Name: Reconstruction Era
Body:
When the Civil War ended in 1865, more than 460,000 newly freed people lived in Georgia. Reconstruction, which lasted until 1871 in Georgia and until 1877 elsewhere in the South, was the struggle over what their freedom would mean ([Bragg](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/reconstruction-in-georgia/)).

For a few years, change came quickly. Freed people sought out schools and built all-Black churches. In Atlanta, 37 Black delegates helped write the state constitution of 1868, which provided for Black voting and free public schools. That year, 32 Black Republicans won seats in the Georgia legislature, including Henry McNeal Turner. White legislators expelled them in September 1868, and they were not reinstated until 1870. The Ku Klux Klan targeted Black leaders, and white conservative Democrats held full control of the state by January 1872 ([Bragg](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/reconstruction-in-georgia/); [Angell](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-mcneal-turner-1834-1915/)).

South-View's founders lived through these years. Jacob McKinley built his businesses during Reconstruction, George W. Graham became one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council in 1871, and Robert Grant co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872 (Henderson 18–21). In 1877, Atlanta's city council ordered the remains of those buried in Oakland Cemetery's "Slave Square" moved (Henderson). Nine years later, formerly enslaved African Americans founded South-View ([South-View Cemetery](https://www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/south-view-cemetery/)).

Name: The Original 33 Expelled
Body: In 1868, three years after the Civil War, Georgia voters elected thirty-three Black men to the state legislature, thirty to the House and three to the Senate ([They Were Expelled](https://images.ajc.com/politics/2026/02/they-were-expelled-from-the-georgia-legislature-now-theyre-honored)). They took their seats in Atlanta that July ([Original 33](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/original-33/)). Two months later, white legislators voted to expel them because of their race ([Original 33](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/original-33/); [I Claim the Rights of a Man](https://www.wabe.org/the-story-of-georgias-original-33-black-legislators/)). On September 3, Rev. Henry McNeal Turner, the first Black chaplain in the Union Army and one of the expelled men, rose to answer them: "Am I a man? If I am such, I claim the rights of a man" ([Am I a Man?](https://www.facingsouth.org/2023/04/1868-speech-expelled-black-georgia-legislator-henry-mcneal-turner); Henderson 135). The Original 33, as they came to be called, retook their seats in 1870 (Henderson 135). Turner later became a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and when he died in 1915, thousands followed his funeral procession to South-View, where he rests (Henderson 134).

Name: Oakland's Slave Square Dug Up
Body: When Atlanta opened Oakland Cemetery, the city set apart a corner of it for "burying the black population," and enslaved and free Black Atlantans were laid to rest in the section that came to be called Slave Square (Henderson 8). In April 1877, with Oakland's other lots filling up, the Atlanta City Council voted to dig up Slave Square, level the ground and sell the space to white families ([Telling the Story of Slave Square](https://www.oaklandcemetery.com/blog/telling-the-story-of-slave-square); Henderson 9). People whose graves had headboards were reburied in the "colored pauper grounds," but those in unmarked graves were apparently moved without their names to a mass grave whose location is still unknown (Henderson 9). Early the next year, Black Atlantans petitioned the city twice, once for more burial space and once for a cemetery of their own (Henderson 9–10). The city gave no answer that has been found. Eight years later, Albert Watts, whose mother had been buried at Oakland in 1876, and five other formerly enslaved men chartered South-View (Henderson 1, 8).
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 1, 7–10.

Name: South-View founded
Body:
In the decades following the Civil War, African Americans in Atlanta built vibrant, self-reliant communities, yet faced constant disrespect—even in death. Under Jim Crow practices, city cemeteries remained strictly segregated. At Oakland Cemetery, Black citizens were initially restricted to "Slave Square." Even after emancipation permitted plot purchases, mistreatment persisted. In 1877, city officials ordered the removal of bodies from Slave Square to make room for white burials, unceremoniously moving marked graves to pauper sections and burying others in mass graves. Years later, at Westview Cemetery, Black families were directed through a back gate to a segregated section named Rest Haven, where "the carriages had driven past the imposing stone gatehouse of Westview Cemetery and through a modest iron gate that stood several hundred yards beyond the main entrance" (Henderson 1). Despite expectations, Rest Haven suffered from severe neglect, as "the lack of maintenance for Westview's African American burials conflicts with the original intention of equal treatment that had been specified in 1884" (Henderson 11). Determined to provide dignity and honor to their loved ones, Albert Watts—whose own family had experienced this indignity—joined forces with five fellow Black businessmen and leaders: Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Rev. Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, and Rev. John Render. Together, they petitioned the city council in February 1886 to create a place for "dignified Christian burials" open to all people regardless of race (Henderson 13).

The establishment of South-View unfolded across several distinct chronological stages:

1. February 20, 1886 Purchase Agreement: The Atlanta Constitution reported that Black Atlantans had initiated the purchase of a 25-acre parcel on McDonough Road for $3,500, having paid $600 down to secure the property as a community investment prior to incorporation.

2. March 18, 1886 Legal Challenge: Shortly after the earliest burials commenced, adjoining landowner A. J. Harper filed a legal complaint seeking an injunction to halt further burials, alleging health hazards and property depreciation. A temporary injunction was granted pending a hearing.

3. April 21, 1886 Charter Approval: Undeterred by the injunction, the founders obtained official state charter approval for the South-View Cemetery Association. Established not only out of necessity but as an enduring community endeavor and business enterprise, South-View operated from its inception as a stockholder corporation, making it one of the oldest African American–owned corporate enterprises in the United States ([Greenmellen](https://www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/south-view-cemetery/)).

4. May 22, 1888 Land Transfer: The founders—Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Rev. Robert Grant, Albert Watts, and the administrator of Charles H. Morgan's estate—formally deeded and transferred the 25-acre tract to the South-View Cemetery Association for $1,250, placing the burial grounds under permanent corporate ownership.

5. August 7, 1893 License Fee Waiver Request: During the Panic of 1893, cemetery president Nicodemus Holmes and the board petitioned the Atlanta City Council to waive South-View's annual $100 license fee, arguing that the cemetery was burying the city's impoverished paupers with minimal compensation. While the city denied the petition, South-View persevered, burying two-thirds of Atlanta's Black dead throughout the economic crisis.

Since its creation, South-View has expanded from its original 25 acres to more than 100 acres and continues to serve the community as an active cemetery ([Greenmellen](https://www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/south-view-cemetery/)).

Name: Panic of 1893
Body: The Panic of 1893 unleashed a severe economic crisis across the United States. Striking an economy that had reached high output per person, the downturn triggered widespread panic as gold reserves dropped, leading depositors to convert bank notes to gold ([Whitten](https://eh.net/encyclopedia/the-depression-of-1893/); [Pamela](https://www.historyinthemargins.com/2026/09/05/the-great-panic-of-1893/)). As loan defaults rose and hundreds of banks failed, the crisis resulted in an estimated 14,000 business insolvencies and an unemployment rate exceeding ten percent for five to six consecutive years—a prolonged disaster matched only by the Great Depression ([Whitten](https://eh.net/encyclopedia/the-depression-of-1893/); [Pamela](https://www.historyinthemargins.com/2026/09/05/the-great-panic-of-1893/)). For the founders and officials of South-View Cemetery, navigating this financial devastation was a monumental undertaking. On August 7, 1893, Nicodemus Holmes and the board of directors petitioned the Atlanta City Council for tax relief. They argued that because of South-View's modest size and its commitment to burying the city’s impoverished paupers, the cemetery should be exempted from its $100 annual license fee. Their appeal was flatly denied. Despite this setback, South-View persevered, interring two-thirds of Atlanta’s African American dead throughout the Panic. The cemetery’s survival owed much to the sheer determination of its founders—men of varying financial means who had endured the far greater adversity of slavery. By 1900, South-View was providing graves for pauper burials at $1.35 per person, compared to at least $2.00 for white pauper burials. When South-View officials increased their bid to $2.00 to seek equal compensation, city council members attempted to negotiate a lower price; however, "South-View officials refused and stood behind their original bid for equal compensation" (Henderson 45). Consequently, the city awarded the contract to Oak View Cemetery at $1.50 per body, while also contracting private undertakers like Lucius L. Lee (Henderson 45–46). Today, many pauper graves lie in overgrown, wooded areas or unmarked plots. As D.L. Henderson observes, "The racial disparities in the cost of burial—in this instance, carried out through the city's control over the necessities of burial—paralleled the oppressive and often demeaning conditions of African American life from the nineteenth to the early twentieth century in Atlanta" (46). Ultimately, South-View's mission of offering a dignified burial could only mitigate municipal bigotry while serving as a crucial sanctuary of respect.
Source:
1.  Henderson, D. L. South-View: An African American City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
2.  Pamela. “History in the Margins.” History in the Margins, 4 Sept. 2026, www.historyinthemargins.com/2026/09/05/the-great-panic-of-1893/.
3.  Whitten, David O. “The Depression of 1893.” *EH.Net Encyclopedia*, edited by Robert Whaples, 14 Aug. 2001, eh.net/encyclopedia/the-depression-of-1893/.

Name: Pittsburgh Riot
Body: In the early morning hours of May 17, 1902, violence erupted in the Pittsburgh neighborhood of Atlanta. Samuel A. Kerlin, a white former police officer, was walking down McDaniel Street when he encountered Will Richardson, an African American store owner whom Kerlin had previously arrested and testified against, causing him to spend months on a chain gang ([National Park Service](https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf)). Richardson threatened Kerlin and fired several shotgun shots; although Kerlin escaped, he returned around 1:30 a.m. with fellow officers and armed civilians to arrest Richardson at his grocery store on the corner of McDaniel and Amy streets ([National Park Service](https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf)). Richardson and his companions barricaded themselves inside with a heavy arsenal. As Kerlin's force approached, Richardson's group opened fire, killing an officer and sparking a full siege involving Atlanta police and thousands of armed civilians who traded an estimated 3,000 rounds over several hours (Henderson 116–17; [National Park Service](https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf)). To force the men out, the block was set on fire. The violence quickly turned into a broader assault on Black residents: "The New York Times reported that three thousand people—at least two thousand of them armed—surrounded the burning block of buildings," while mob members hunted residents, including James Harrison, who was chased along railroad tracks and "shot hundreds of times as he tried to escape the mob" (Henderson 116–17). Richardson perished inside the burning store, and his body was almost entirely cremated in the fire (Henderson 116–17; [National Park Service](https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf)). Tensions remained high following the destruction: "After the burned body of the negro was found, an angry mob of white men seized it and started with it towards the city," until Chief Ball formed a police cordon at the city limits to intercept the crowd and transport the body by wagon (Hartzog). In total, nine people died during the riot, and state militia troops were deployed to patrol the Pittsburgh community to maintain order (Henderson 116–17; [National Park Service](https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf)).
Source:
1.  Hartzog, Henry S. “Negro’s Deadly Aim: Ends Earthly Career of Three Officers and a Citizen.” The Bamberg Herald, 22 May 1902.
2.  Henderson, D. L. South-View: An African American City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
3.  *Pittsburgh Historic District*. National Register of Historic Places Registration Form, National Park Service, https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf.

Name: 1906 Atlanta Massacre
Body:
At the turn of the twentieth century, Atlanta promoted itself as the gleaming hub of the "New South"—a vibrant city of economic progress and modern opportunity. Yet beneath this optimistic façade lay deep-seated racial segregation and prejudice. As the city's African American population expanded to tens of thousands, Black Atlantans built thriving businesses, churches, schools, and self-managed institutions like South-View Cemetery. However, this remarkable progress ignited resentment among some white residents, sparking fierce economic competition and racial friction across all levels of society.

By the summer of 1906, political strife reached a boiling point during a contentious gubernatorial campaign. Sensationalized newspaper headlines falsely accused Black men of attacking white women, stoking fears and racial animosity throughout the city. On the evening of September 22, tensions exploded as a mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys flooded downtown Atlanta. For hours, violence consumed streets like Decatur, Pryor, and Peachtree. Black-owned businesses were looted and vandalized, streetcars were raided, and innocent residents—including young messenger Frank Smith—were brutally attacked and killed.

As night fell, heavy rains helped disperse the downtown mobs, but the terror spread toward Black neighborhoods like Brownsville. Defending their homes and families, local residents organized resistance. When police officers and armed civilians invaded Brownsville on September 24, a deadly skirmish ensued. State militia moved in, disarming the community and arresting hundreds of Black residents, including educators and leaders like Dr. J.W.E. Bowen and Luther Judson Price, while Civil War veteran George Union Wilder was murdered in the unrest.

When the violence finally subsided, dozens of Black citizens lay dead and countless others were wounded or displaced. The massacre shattered Atlanta's progressive image on the national stage. In response, local Black and white leaders formed interracial committees to restore peace, yet systemic disenfranchisement soon followed through restrictive voting laws in 1908. Despite these crushing setbacks, community institutions like South-View Cemetery endured—serving as both a final resting place for victims and heroes, and an enduring monument to resilience, memory, and the ongoing pursuit of justice.
Source:
1. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001.
2. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.
3. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: The Odd Fellows Building Opens on Auburn Avenue
Body: In the early 1900s the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows was perhaps the wealthiest Black fraternal order in Atlanta, paying sick and burial benefits to its members (Henderson 103–4). Led by Benjamin J. Davis Sr., the Georgia lodge's district grand secretary and editor of the Atlanta Independent, the order built a six-story headquarters on Auburn Avenue in 1912, followed by an annex with an auditorium ([Testament to Black Businesses](https://www.ajc.com/news/local/testament-black-businesses-odd-fellows-building-observes-centennial/KZOTWB0gR8q2JV2szDe7mJ); [NRHP Nomination](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/cccd3162-d0fa-46e3-9694-7af5919e3343); [The Odd Fellow City](https://guoof.org/?p=1157); Henderson 104). Robert E. Pharrow, a Black contractor and Odd Fellow, built it, and Booker T. Washington spoke at its dedication (Henderson 104; [The Odd Fellow City](https://guoof.org/?p=1157)). The building held offices, stores, and a roof garden, and its rents became a major source of the order's income (Henderson 104). In 1914 pharmacist Moses Amos opened his Gate City Drugstore there, said to be the finest Black-owned drugstore in the South (Henderson 148). Davis, Pharrow, and Amos all rest at South-View, as does George Wilder, a Civil War veteran whose gravestone carries the Odd Fellows' three linked rings (Henderson 104, 119, 171, 235). The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1975 ([Odd Fellows Building, HistoryPointer](https://historypointer.com/nris/resource/75000594)).

Name: Grady's Training School for Black Nurses
Body: Grady Memorial Hospital opened a nursing school in 1898, but it offered no training to Black women until 1914, when nurse Ludie Clay Andrews organized the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses (Henderson 171; [Timeline of Major Events](https://exhibits.library.gsu.edu/grady-exhibit/timeline-of-major-events/)). Its students took classes at Spelman and trained in Grady's wards for Black patients, and the school received its state charter in 1917 ([Timeline of Major Events](https://exhibits.library.gsu.edu/grady-exhibit/timeline-of-major-events/)). Georgia would not let Black nurses sit for the licensing exam that white nurses took, so while she built the school, Andrews fought the state nursing board for ten years at her own expense ([National Conclave of Grady Nurses](https://aspace-aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/125)). She won in 1920, the year the school's first class graduated, and became Georgia's first Black registered nurse ([National Conclave](https://aspace-aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/125); [Ludie Clay Andrews](https://www.georgiawomen.org/ludie-clay-andrews)). The school ran separately until 1965, when Grady combined it with the school for white nurses (Henderson 171). Andrews rests at South-View (Henderson 6).

Name: Atlanta Branch of the NAACP Founded
Body: The Atlanta branch of the NAACP was chartered in 1917, eleven years after the massacre of 1906 ([NAACP Atlanta Branch Records](https://aspace-aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/9)). Its organizers included Harry Pace, Dr. Louis Wright, and a young insurance clerk named Walter White, who became its secretary, along with Rev. Adam Daniel Williams of Ebenezer Baptist Church, the grandfather of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. ([NAACP Atlanta Branch Records](https://aspace-aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/9); [Walter White](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/walter-white-1893-1955); Henderson 254). Its first fight came that year. The school board planned to drop the seventh grade from the city's Black public schools to help pay for a new high school for white students, and the branch's protest stopped it ([Walter White](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/walter-white-1893-1955); [White, Walter F.](https://www.blackpast.org/aah/white-walter-f-1893-1955)). White went on to lead the national NAACP, while Williams later served as the Atlanta branch's president (Henderson 254; [Walter White](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/walter-white-1893-1955)). Several South-View residents carried the branch's work forward, among them Virgil W. Hodges and later presidents Rev. Samuel W. Williams and John H. Calhoun Jr., and Walter White's parents also rest at South-View (Henderson 120, 185, 212, 254).

Name: The Great Atlanta Fire of 1917
Body: On May 21, 1917, several fires broke out across Atlanta, and one that began in a downtown warehouse spread through the Old Fourth Ward ([The Great Fire of 1917](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/thisweek/this-week-in-atlanta-history-the-great-fire-o/); [The History That Shaped the Atlanta Neighborhood](https://www.wabe.org/the-history-that-shaped-the-atlanta-neighborhood-where-mlk-was-raised/)). The fire burned about 300 acres and close to 1,900 buildings, most of them homes, and left more than 10,000 people homeless ([100 Years After the Fire](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/new-entry); [The Great Fire of 1917](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/thisweek/this-week-in-atlanta-history-the-great-fire-o/)). First aid stations opened in the Odd Fellows Hall on Auburn Avenue ([The Great Fire of 1917](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/thisweek/this-week-in-atlanta-history-the-great-fire-o/)). The fire destroyed Wheat Street Baptist Church (Henderson 182; [Wheat Street Baptist Church](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/geh_goldfarb_13)). Its pastor, Rev. Peter James Bryant, led the congregation in building a new Gothic Revival church with seats for 2,500, which opened on Auburn Avenue in 1921 (Henderson 182; [Wheat Street Baptist Church](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/geh_goldfarb_13)). Across the neighborhood, many homeowners never rebuilt, and renters and apartment buildings took their place ([The History That Shaped the Atlanta Neighborhood](https://www.wabe.org/the-history-that-shaped-the-atlanta-neighborhood-where-mlk-was-raised/)).

Name: Citizens Trust Bank Opens on Auburn Avenue
Body: On August 16, 1921, businessman Heman E. Perry and four partners opened Citizens Trust Bank on Auburn Avenue, at a time when Black business owners had great difficulty getting loans from white-owned banks ([Citizens Trust Bank](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/business-economy/citizens-trust-bank); [Funderburg, I. Owen](https://www.encyclopedia.com/education/news-wires-white-papers-and-books/funderburg-i-owen-1924-2002)). The bank reorganized in 1927 with Clayton R. Yates as chairman and Lorimer D. Milton as cashier, and Milton later became its president ([Citizens Trust Bank](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/business-economy/citizens-trust-bank)). In 1934 it became the first Black-owned bank insured by the FDIC, and in the late 1940s the first to join the Federal Reserve System ([Citizens Trust Bank marker](https://www.georgiahistory.com/?p=67812); [Citizens Trust Bank, NGE](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/business-economy/citizens-trust-bank)). Yates and Milton were also partners in the Yates and Milton drugstores, and in the 1960s student organizers of the civil rights movement met at their Auburn Avenue store to plan in secret (Henderson 148). Both men served on South-View's board, Yates as its president, and by 1961 Citizens Trust held South-View's perpetual care fund (Henderson 32–33, 258). Yates and Milton rest at South-View.

Name: Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Founded
Body: White-owned banks rarely made home loans to Black Atlantans, so in 1925 a group of Black businessmen who met at the Butler Street YMCA set out to lend to their own community (Henderson 208; [Atlanta's Historic Auburn Ave. at Crossroads](https://www.bet.com/article/8jmtl2/atlanta-s-historic-auburn-ave-again-at-crossroads)). Clarence C. Hart, Atlanta's first licensed Black plumber, invested $100 to help start the Mutual Federal Building and Loan Association, and accountant Jesse B. Blayton Sr. was a co-founder (Henderson 175, 208; [Our History](https://www.sweetauburnworks.com/about-us/our-history/)). Blayton later served as its president (Henderson 175; [Citizens Advisory Committee for Urban Renewal](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/mayoral-records/traditional/items/show/5513)). In the early 1960s the Mutual Federal office on Auburn Avenue was the headquarters of the Citizens Student Defense Fund, which raised money for Atlanta University students who protested segregation ([Tour Atlanta's Historic Auburn Avenue](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/1996-annual-meeting-tour-atlantas-historic-auburn-avenue/)). By the 1990s Mutual Federal was one of the leading Black-owned companies in the country (Henderson 208). In 2000 Citizens Trust Bank took over its deposits ([FDIC Approves Assumption](https://archive.fdic.gov/view/fdic/1743)). Blayton rests at South-View (Henderson 175). Note: the 1925 founding year comes from Henderson (208); outside records consulted so far confirm the association and its founders but not the year.

Name: The Lynching of Dennis Hubert
Body: Dennis Taylor Hubert was eighteen, a divinity student at Morehouse College, and the son of a prominent Baptist minister, Rev. G.J. Hubert (Henderson 214; [A Black 18-Year-Old College Student](https://kvia.com/cnn-national/2025/05/25/a-black-18-year-old-college-student-was-lynched-on-a-playground-95-years-ago-his-nephew-just-accepted-his-posthumous-degree/)). On June 15, 1930, on the playground of the segregated Crogman School in the Pittsburgh neighborhood, seven white men confronted him over a claim that he had insulted a white woman, and one of them shot and killed him (Henderson 214; [Killing of Dennis Hubert](https://crrjarchive.org/incidents/196)). As Black Atlanta pressed for justice, the Huberts' home was burned to the ground two days after the accused men were denied bail, and a white mob attacked a Black church with tear gas during a fundraiser for the family ([A Black 18-Year-Old College Student](https://kvia.com/cnn-national/2025/05/25/a-black-18-year-old-college-student-was-lynched-on-a-playground-95-years-ago-his-nephew-just-accepted-his-posthumous-degree/); Henderson 214). Juries convicted the shooter of voluntary manslaughter and six other men as accessories (Henderson 214; [Killing of Dennis Hubert](https://crrjarchive.org/incidents/196)). In 2022, a historical marker was placed in his memory, and in 2025 Morehouse College awarded him a posthumous degree ([Lynching of Dennis Hubert marker](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=227409); [Morehouse College Student Given Degree](https://www.ajc.com/education/morehouse-college-student-given-degree-95-years-after-his-lynching/LA7YEFCXTBF5FDEH4AAGEW52UQ/)). He rests at South-View (Henderson 214).

Name: King Sr.'s March on City Hall
Body: In 1935, Rev. Martin Luther King Sr., pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, worked with Ruby Blackburn, Selena Sloan Butler, and the Atlanta branch of the NAACP on a voter registration drive that started on Auburn Avenue ([Atlanta NAACP Leads Voter Registration Drive](https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/atlanta-naacp-leads-voter-registration-drive); [Tour Atlanta's Historic Auburn Avenue](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/1996-annual-meeting-tour-atlantas-historic-auburn-avenue/)). In March 1936 he spoke at an NAACP mass meeting at Wheat Street Baptist Church ([King, Sr., Speaks at NAACP Mass Meeting](https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/king-sr-speaks-naacp-mass-meeting-atlanta)). That year he led several hundred Black Atlantans on a march to City Hall to demand the right to vote (Henderson 220; [Rev. Martin Luther King, Sr.](https://11alive.com/article/news/local/black-history/rev-martin-luther-king-sr-advocate-for-social-change/85-68774415)). Also in 1936, John Wesley Dobbs founded the Atlanta Civic and Political League at Big Bethel AME Church, and King Sr. joined its executive committee in 1938 ([Tour Atlanta's Historic Auburn Avenue](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/1996-annual-meeting-tour-atlantas-historic-auburn-avenue/); [King, Sr., Elected to Atlanta Civic and Political League](https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/king-sr-elected-atlanta-civic-and-political-league)). King Sr. rests at South-View (Henderson 115).

Name: The Green Book in Atlanta
Body: Under segregation, a Black family driving through the South could be turned away at a gas station, a restaurant, or a hotel, and some towns were unsafe for them after dark. From 1936 to 1966, Victor Hugo Green, a Harlem postal worker, published the Green Book, a guide to the businesses where Black travelers would be served ([In Segregation-Era Atlanta](https://wabe.org/?p=45670)). In Atlanta, one of the few gas stations listed was Harden's Service Station on Hunter Street, owned by John and Willie Lee "Billie" Harden, where Black drivers could safely fill up and get repairs ([Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlanta-in-the-negro-motorist-green-book/)). John Harden was the first African American to own and operate a gas station in Atlanta, and the Hardens also owned the Atlanta Black Crackers baseball team (Henderson 206). Both rest at South-View.

Name: The Prince Hall Masonic Temple Rises on Auburn Avenue
Body: For years Atlanta's Prince Hall Masons, the Black Masonic order, met in a temple on Ivy Street (Henderson 100). In 1937, under Grand Master John Wesley Dobbs, they began building a new grand lodge at 330 Auburn Avenue, paid for with money Dobbs raised (Henderson 100; [Protecting the Cultural Resources](https://www.nps.gov/malu/protecting-the-cultural-resources.htm)). The building was finished in 1940, and an addition followed in 1941 ([Protecting the Cultural Resources](https://www.nps.gov/malu/protecting-the-cultural-resources.htm); [Prince Hall Masonic Grand Lodge](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/prince-hall-history/)). Its tenants included a Madam C.J. Walker beauty school, WERD, the first radio station owned by African Americans, and the headquarters of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, led by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. ([Protecting the Cultural Resources](https://www.nps.gov/malu/protecting-the-cultural-resources.htm); [Prince Hall Masonic Lodge, Once MLK's SCLC Offices](https://www.ajc.com/uatl/prince-hall-masonic-lodge-once-mlks-sclc-offices-on-road-to-restoration/WDDHAG3EERH5NHFAUP3RNZLHZA)). In 2018 the building became part of the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park ([Historic Preservation on Auburn Avenue](https://saportareport.com/?p=1056114)). Dobbs led the Prince Hall Masons of Georgia for thirty years, until his death in 1961, and in 1963 the order marked his grave at South-View with a broken column, a monument reserved for grand masters (Henderson 100–101).

Name: Atlanta's Tuskegee Airmen
Body: During World War II, the Army Air Forces trained Black pilots at Tuskegee, Alabama, and many of them flew in combat with the 332nd Fighter Group ([Walter Drake Westmoreland](https://cafriseabove.org/walter-drake-westmoreland/); Henderson 250). Two Atlanta men among them rest at South-View. Walter D. Westmoreland, a Morehouse graduate, earned his wings in July 1943 and flew a P-51C nicknamed "Dopey" with the 302nd Fighter Squadron from Italy ([Walter Drake Westmoreland](https://cafriseabove.org/walter-drake-westmoreland/); [Tuskegee Airmen](https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Upcoming/Photos/igphoto/2000981892/)). On October 13, 1944, enemy ground fire shot down his plane near Lake Balaton, Hungary, as he returned from an escort mission to Blechhammer, Germany, and he was killed ([Walter Drake Westmoreland](https://cafriseabove.org/walter-drake-westmoreland/); [Tuskegee Airmen](https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Upcoming/Photos/igphoto/2000981892/); Henderson 250). His body came home to Atlanta in 1949 (Henderson 250). Horace A. Bohannon, who as a boy watched pilots at Candler Field, earned his wings in December 1944 and flew with the 332nd at Godman Field, Kentucky; the war ended before he went overseas (Henderson 176; [Horace A. Bohannon](https://cafriseabove.org/?p=45307)). He later helped found the Atlanta chapter of Tuskegee Airmen, Inc. ([Wreaths Across America](https://www.dobbins.afrc.af.mil/News/Photos/igphoto/2000298187)).

Name: The 1946 Voter Registration Drive
Body: For decades, Georgia's Democratic Party barred Black citizens from voting in its primary elections ([Black Suffrage in the Twentieth Century](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/black-suffrage-in-the-twentieth-century/)). In October 1945, after Primus King of Columbus sued, a federal judge ruled the white primary unconstitutional, and an appeals court upheld the ruling in 1946 ([Atlanta Negro Voters League: Strength in Unity](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlanta-negro-voters-league-strength-in-unity/); [Black Suffrage](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/black-suffrage-in-the-twentieth-century/)). Black Atlanta organized at once. A coalition led by the Atlanta Urban League, whose executive director was Grace Towns Hamilton, registered 14,368 new Black voters in about two months, and the All-Citizens Registration Committee, chaired by historian Clarence A. Bacote, raised the number of Black voters in the city from 6,976 to 21,244 in less than five months ([Black Suffrage](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/black-suffrage-in-the-twentieth-century/); [Clarence A. Bacote](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/clarence-a-bacote-1906-1981/); Henderson 204). By June 1946, Black voters were more than a quarter of Atlanta's electorate ([Strength in Unity](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlanta-negro-voters-league-strength-in-unity/)). In 1949, John Wesley Dobbs and attorney A.T. Walden founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League to turn those numbers into political power, and John H. Calhoun Jr. and Q.V. Williamson Sr. were among its leaders ([Atlanta Negro Voters League](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/atlanta-negro-voters-league-anvl/); Henderson 185, 255).

Name: Atlanta's First Black Police Officers
Body: Atlanta hired its first Black police officers in 1948, after pressure from Black civic leaders, including Rev. William Holmes Borders of Wheat Street Baptist Church (Henderson 177). Eight men joined the force that spring: Henry Hooks, Claude Dixon, Ernest H. Lyons, Robert McKibbens, Willard Strickland, Willie T. Elkins, Johnnie P. Jones, and John Sanders ([Tracing the Atlanta 8](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/tracing-the-atlanta-8-through-sweet-auburn/)). About four hundred people turned out to watch their first patrol on April 3, 1948 ([Tracing the Atlanta 8](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/tracing-the-atlanta-8-through-sweet-auburn/)). The eight were not allowed in police headquarters, so they worked out of the basement of the Butler Street YMCA. They could not wear their uniforms to and from work or drive squad cars, and they walked their beats in Black neighborhoods (Henderson 242). If they stopped a white suspect, they had to call a white officer, and they could not arrest white people until 1962 ([Tracing the Atlanta 8](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/tracing-the-atlanta-8-through-sweet-auburn/)). Willard Strickland, one of the eight, rests at South-View (Henderson 242–43).

Name: WERD, the First Black-Owned Radio Station
Body: In 1949 Jesse B. Blayton Sr., Georgia's first Black certified public accountant, bought Atlanta radio station WERD for $50,000, making it the first radio station in the United States owned by African Americans (Henderson 175; [WERD](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/werd); [Jesse B. Blayton, Sr.](https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/blayton-sr-jesse-b-1897-1977/)). He took over the station on October 3, 1949 ([Jesse B. Blayton, Sr.](https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/blayton-sr-jesse-b-1897-1977/)). The station's first building would not let Black staff use its restrooms, so the Blaytons moved WERD to the second floor of the Prince Hall Masonic Temple on Auburn Avenue ([Atlanta Magazine](https://atlantamagazine.mydigitalpublication.com/atlanta-magazine-november-2023/page-24); [WERD](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/werd)). His son, Jesse B. Blayton Jr., managed the station for twenty years (Henderson 175–76; [WERD](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/werd)). In the 1960s WERD shared the building with the Southern Christian Leadership Conference ([WERD](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/werd)). Blayton sold the station in 1968 and was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995 ([Jesse B. Blayton, Sr.](https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/blayton-sr-jesse-b-1897-1977/); Henderson 175). Blayton and his son rest at South-View (Henderson 175–76).

Name: Civil Rights Movement
Body:
The struggle for civil rights is not a self-contained chapter in history, but a continuous story that connects the era of Reconstruction through the 1960s to the present day. To understand this movement fully, we must look beyond the most celebrated figures and examine both nationwide efforts and the deeply rooted local activism in cities like Atlanta.

While leaders such as Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Thurgood Marshall, and John Lewis helped shape the public consciousness, countless less heralded figures—including Ralph David Abernathy Sr., Joseph Lowery, Herman Russell, C.T. Vivian, Hosea Williams, Andrew Young Jr., Julian Bond, Joseph E. Boone, Lonnie C. King Jr., and Dr. Roslyn Pope—fought tirelessly against everyday indignities. Organizations as different as the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and the Black Panther Party carried the struggle forward in their own ways.

Many of the people who carried this struggle in Atlanta now rest at South-View, the cemetery that formerly enslaved Black Atlantans founded in 1886 so their families could bury their dead with dignity. Among them are ministers William Holmes Borders and Samuel W. Williams, student organizers Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson and Fred C. Bennette Jr., businessmen Jesse Hill Jr. and Herman J. Russell, Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King, and Congressman John Lewis. Dr. King himself was first laid to rest here in 1968 (Henderson 6, 114–15).

From the Montgomery Bus Boycotts and sit-ins to pivotal marches across historic locations like the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma and the March on Washington, these events transformed the nation. By honoring both the major milestones and the smaller, overlooked personal stories, we preserve a richer, more accurate history of the ongoing fight for equality.

Name: Southern Christian Leadership Conference Founded
Body: In January 1957, soon after the Montgomery Bus Boycott, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and other leaders called about sixty Black ministers and activists to Atlanta to carry the boycott's nonviolent methods across the South ([This Far by Faith](https://www.pbs.org/thisfarbyfaith/popup/4_sclc.html)). They met at Ebenezer Baptist Church, where King's father was pastor ([Reasons to Celebrate Black History Month: SCLC](https://www.ajc.com/lifestyles/reasons-celebrate-black-history-month-sclc/ZhIaBVoyRuhzlPiE7e91CK/); Henderson 220). Later that year the group took the name Southern Christian Leadership Conference, with King as its first president, and it set out to end segregation through nonviolent direct action ([Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)](https://encyclopedia.com/history/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/southern-christian-leadership-conference-sclc); [Martin Luther King Jr. Fast Facts](https://keyt.com/news/national-world/cnn-national/2026/01/07/martin-luther-king-jr-fast-facts/)). Its first headquarters was on Auburn Avenue in the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, which the Masons had built under the leadership of John Wesley Dobbs (Henderson 100; [Prince Hall Masonic Temple](https://exploregeorgia.org/atlanta/history-heritage/african-american/prince-hall-masonic-temple)). Several South-View residents helped carry its work: Rev. Samuel W. Williams held leadership roles in the SCLC, Rev. A.D. King served on its board, Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr. directed its voter registration drives and was the first director of its Operation Breadbasket, and Herman J. Russell was a major donor (Henderson 174, 219, 239, 254).

Name: Triple L Movement
Body: In Atlanta, Black riders were made to sit at the back of city buses. In January 1957, soon after the Montgomery Bus Boycott, a group of Black ministers led by Rev. William Holmes Borders of Wheat Street Baptist Church launched the Love, Law, and Liberation (Triple L) Movement to change that. On January 8, Borders told a crowd of more than 1,200 at Wheat Street, "We are going to ride until these buses are desegregated" ([Bus Desegregation in Atlanta](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/bus-desegregation-in-atlanta/)). The next day, six ministers boarded a downtown bus and took the front seats, and police arrested them the following afternoon, creating the test case the ministers had planned for. Two years later, on January 9, 1959, a federal court ruled in their favor, and Atlanta's buses opened to every rider ([Bus Desegregation in Atlanta](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/bus-desegregation-in-atlanta/)). Borders and Rev. Samuel W. Williams, one of the plaintiffs in the bus case, both rest at South-View (Henderson 177, 254).

Name: Atlanta Public Library Desegregated
Body: For decades, Black Atlantans could not borrow books from the city's main library and could read there only in the basement ([The Woman Who Desegregated Atlanta's Library System](https://theatlanta100.com/history/2018/02/20/desegregation-of-atlantas-library-system/15230)). They were served instead at separate branches, such as the Auburn Avenue Branch, whose first librarian in 1921 was Alice Dugged Cary, and the West Hunter Branch, managed from 1949 by Annie L. McPheeters (Henderson 187, 228). In March 1959, Spelman history professor Howard Zinn and Atlanta University dean Whitney Young began a federal lawsuit against the library with two plaintiffs, Spelman professor Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss, a Morehouse theology student (Henderson 216). Rather than fight in court, the library board agreed to desegregate. Jackson became the first African American to receive a card from the main branch, and music professor Earl A. Sanders received his at the same time (Henderson 216). Jackson's daughter Constance later recalled threatening phone calls and drive-by harassment in the days that followed (Henderson 216). In 1976, Ella Gaines Yates became the first African American director of the Atlanta-Fulton Public Library system (Henderson 258). Jackson, Cary, McPheeters, and Yates all rest at South-View.

Name: Atlanta Student Movement
Body: In 1960, Black Atlantans could shop at downtown stores like Rich's but were refused a seat at their lunch counters and restaurants. That February, students at Atlanta's six historically Black colleges began to organize, and on March 9 they published "An Appeal for Human Rights" in all three of the city's daily newspapers ([Atlanta Sit-ins](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/atlanta-sit-ins/)). Six days later, nearly 200 students sat in at ten downtown lunch counters, and police arrested 77 of them. On October 19, students returned, this time to Rich's whites-only Magnolia Room, and police arrested more than fifty people, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and his brother A.D. King ([Atlanta Sit-ins](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/atlanta-sit-ins/)). Fred C. Bennette Jr., a Morris Brown student, led the Rich's campaign (Henderson 174); Rev. William Holmes Borders chaired the adults who advised the students (Henderson 177); and Jesse Hill Jr. helped launch the Atlanta Inquirer as a newspaper of protest (Henderson 212). In March 1961 the city's leaders agreed to open the lunch counters, and they did so that October ([Atlanta Sit-ins](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/atlanta-sit-ins/)).

Name: Atlanta Schools and UGA Desegregated
Body: Seven years after the Supreme Court's 1954 ruling in Brown v. Board of Education, Georgia's schools and colleges were still segregated. Dr. Horace Mann Bond, who later led Atlanta University's school of education, had helped research the Brown case for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund (Henderson 177). In 1961, the barriers began to fall. After a two-year legal fight by the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund and Atlanta lawyers Donald Hollowell, Vernon Jordan, and Horace Ward, federal judge William Bootle ordered the University of Georgia on January 6 to admit Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter ([Charlayne Hunter-Gault](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/people/charlayne-hunter-gault-b-1942/)). Jesse Hill Jr. had met the two Turner High School graduates in 1959 and helped them look for a white Georgia college to desegregate ([Hamilton Holmes](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/education/hamilton-holmes-1941-1995/)). When they arrived to register on January 9, they were met with taunts and slurs. Two days later, after a basketball game, a crowd gathered outside Hunter's dormitory and smashed windows, and the university suspended both students until a new court order returned them to class ([Charlayne Hunter-Gault](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/people/charlayne-hunter-gault-b-1942/); [Ernest Vandiver](https://lib-umbra-prd-app-01.oit.umn.edu/catalog/e96cf1eeea4b5a3f7304abb6dbf423eb71c14709)). That August, after an NAACP lawsuit first filed in 1958, nine Black students entered four all-white Atlanta high schools, Brown, Grady, Murphy, and Northside, on August 30, 1961 ([NAACP and School Desegregation](https://scholarblogs.emory.edu/woodruff/fyi/naacp-and-school-desegregation)). Remembered as the Atlanta Nine, they were Madelyn Nix, Thomas Welch, Willie Jean Black, Arthur Simmons, Donita Gaines, Lawrence Jefferson, Mary McMullen, Martha Ann Holmes, and Rosalyn Walton ([How Atlanta Public Schools Integrated](https://ajc.com/education/photos-how-atlanta-public-schools-integrated-in-1961/D7DZPW7P2VCT5CLWYYC5PAPNPI)). Hill and Bond rest at South-View.

Name: Peyton Road Wall
Body: In December 1962, Dr. Clinton Warner, a Black surgeon, bought a home in Peyton Forest, a white section of Cascade Heights in southwest Atlanta ([Atlanta's Berlin Wall](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlantas-berlin-wall/)). White homeowners asked the city to keep more Black families out, and on December 17 the Board of Aldermen approved their plan. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. then had barricades built across Peyton Road and Harlan Road, cutting the white streets off from the Black neighborhood next to them ([Atlanta's Berlin Wall](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlantas-berlin-wall/); [Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/civilrights/atlantas-berlin-wall/)). Black Atlantans called it "Atlanta's Berlin Wall" ([Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/civilrights/atlantas-berlin-wall/)). Attorney Donald Hollowell took the city to court, and on March 1, 1963, Judge George P. Whitman ruled the barricades unconstitutional; the mayor had them torn down within minutes ([Civil Rights Giant](https://atlinq.com/civil-rights-giant-and-activist-clinton-e-warner-jr-md-succumbs-at-age-87/); [Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/civilrights/atlantas-berlin-wall/)). The wall stood for less than three months. Historian Ronald Bayor writes that Allen allowed it as part of an effort to keep the neighborhood white ([Ivan Allen Jr. Biography](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/biography/peyton-road-wall)).

Name: Grady Hospital Desegregated
Body: Grady Memorial Hospital opened in 1892 in the heart of Black Atlanta, but for more than seventy years it kept Black and white patients in separate and unequal facilities, so that Atlantans called it "the Gradies" (Lovasik et al.; [Grady Health System](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/science-medicine/grady-health-system/)). Even the "New Grady" that opened in 1958 split patients by race, wing by wing (Lovasik et al.). In 1962, Atlanta dentist Dr. Roy C. Bell sued in federal court, joined by seven other Black medical professionals, applicants turned away from Grady's nursing school, and three Black citizens who had been denied emergency treatment ([Timeline of Major Events](https://exhibits.library.gsu.edu/grady-exhibit/timeline-of-major-events/); [Roy Charles Bell](https://ajc.com/news/local/roy-charles-bell-pioneering-dentist-and-civil-rights-leader/QJGlfs0QHKcbSa1nIQyoVN)). On June 1, 1965, a quiet memo from superintendent Bill Pinkston announced, "All phases of the hospital are on a non-racial basis, effective today" (Lovasik et al.). That same year Grady's two nursing schools were combined, ending the separate school for Black nurses that Ludie Clay Andrews had organized in 1914 (Henderson 171). Andrews rests at South-View, as do Eula Benning, a Grady-trained nurse, and Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr., who in 1958 became the first Black doctor at Grady and in 1972 its medical director (Henderson 171, 174, 257–58).

Name: The Civil Rights Act Tested in Atlanta
Body: On July 2, 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which barred businesses open to the public from turning people away because of their race ([Pickrick Showdown](https://sites.gatech.edu/pickrickproject/pickrick-showdown)). The next day, three Black ministry students at Atlanta's Interdenominational Theological Center, George Willis, Albert Dunn, and Woodrow T. Lewis, drove to Lester Maddox's Pickrick restaurant to be served. Maddox met them with a pistol and called on his customers to grab the ax handles he kept by the door, and the three were driven off ([Pickrick Showdown](https://sites.gatech.edu/pickrickproject/pickrick-showdown); [Atlanta Restaurant Suit to Test New Rights Act](https://ldfrecollection.org/archives/archives-search/archives-item/fa5d67ad-3c25-4068-8e91-55fad85793ae/atlanta-restaurant-suit-to-test-new-rights-act)). On July 4, Moreton Rolleston's Heart of Atlanta Motel turned away two more Black ministers ([Heart of Atlanta Motel Incident](https://sites.gatech.edu/pickrickproject/heart-of-atlanta-motel-incident)). The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund sued Maddox ([Atlanta Restaurant Suit](https://ldfrecollection.org/archives/archives-search/archives-item/fa5d67ad-3c25-4068-8e91-55fad85793ae/atlanta-restaurant-suit-to-test-new-rights-act)), and Rolleston sued to overturn the law. On December 14, 1964, a unanimous Supreme Court upheld the law in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States ([Heart of Atlanta v. United States](https://encyclopedia.com/law/legal-and-political-magazines/heart-atlanta-motel-v-united-states-1964)). T.M. Alexander Sr., an Atlanta insurance leader whom President Johnson appointed to a national citizens' committee to help put the new law into practice, rests at South-View (Henderson 170).

Name: Summerhill Uprising
Body: On September 6, 1966, Atlanta police shot Harold Prather, a 25-year-old Black man, as they tried to arrest him in the Summerhill neighborhood ([The Summerhill Riot or the Atlanta Rebellion?](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/mayoral-records/traditional/exhibits/show/summerhill-riots); [The Truth](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/mayoral-records/traditional/items/show/8535)). Hundreds of residents gathered to protest. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. came to Summerhill and climbed onto a police car to urge the crowd to go home, but he was heckled and knocked off the car ([Ivan Allen Jr. Digital Collection](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/artifacts/items/show/373)). Allen blamed the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC); police raided SNCC's office, and its chairman, Stokely Carmichael, was convicted of inciting a riot ([Ivan Allen Jr. Digital Collection](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/artifacts/items/show/373)). SNCC said none of its members were there when the crowd first gathered ([The Truth](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/mayoral-records/traditional/items/show/8535)). Allen called it a riot. Many Black Atlantans saw an uprising against police violence and the deep inequity of the "City Too Busy to Hate," and it is also remembered as the Atlanta Rebellion ([The Summerhill Riot or the Atlanta Rebellion?](https://ivanallen.iac.gatech.edu/mayoral-records/traditional/exhibits/show/summerhill-riots)). Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson, a SNCC leader, grew up in Summerhill, and Charles Walter "Pete" Greenlea co-founded Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., a community development corporation; both rest at South-View (Henderson 203, 238).

Name: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. and Dr. King Laid to Rest at South-View
Body:
On April 4, 1968, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee. He had traveled to Memphis to support roughly 1,300 Black municipal sanitation workers striking against deplorable working conditions, discriminatory pay, and severe safety hazards highlighted by the recent deaths of two workers crushed in a malfunctioning garbage truck. King’s murder triggered an immediate wave of national mourning and civil unrest across more than one hundred cities. In the immediate aftermath, the national crisis galvanized Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1968, enacting critical Fair Housing protections. Following national funeral rites in Atlanta on April 9, King was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in a marble crypt along Jonesboro Road, where he remained until his reinterment near Ebenezer Baptist Church in 1970.

On April 9, 1968, five days after he was assassinated in Memphis, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was carried on a mule-drawn farm wagon to South-View Cemetery ([Plan Your Visit](https://thekingcenter.org/visit/)). His burial drew the largest gathering in South-View's history; photographers climbed onto nearby mausoleums to see over the crowd (Henderson 114). He was laid to rest in a marble crypt on mausoleum row, its inscription stenciled at first because it was needed so quickly, and an eternal flame and a guard were later added (Henderson 69, 115). On what would have been his fortieth birthday, January 15, 1969, about three hundred people gathered at his grave, and thousands more came that year. In January 1970 his body was moved to a tomb near Ebenezer Baptist Church, now part of the King Center (Henderson 115). His parents, Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King, were later laid to rest at South-View in the same crypt where their son first rested (Henderson 115).

Name: Maynard Jackson Elected Mayor
Body:
On October 16, 1973, thirty-five-year-old attorney Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr. made history by defeating incumbent mayor Sam Massell in a runoff election, becoming Atlanta's first African American mayor and the first Black chief executive of any major Southern city. Jackson ultimately served three transformative terms as mayor (1974–1982 and 1990–1994), reshaping Atlanta's municipal landscape and creating an enduring national model for minority economic empowerment. Under his leadership, the city enacted progressive policies that drastically expanded municipal contracting opportunities for minority-owned businesses, increasing minority firm participation from less than one percent to over thirty percent. A crowning achievement of his tenure was the timely construction of the new midfield airport terminal, completed on schedule and within budget while ensuring unprecedented minority business participation. In 2003, the city honored his enduring contributions by renaming the facility Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

Jackson's milestone victory was deeply rooted in generations of Black political organizing in Atlanta. His maternal grandfather was John Wesley Dobbs, the renowned civic leader often celebrated as the unofficial "mayor of Sweet Auburn." Dobbs dedicated decades to organizing the Atlanta Negro Voters League and mobilizing tens of thousands of Black registered voters across the city. Dobbs, who is buried at South-View Cemetery, established the vital civic and voting infrastructure that empowered the Black electorate, directly forging the path for his grandson's historic triumph. Jackson's election thus stood as both a landmark personal achievement and the triumphant culmination of earlier generations' relentless struggle for civil rights and political representation.

Name: Atlanta's 1973 City Charter
Body: In 1973 Atlanta replaced its century-old city charter, and State Representative Grace Towns Hamilton was a principal architect of the new one (Henderson 205; [Grace Towns Hamilton, NGE](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/grace-towns-hamilton-1907-1992/)). The new charter made the mayor the head of a stronger executive branch, cut back the number of council seats elected citywide, and added seats elected by district ([Hamilton Papers, AHC](https://ahc.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/3134); [Hamilton, Grace Towns, AHC](https://www.umbrasearch.org/catalog/edef50a30e6b4b852720db33ce9cafed0ececcd0)). For the first time, Black Atlantans were elected to the City Council in numbers that matched their share of the population (Henderson 205; [Hamilton Papers, AUC](https://findingaids.auctr.edu/repositories/2/resources/144); [Grace Towns Hamilton, NGE](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/grace-towns-hamilton-1907-1992/)). In 1973 John H. Calhoun Jr., at seventy-four, won a seat on the council (Henderson 185). That same year Atlanta elected Maynard Jackson its first Black mayor (Henderson 216; [ATLVault: Maynard Jackson](https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2023/10/16/hfr-atlvault-maynard-jackson-made-american-history-50-years-ago)). Hamilton and Calhoun rest at South-View (Henderson 185, 205).

Name: Hank Aaron's 715th Home Run
Body: Hank Aaron ended the 1973 season one home run short of Babe Ruth's record of 714. That winter he received racist hate mail and threats on his life, and he needed bodyguards and police protection to keep playing ([Watch: Hank Aaron](https://www.si.com/mlb/strike-zone/2014/04/08/video-hank-aaron-715th-homer-40th-anniversary-babe-ruth)). His teammates feared someone would shoot him on the field ([Odum](https://www.wabe.org/hank-aaron-rose-above-racist-hate-mail-and-threats-in-pursuit-of-ruths-home-run-record-50-years-ago/)). Aaron reached this milestone while facing racist threats and hate mail during the record chase. On April 8, 1974, before a sellout crowd of 53,775 spectators at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, Henry Louis Aaron hit his 715th career home run in the fourth inning against Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Al Downing, and the Braves went on to win the game. He ultimately finished his major league career with 755 home runs ([Watch: Hank Aaron](https://www.si.com/mlb/strike-zone/2014/04/08/video-hank-aaron-715th-homer-40th-anniversary-babe-ruth)). Aaron married Billye Williams, the widow of Rev. Samuel W. Williams (Henderson 254). In January 2021 his funeral was held at Friendship Baptist Church, where Rev. Williams had once been pastor, and he was laid to rest at South-View ([Hank Aaron's funeral](https://ajc.com/sports/hank-aarons-funeral-a-tribute-to-more-than-a-baseball-great/NTMY77KPAFCWFHKNE4LJRBSGS4/)).

Name: Alberta Williams King's Funeral
Body:
On June 30, 1974, tragedy struck Ebenezer Baptist Church when Alberta Williams King was fatally shot while playing the organ during Sunday morning services. As the wife of long-serving pastor Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and mother of civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., she had devoted decades of service to Ebenezer as an accomplished choir organizer, musical director, and church organist.

Her funeral took place at Ebenezer Baptist Church on July 3, 1974, bringing together family members, civil rights figures, and national dignitaries to celebrate her lifelong dedication to faith and music. Following the service, she was laid to rest at historic South-View Cemetery in the crypt that had initially held her son Martin Luther King Jr., resting alongside her family.

Name: Albert Hawes Watts Becomes South-View's President-Treasurer
Body:
In 1977, Albert Hawes Watts assumed executive leadership as president-treasurer of the South-View Cemetery Association, succeeding earlier generations of his family. The grandson of co-founder Albert Watts and son of longtime secretary-treasurer Lewis Gould Watts, he had spent decades learning every facet of cemetery operations firsthand. Beginning his career as a laborer digging graves on the grounds, he steadily advanced through multiple supervisory, maintenance, and administrative positions across several decades before taking the helm.

Watts served as president-treasurer until his death in 2001, guiding the historic institution through modernization while maintaining its founding mission as a dignified, African American-owned sanctuary. His tenure represented a vital continuation of the Watts family's multigenerational stewardship, extending an enduring legacy of leadership that helped sustain South-View across four generations.

Name: Henry Ossian Flipper Reburied with Military Honors
Body: In 1877, Henry Ossian Flipper became the first Black graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point. Following his court-martial and dismissal from the Army in 1882, he pursued engineering, surveying, and government service while seeking to clear his military record. His discharge was officially corrected to honorable in 1976. After being buried at South-View following his death in 1940, Flipper was reburied with full military honors in his hometown of Thomasville, Georgia, on February 11, 1978.

Name: Atlanta Child Murders
Body:
In the late 1970s, a quiet anxiety began to shadow Atlanta’s low-income Black neighborhoods as crime rates climbed with little national notice. Between 1979 and 1981, that shadow deepened into a terrifying crisis when nearly thirty young African American children, teenagers, and young adults went missing. The horror began in late July 1979 with the disappearances of 14-year-old Edward Hope Smith and 13-year-old Alphred James Evans, both found dead shortly after. Over the next twenty-two months, young residents vanished in plain daylight from public places, their bodies later discovered in isolated areas. The fear grew unbearable as more children—14-year-old Milton Harvey and 9-year-old Yusef Bell—were lost to the darkness. As noted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, during this period "at least 28 African-American children, teenagers, and young adults... were killed in the Atlanta area" ([Serial Killers, Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). Desperate for answers, grieving parents and grassroots community leaders banded together on April 15, 1980, forming the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP) to run hotlines, raise public awareness, and press law enforcement into recognizing a pattern ([Atlanta Child Murders](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/atlanta-child-murders/)). While local police initially treated each case independently, the overwhelming crisis eventually compelled the Atlanta Police Department to establish the Missing and Murdered Task Force in August 1980 ([Atlanta Child Murders](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/atlanta-child-murders/)).

Federal help arrived after the June 1980 abduction of a 7-year-old girl prompted local officials to request broader support. Special Agent in Charge John Glover—the first African American to lead an FBI field office—pledged full institutional backing, bringing over two dozen full-time agents into a major federal inquiry by late autumn ([Serial Killers, Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). As investigators pieced together the clues, they realized a single perpetrator was likely targeting young Black males. By spring 1981, when the killer began discarding victims in the Chattahoochee River, law enforcement set up tense, round-the-clock stakeouts across fourteen metro river bridges ([Serial Killers, Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). The turning point came at 2:52 a.m. on May 22, 1981, when officers stationed near a bridge heard a loud splash and spotted a car speeding away ([Serial Killers, Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). They pulled over 23-year-old Wayne Williams. Though initially let go, the recovery of Nathaniel Cater’s body downstream two days later centered the investigation squarely on Williams ([Serial Killers, Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). With circumstantial evidence mounting—including hair and fiber matches, a lack of an alibi, and failed polygraph tests—authorities arrested Williams on June 21, 1981 ([Atlanta Child Murders](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/atlanta-child-murders/)). As documented on the Atlanta Child Murders memorial site, "Williams was convicted of the murders of two adults... and the police attributed most of the remaining child murders to him as well" ([Atlanta’s Missing & Murdered](https://atkid.weebly.com/)). Though he was sentenced to consecutive life terms, bringing a close to the official investigation, the profound pain and systemic inequalities exposed during those tragic years left an indelible mark on the city of Atlanta.

Williams was convicted in 1982 of the murders of two adults. He has never been convicted in any of the children’s deaths, and he has always maintained his innocence. In 2019, Atlanta officials announced that evidence from the murders would be re-tested ([Atlanta Child Murders Case Reopened](https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-news/atlanta-child-murders-case-reopened-mindhunter-874051/)).

Name: Dr. King's Birthday Becomes a National Holiday
Body: Four days after Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968, Michigan congressman John Conyers introduced the first bill to make King's birthday a national holiday ([How the Martin Luther King Jr. Birthday Became a Holiday](https://constitutioncenter.org/amp/blog/how-martin-luther-king-jr-s-birthday-became-a-holiday-3)). It took fifteen years. On November 2, 1983, President Ronald Reagan signed the bill in the White House Rose Garden, with Coretta Scott King and about two hundred civil rights leaders looking on, and set the holiday on the third Monday in January ([Reagan Signs King Holiday](https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/11/02/Reagan-signs-King-holiday/1735436597200/); [What Goes into Making a Federal Holiday](https://reagan.blogs.archives.gov/2017/01/16/what-goes-into-making-a-federal-holiday-ronald-reagan-and-martin-luther-king-jr-day)). The nation first observed it in 1986, but some states held out, and not until 2000 did every state observe it ([How the Martin Luther King Jr. Birthday Became a Holiday](https://constitutioncenter.org/amp/blog/how-martin-luther-king-jr-s-birthday-became-a-holiday-3)). Dr. King was first laid to rest at South-View in 1968, and his parents, Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King, rest there today (Henderson 114–15).

Name: Martin Luther King Sr. Buried at South-View
Body: On November 11, 1984, Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. passed away in Atlanta and was laid to rest at historic South-View Cemetery. Known affectionately as "Daddy King," he served as pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for more than four decades from 1931 to 1975, transforming the congregation into a major spiritual center of the civil rights movement. Throughout his life, King Sr. championed racial equality, leading historic voter registration campaigns, including a 1936 march on Atlanta City Hall, and successfully fighting for equal salaries for Black public school teachers through the NAACP. He was a foundational figure in Atlanta's civic affairs and played an influential advisory role during pivotal moments of the national struggle for civil rights. At South-View, he was interred beside his beloved wife, Alberta Williams King, who was laid to rest there in 1974 after her tragic death at Ebenezer Baptist Church.

Name: Forsyth County Brotherhood Marches
Body: In 1912, white residents of Forsyth County, north of Atlanta, drove out all 1,098 of the county's Black residents, and for decades afterward the county kept Black people out ([In 1912, This Georgia County Drove Out Every Black Resident](https://www.history.com/articles/georgia-racial-expulsion-stacey-abrams); [Remembering the Brotherhood March](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/exhibitions/remembering-the-brotherhood-march-35-years-later/)). In January 1987, as the nation marked its second King holiday, local residents and Atlanta civil rights leader Hosea Williams organized a Brotherhood March there ([Brotherhood March](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/brotherhood-march/)). On January 17, about seventy-five marchers, Black and white, set out for the courthouse in Cumming; counter-protesters, some in Klan robes, threw rocks, bottles and bricks until the march was called off ([Brotherhood March](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/brotherhood-march/); [Remembering the Brotherhood March](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/exhibitions/remembering-the-brotherhood-march-35-years-later/)). A week later, on January 24, more than fifteen thousand people returned, among them Coretta Scott King and Congressman John Lewis, who now rests at South-View ([Brotherhood March](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/brotherhood-march/)). Williams led a third march in 1988 ([Remembering the Brotherhood March](https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/exhibitions/remembering-the-brotherhood-march-35-years-later/)).

Name: 1906 Massacre Centennial Remembrance
Body: For most of the twentieth century, Atlanta said little about the 1906 massacre, and many Black families also chose to put it behind them ([Atlanta 1906 Race Riot Remembered](https://www.ajc.com/news/atlanta-1906-race-riot-remembered-citys-bloody-stain-seen-with-new-eyes/PWIJXP7XT5FRBJ5EAJ7K6MLSXI/)). As the hundredth anniversary approached, civic leaders, historians, genealogists and educators formed the Coalition to Remember the 1906 Atlanta Race Riot and planned a Centennial Remembrance Weekend for September 21–24, 2006 ([Atlanta Marks Centennial](https://www.voanews.com/a/a-13-2006-09-21-voa46/399420.html); [Centennial Remembrance Weekend](https://egrove.olemiss.edu/atrr_docs/6)). On Thursday, September 21, a memorial service was held at South-View for the Black victims of the massacre (Henderson 120). Mourners also gathered at the old Ebenezer Baptist Church and followed a funeral procession to the cemetery ([Reasons to Celebrate Black History Month](https://ajc.com/lifestyles/reasons-celebrate-black-history-month-the-1906-atlanta-riot/kbBasrl5ynpbBjsrNwPixM/)). Burial records show that ten Black victims were laid to rest at South-View in 1906, though only the graves of George Wilder and Frank Smith have been found (Henderson 119). Remembrance at South-View has continued since; in 2024 the annual commemoration included a theatrical tour of the cemetery and the Praise House Project ([Atlanta Race Massacre Remembrance](https://roughdraftatlanta.com/2024/09/20/atlanta-race-massacre-remembrance/)).

Name: South-View Historical Marker Dedicated
Body: On April 30, 2016, the Georgia Historical Society and the Historic South-View Preservation Foundation dedicated a historical marker on the grounds of South-View Cemetery. The marker commemorated the cemetery's 1886 founding by formerly enslaved African Americans and Black community leaders who sought a dignified resting place in response to discrimination at segregated burial grounds. It also recognized notable figures buried at South-View, including Atlanta Life Insurance Company founder Alonzo Franklin Herndon, Reconstruction legislator and AME bishop Henry McNeal Turner, and the parents of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King. The dedication highlighted the ongoing importance of preserving and sharing South-View's profound historical legacy.

Name: John Lewis Laid to Rest at South-View
Body: John Lewis (1940–2020) chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, was beaten by Alabama state troopers as he led marchers across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma in 1965, and later represented Atlanta in Congress for more than thirty years ([Moye](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/john-lewis-1940-2020/)). After he died on July 17, 2020, his casket crossed that same bridge on a horse-drawn caisson, and he became the first Black lawmaker to lie in state in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol ([America Paid Homage](https://www.culturetype.com/2020/07/31/america-paid-homage-to-civil-rights-icon-john-lewis-this-week-in-multi-city-homegoing-worthy-of-a-head-of-state/); [Former Presidents Pay Tribute](https://www.voanews.com/usa/former-presidents-pay-tribute-civil-rights-icon-john-lewis)). On July 30, after a funeral at Ebenezer Baptist Church where three former presidents honored him, he was laid to rest at South-View beside his wife, Lillian Miles Lewis ([John Lewis: A Founding Father](https://www.ajc.com/john-lewis/john-lewis-a-founding-father-of-a-better-america/2PYQEPHYIRH7NE4R6B5SS2JPZU/); Henderson 223). His own card tells the full story of his life in the movement.

Name: Hank Aaron Laid to Rest at South-View
Body: Henry "Hank" Aaron (1934–2021) broke Babe Ruth's home run record in Atlanta on April 8, 1974, after a winter of racist hate mail and threats ([Watch: Hank Aaron](https://www.si.com/mlb/strike-zone/2014/04/08/video-hank-aaron-715th-homer-40th-anniversary-babe-ruth)). He died in January 2021, at eighty-six ([Hank Aaron Laid to Rest](https://11alive.com/article/news/local/hank-aaron-final-resting-place/85-834bd507-a782-4a20-8977-9ab73606cb0b)). On January 27 his funeral was held at Friendship Baptist Church, once led by Rev. Samuel W. Williams, who also rests at South-View ([Hank Aaron's Funeral](https://ajc.com/sports/hank-aarons-funeral-a-tribute-to-more-than-a-baseball-great/NTMY77KPAFCWFHKNE4LJRBSGS4/); Henderson 254). On the way to the cemetery, his funeral procession stopped at the marker for his 715th home run, at the site of the old Atlanta–Fulton County Stadium ([Hank Aaron Hearse Makes Stop](https://11alive.com/article/sports/mlb/atlanta-braves/hank-aaron-hearse-715-homerun-spot/85-19414170-e24c-4962-82d0-a1d50fbcf0ac)). He rested in a temporary crypt at South-View while his tomb was finished, and on January 5, 2022, he was laid in his final resting place near the crypt of Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King ([Braves Legend Hank Aaron Moved](https://www.wrdw.com/2022/01/06/braves-legend-hank-aaron-moved-final-resting-place/)). His own card and the 715th Home Run card tell the rest of his story.

Name: 1906 Massacre Victims Identified
Body: For more than a century, some of the Black Atlantans killed in the 1906 massacre were remembered only as "unknown" ([Two Victims in 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre Identified](https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/two-victims-1906-atlanta-race-massacre-identified-nearly-120-years-later/5LVMJY55DFBPZP76CKLWA57T5Y/)). In September 2023, researchers from the National Center for Civil and Human Rights, Emory University's Georgia Civil Rights Cold Cases Project, and the Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society announced two more names, found in Fulton County death certificates ([Unearthing the Past](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/); [Klibanoff Helps Identify Two Victims](https://scholarblogs.emory.edu/emoryhistorynews/2023/10/30/klibanoff-helps-identify-two-victims-of-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/)). Marshall Carter was a thirteen-year-old schoolboy who lived with his family on Love Street near Summerhill, and Stinson Ferguson, twenty-five, lived on Thurmond Street ([Unearthing the Past](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/)). The white mob killed both on the first night of the massacre, September 22, 1906, and both were laid to rest at South-View ([Unearthing the Past](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/); [New Victims Identified](https://www.axios.com/local/atlanta/2023/09/19/atlanta-race-massacre-victims)). The researchers sent their names to the Equal Justice Initiative so that they can replace "unknown" on its record of racial terror lynchings in Fulton County ([Unearthing the Past](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/)).
