Name: South-View Listed on the National Register
Body: In 1886, Albert Watts and five other Black Atlantans founded South-View because the city's cemeteries, including Oakland and Westview, segregated and neglected Black burials (Henderson 1, 11, 13). Located at 1990 Jonesboro Road SE in Atlanta, Georgia, the cemetery expanded from its original 25 acres to more than 100 acres, serving as the burial place for generations of Atlanta families and guided across generations by descendants of the founders who continued to participate in its leadership ([Our History](https://southviewcemetery.com/our-history/)). The National Register recognition followed the dedication of a Georgia Historical Society historical marker on the grounds in 2016 ([Georgia Historical Society](https://www.georgiahistory.com/georgia-historical-society-to-recognize-south-view-cemetery-with-historical-marker-dedication-this-saturday/)). In 2024, the Atlanta Preservation Center and the South-View Cemetery Association began working to place the cemetery on the National Register of Historic Places in time for its 140th anniversary ([Advocates Begin Process](https://www.axios.com/local/atlanta/2024/07/19/advocates-begin-process-to-include-south-view-cemetery-on-historic-places-list); [Cemetery Established by Formerly Enslaved Black Atlantans](https://www.ajc.com/news/south-view-cemetery-applying-for-historic-recognition/PGJTI6ZETNGEVCNDON6OUDGZAY/)). By May 2026 South-View was on the Georgia Register of Historic Places, and on July 6, 2026—140 years after its founding—the National Park Service officially listed it on the National Register of Historic Places, where it now stands beside Oakland and Westview ([South-View Seeks National Recognition](https://roughdraftatlanta.com/2026/05/05/south-view-cemetery-historic-atlanta/); [Weekly List 2026 07 10](https://home.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/weekly-list-2026-07-10.htm); [Advocates Begin Process](https://www.axios.com/local/atlanta/2024/07/19/advocates-begin-process-to-include-south-view-cemetery-on-historic-places-list)). Today it covers 101 acres and holds about 80,000 graves, and it was the first privately owned Black cemetery corporation in Georgia after the Civil War ([National Register](https://www.fox5atlanta.com/news/national-register-historic-places-adds-4-georgia-landmarks)).

Name: A.D. Williams King
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Alfred Daniel Williams King was an influential Baptist pastor, grassroots civil rights organizer, and stalwart leader in the Black freedom movement. As the younger brother of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., he played a pivotal role in direct-action protests, community mobilization, and pastoral leadership across the American South, providing essential moral fortitude and strategic guidance during some of the movement's most perilous campaigns.

Life and Contributions:
Born on July 30, 1930, in Atlanta, Georgia, Alfred Daniel Williams King was the son of Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King. Growing up immersed in the spiritual life of Ebenezer Baptist Church, he completed his education at Morehouse College, graduating with a bachelor's degree in sociology in 1959. Drawn to the ministry, King was ordained at Ebenezer and assumed pastorates at several congregations, including First Baptist Church in Ensley, Alabama, and later Zion Baptist Church in Louisville, Kentucky.

Throughout the 1960s, King was an active and courageous front-line leader in major civil rights demonstrations. During the 1960 Atlanta Student Movement, he joined student organizers in sit-ins at downtown department stores, willingly enduring arrest to challenge racial segregation. In Birmingham, Alabama, King served as a key local organizer during the historic 1963 campaigns led by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). On the night of May 11, 1963, segregationist vigilantes bombed his Ensley home while his wife Naomi and five children were inside; miraculously, the family survived, and King immediately took to the streets to preach nonviolence to outraged residents.

Relocating to Louisville in 1965, King directed a prominent open-housing campaign that mobilized thousands of demonstrators and pressured municipal authorities into passing fair-housing legislation. In 1968, following the tragic assassination of his brother Martin, A.D. returned to Atlanta to serve as co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church alongside his father, providing vital stability to the congregation and community. Tragically, on July 21, 1969, King drowned in his home swimming pool at the age of thirty-eight, cutting short a dedicated life of Christian ministry, social justice advocacy, and civil rights leadership.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
A.D. Williams King maintained deep, lifelong roots in Atlanta as a native son, Morehouse College graduate, and co-pastor of historic Ebenezer Baptist Church on Auburn Avenue. Following his tragic passing on July 21, 1969, thousands of mourners gathered for his funeral service at Ebenezer Baptist Church. King was interred at South-View Cemetery, where generations of his distinguished family are commemorated (Henderson 219). His resting place at South-View stands alongside foundational leaders of Atlanta’s faith and civil rights traditions.

Name: Aaron Jackson
Body:
Overview:
Aaron Jackson was a nine-year-old African American child from Atlanta whose tragic abduction and murder in November 1980 made him one of the devastating casualties of the Atlanta Child Murders. His heartbreaking death intensified community outrage, galvanizing working-class families and civil rights organizers to demand municipal accountability and protective measures for vulnerable children throughout the metropolitan area.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, Aaron Jackson grew up in a working-class neighborhood during the late 1970s. As a nine-year-old child, Aaron was a beloved member of his family and local community, attending neighborhood public schools and participating in neighborhood childhood activities. In the autumn of 1980, the city of Atlanta was gripped by an unprecedented crisis of fear as Black children and teenagers were systematically targeted, abducted, and murdered across the metropolitan area.

On November 1, 1980, Aaron disappeared after leaving his home, vanishing without a trace. His sudden disappearance sent shockwaves through his neighborhood and heightened the acute panic experienced by Atlanta parents, who were already enforcing strict curfews and organizing community search parties. Tragically, on November 2, 1980, Aaron's body was discovered on a riverbank near Moreland Avenue and the South River in DeKalb County. Medical examiners determined that the young boy had died from asphyxiation.

Aaron's death was formally investigated by the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force, a joint multi-agency investigative team comprising the Atlanta Police Department, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. His murder became a central focal point for local activist groups, most notably the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP), established by grieving mothers who rallied to demand enhanced protective resources, street lighting, and social services for Atlanta's Black neighborhoods. Though decades have passed, Aaron Jackson’s tragic loss remains an enduring symbol of community grief and the collective struggle for justice and accountability.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Aaron Jackson was an Atlanta native whose tragic life and untimely death took place entirely within the metropolitan community during the harrowing 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Following the discovery of his remains, his grieving family and neighbors held services in Atlanta. Jackson was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, which provided solemn, sacred grounds for several young victims of the Atlanta Child Murders (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His resting place connects South-View directly to the collective mourning of Atlanta’s African American community.

Name: Aaron Wyche
Body:
Overview:
Aaron Wyche was a gentle ten-year-old African American boy from Atlanta whose tragic disappearance and death in June 1980 deeply intensified the terror of the Atlanta Child Murders. His loss demonstrated that children of varying ages were being targeted indiscriminately, galvanizing neighborhood mothers and civic organizers to unite in demanding rigorous investigative resources and child protections.

Life and Contributions:
Aaron Wyche was born in 1970 in Atlanta, Georgia, and was raised by his family in a close-knit south Atlanta neighborhood. Known to relatives and friends as an observant and soft-spoken youth, Aaron was an elementary school student who enjoyed spending time outdoors and assisting neighbors with everyday errands. In early 1980, widespread dread had begun to settle over Black neighborhoods across Atlanta following the unexplained disappearances of several youths.

On June 23, 1980, ten-year-old Aaron was last seen near a neighborhood grocery store on Pryor Road in south Atlanta, where he had walked during a warm afternoon. When he failed to return home, his family launched immediate neighborhood searches and alerted the authorities. The following day, on June 24, 1980, searchers discovered Aaron’s body beneath a railway trestle along the Interstate 20 corridor near Moreland Avenue. Medical examiners concluded that he had suffered fatal neck trauma and asphyxiation.

Aaron's tragic death marked a critical turning point in the city's recognition of the unfolding crisis. It served as a stark, horrifying confirmation that the mysterious predator was operating across disparate neighborhoods and abducting younger children. In response, Atlanta mothers, led by Camille Bell, organized the Committee to Stop Children's Murders, forcing municipal and national leaders to devote substantial investigative manpower to the cases. The FBI Vault and the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force subsequently included Aaron's case among the official list of investigated victims, leaving a legacy of enduring sorrow and community solidarity.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Aaron Wyche spent his childhood in Atlanta, and his tragic death in June 1980 occurred within the city during the height of the missing and murdered crisis. Following his death, community members gathered in south Atlanta to support his family, and Aaron was interred at South-View Cemetery, where multiple victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were laid to rest in sacred peace (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His grave at South-View preserves the memory of an innocent youth taken far too soon.

Name: Adam Daniel Williams
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Adam Daniel Williams was a pioneer Baptist minister, civil rights organizer, and community builder who served as pastor of Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church for thirty-seven years. The maternal grandfather of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Williams transformed Ebenezer into a major institutional congregation and co-founded the Atlanta NAACP branch, laying essential foundations for twentieth-century Black civic activism.

Life and Contributions:
Born on January 2, 1863, in Greene County, Georgia, into slavery, Adam Daniel Williams was the son of Willis and Lucrecia Williams. Following the Civil War, Williams demonstrated an exceptional passion for learning and spiritual calling. He moved to Atlanta during Reconstruction to pursue ministerial education, studying at the Atlanta Baptist Seminary (later Morehouse College). In 1888, he was licensed to preach, and in March 1894, he was called to the pastorate of Ebenezer Baptist Church, which then had only a few dozen congregants.

Over the next nearly four decades, Williams exhibited visionary leadership, transforming Ebenezer into one of the largest and most influential African American institutional churches in the South. In 1914, under his direction, the congregation constructed its iconic Gothic revival brick sanctuary on Auburn Avenue, which became a vital anchor of Sweet Auburn. Williams believed firmly in the Social Gospel, establishing community aid programs, public health clinics, and educational forums within the church.

Williams was equally prominent as a civil rights militant. In 1906, following the devastating Atlanta Race Massacre, he worked with civic leaders to protect Black residents and organize legal defense. In 1917, Williams co-founded the Atlanta branch of the NAACP, serving as its first president and mobilizing mass community protests that successfully halted the school board's discriminatory plan to eliminate seventh-grade education in Black public schools. Williams married Jennie Celeste Parks in 1899; their daughter, Alberta Christine Williams, married Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. Williams passed away on March 21, 1931, leaving an enduring institutional, theological, and generational legacy.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Adam Daniel Williams lived and ministered on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta for more than four decades, anchoring Ebenezer Baptist Church and establishing the Atlanta NAACP in 1917. When he died suddenly in March 1931, thousands of citizens filled Ebenezer Baptist Church to pay their respects. Williams was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside his wife Jennie, his daughter Alberta Williams King, and generations of the King family (Henderson 234, 253–54). His resting place at South-View symbolizes the foundational roots of Atlanta’s civil rights leadership.

Name: Albert Hawes Watts
Body:
Overview:
Albert Hawes Watts was an executive, community trustee, and dedicated steward of South-View Cemetery who served as president-treasurer of the South-View Cemetery Association for twenty-four years. As the grandson of founding organizer Albert Watts, his lifelong career ensured the financial endurance, physical preservation, and dignified management of the historic African American corporation into the twenty-first century.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, on July 10, 1913, Albert Hawes Watts was the son of Lewis Gould Watts and grandson of South-View co-founder Albert Watts. Immersed from early childhood in the family tradition of community stewardship, Watts attended local public schools and pursued higher education in Atlanta, earning his bachelor's degree from Clark College and undertaking graduate studies at Atlanta University.

After completing his education, Watts committed his entire career to South-View Cemetery, learning its operations through rigorous hands-on service. He began his employment on the grounds as a gravedigger, manual laborer, and maintenance worker, acquiring an intimate understanding of the physical terrain, burial traditions, and engineering requirements of the cemetery. Watts subsequently advanced to grounds superintendent, office manager, and assistant treasurer, modernizing administrative records and overseeing expanded cemetery landscaping.

In 1977, upon the transition of senior leadership, Watts was elected president and treasurer of the South-View Cemetery Association. Over the next twenty-four years, he guided South-View through substantial economic, municipal, and demographic changes. Watts maintained the cemetery's financial self-sufficiency, expanded its perpetual care trust funds, and preserved its historic core while opening new memorial gardens. Dedicated to community service, Watts also supported Clark College, local youth initiatives, and fraternal organizations. He remained in active executive leadership until his passing on November 20, 2001, at the age of eighty-eight, concluding an extraordinary tenure that sustained South-View as one of the oldest Black-owned corporations in the nation.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Albert Hawes Watts spent his entire life in Atlanta, dedicating more than six decades of professional service directly to South-View Cemetery. Serving as the cemetery's president-treasurer from 1977 until 2001, he stewarded the final resting place of thousands of African American citizens, civil rights icons, and community pioneers. Following his passing in November 2001, Watts was interred in the historic Watts family plot at South-View Cemetery, resting alongside his father Lewis Gould Watts and grandfather Albert Watts (Henderson 22; [Celebration of Life Honoring Watts](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/aarl_afpc_wattsalberthawes20011126)). His life represents unbroken familial devotion to Black memorial heritage.

Name: Albert Watts
Body:
Overview:
Albert Watts was an entrepreneur, civic leader, and the principal organizer and founding treasurer of South-View Cemetery. Motivated by the discriminatory treatment and desecration of Black burial grounds in municipal cemeteries, Watts mobilized fellow African American leaders in 1886 to charter South-View, establishing an enduring corporate enterprise and multi-generational family legacy of Black self-determination.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery around 1843 in Clarke County, Georgia, Albert Watts was the son of Sterling and Emily Watts. Following emancipation at the conclusion of the Civil War, Watts relocated to Atlanta, appearing on freight house employment records in 1870 as an industrious railroad laborer. Practicing rigorous personal thrift, Watts accumulated independent capital and established a prosperous grocery store on Fraser Street by 1874, serving working-class Black families in south Atlanta.

Watts emerged as an influential civic and moral leader in municipal politics. He served as an outspoken advocate for the temperance movement, chairing the Third Ward Colored Prohibition Club and mobilizing Black voters around community welfare. Watts married Sarah Andrews, and together they raised six children. Personal tragedy, however, catalyzed his most enduring achievement. In 1876, his mother Emily was buried in Oakland Cemetery's segregated "Slave Square," which was later dug up and desecrated by the city council in 1877. In October 1885, when his father Sterling died, Watts was forced to bring the casket through a segregated rear gate at Westview Cemetery into the neglected "Rest Haven" section.

Incensed by this persistent indignity, Watts rallied five fellow Black leaders—Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Rev. Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, and Rev. John Render—to petition the Atlanta City Council in February 1886. In April 1886, they secured a corporate charter for the South-View Cemetery Association, open to all people without racial restriction. Watts served as founding treasurer from 1886 until his death in 1903, overseeing its expansion from twenty-five acres into a thriving institution and establishing an unbroken family dynasty of cemetery stewardship.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Albert Watts lived and operated his businesses in Atlanta for over three decades, conceptualizing and establishing South-View Cemetery after enduring segregated cemetery practices at Oakland and Westview. As South-View's founding treasurer from 1886 until 1903, he secured land purchases, defeated discriminatory legal injunctions, and built a permanent sanctuary for Atlanta's African American community. Upon his death in 1903, Watts was buried in the Watts family plot at South-View Cemetery, where four generations of his family have since been interred (Henderson 1, 22).

Name: Alberta Whitman
Body:
Overview:
Alberta Whitman was an acclaimed African American dancer, composer, entertainer, and male impersonator who starred in the celebrated Whitman Sisters Revue. Known on stage as "Bert," her dynamic flash-dancing and tailored masculine attire made her a headlining sensation across the nation, cementing the Whitman troupe as the preeminent act in early twentieth-century Black vaudeville.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1887 in Lawrence, Kansas, Alberta Whitman was the daughter of Rev. Albery Allson Whitman, an esteemed AME minister and poet, and Caddie Whitman. Raised in a profoundly musical and literary household, Alberta and her sisters—Mabel, Essie, and Alice—began performing religious songs and jubilee spirituals at church revivals and Chautauqua circuits across the country during the late 1890s.

As the sisters transitioned into secular vaudeville, they organized the Whitman Sisters Comedy Company, which evolved into one of the longest-running, highest-paid, and most influential touring companies on the Theater Owners Booking Association (TOBA) circuit. Within the revue, Alberta emerged as a brilliant, multifaceted talent. Performing under the stage persona "Bert," she gained national renown as a male impersonator, striding across stages in impeccably tailored tuxedos, top hats, and walking sticks, executing dazzling flash-dancing routines and high-speed struts that captivated both Black and white audiences.

Beyond her performance artistry, Alberta served as a primary musical composer for the troupe. She wrote and arranged original songs, jazz tunes, and comedic skits that formed the core of the company's repertoire, blending popular ragtime, blues, and rhythm into their nationwide productions. Alberta also played a crucial role in talent development, helping identify, recruit, and mentor young Black performers, including legendary tap dancers and singers who got their first professional start in the Whitman Sisters Revue. She continued performing and composing with the troupe through the 1930s and 1940s, leaving an indelible imprint on American theatrical history before her death in 1964.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Alberta Whitman and the Whitman Sisters maintained deep, lasting connections to Atlanta as a primary performance hub, regional headquarters, and winter gathering site along the southern vaudeville circuit. When the family retired from the stage, they chose Atlanta as their permanent home. Following her death in 1964, Alberta was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests alongside her sisters in the historic Whitman family plot (Henderson 252). Her burial at South-View links the grounds to the pioneering golden era of African American entertainment.

Name: Alberta Williams King
Body:
Overview:
Alberta Williams King was an accomplished educator, pianist, organist, and choir director who served as the musical and spiritual heart of Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church. As the mother of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., she nurtured her family's moral commitments, anchored community life, and led faith programs until her tragic death in 1974.

Life and Contributions:
Born on September 13, 1904, in Atlanta, Georgia, Alberta Christine Williams was the only surviving child of Rev. Adam Daniel Williams, pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, and Jennie Celeste Parks Williams. Growing up in Sweet Auburn, Alberta was surrounded by sacred music and education. She attended Spelman Seminary, earned her teaching credentials at Hampton Institute in Virginia in 1924, and later completed a bachelor’s degree in education from Morris Brown College in 1938.

On Thanksgiving Day in 1926, she married Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. at Ebenezer Baptist Church. The couple had three children: Christine, Martin Jr., and Alfred Daniel (A.D.). While raising her family, King pursued a teaching career and dedicated herself to Ebenezer’s music ministry. She served as the church’s primary organist and choir director from 1932 until 1974, founding the Ebenezer Choir and organizing the Women's Committee. Her home was an open sanctuary for visiting civil rights figures, ministers, and students.

King endured profound family grief with extraordinary grace, supporting her son Martin through the perilous trials of the civil rights movement, mourning his assassination in 1968, and grieving the sudden drowning of her son A.D. in 1969. Tragically, on June 30, 1974, while playing "The Lord’s Prayer" on the organ during Sunday services at Ebenezer, she was fatally shot by an armed assailant. Her loss plunged Atlanta and the nation into mourning, while her lifetime of quiet grace, musical excellence, and spiritual resilience remains an enduring inspiration.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Alberta Williams King lived her entire life in Atlanta, dedicating seven decades to the educational, civic, and spiritual life of the Sweet Auburn community at Ebenezer Baptist Church. Following her tragic death on June 30, 1974, thousands of mourners attended her funeral at Ebenezer. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery beside her son Martin's original crypt, where her husband Martin Luther King Sr. was later interred beside her; her epitaph reads "Her life shall be filled with music" (Henderson 69, 115, 220).

Name: Alice Dugged Cary
Body:
Overview:
Alice Dugged Cary was a pioneer educator, librarian, author, and suffragist who broke significant institutional barriers for African Americans in Georgia. She served as Atlanta's first Black woman public school principal, co-founded the city’s first free Black kindergarten, and became the founding head librarian of the historic Auburn Avenue Branch Library in 1921.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1859 in New London, Indiana, Alice Dugged was the daughter of free African American parents John R. and Josie Dugged. Committed to intellectual advancement, she attended public schools and graduated from Wilberforce University in Ohio in 1881. After teaching in Kansas, she married Rev. Jefferson A. Cary, an AME minister, and relocated to Atlanta, Georgia, in the mid-1880s, where she embarked on a transformative educational career.

In 1886, Cary made history when the Atlanta Board of Education appointed her principal of Mitchell Street School, making her the first African American woman to serve as a public school principal in Atlanta. For decades, Cary championed early childhood education and educational equity for Black youth. In 1900, she partnered with civic groups to establish Atlanta's first free kindergarten for African American children. She also taught education and literature at Morris Brown College, serving as principal of its normal department and mentoring future teachers across the state.

Beyond the classroom, Cary was a prominent civic organizer, serving as president of the Georgia State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs and advocating nationally for women's suffrage and temperance. In 1921, when the Carnegie Corporation funded the opening of the Auburn Avenue Branch of the Atlanta Public Library—the city's first public library for Black citizens—Cary was appointed its first head librarian. She transformed the branch into a cultural beacon and intellectual salon for Sweet Auburn before her passing in 1941.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Alice Dugged Cary spent more than fifty-five years in Atlanta transforming its public education, higher education at Morris Brown College, and public library access along Auburn Avenue. When she passed away in Atlanta on September 25, 1941, educators, civic clubs, and community leaders paid tribute to her pioneering leadership. Cary was interred at South-View Cemetery, where she rests alongside generations of educators and civic trailblazers who built Atlanta's Black institutional life (Henderson 187). Her grave at South-View commemorates a lifetime of barrier-breaking public service.

Name: Alonzo Herndon
Body:
Overview:
Alonzo Franklin Herndon was an entrepreneur, real estate investor, and civic benefactor who rose from chattel slavery to become Atlanta's first African American millionaire. As the founder and president of the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, Herndon established one of the nation's premier Black-owned corporate powerhouses, funding community institutions and expanding economic opportunity throughout the South.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on June 26, 1858, in Social Circle, Walton County, Georgia, Alonzo Herndon was the son of an enslaved woman, Sophenie, and her white enslaver. Emancipated in 1865 at age seven, Herndon labored as a farmhand and sharecropper to help support his family before learning the barbering trade in Jonesboro. In 1883, Herndon arrived in Atlanta with eleven dollars in savings, quickly finding work in local barbershops.

Demonstrating extraordinary business acumen and thrift, Herndon acquired his own shop and by 1902 owned three upscale Atlanta barbershops. His flagship establishment at 66 Peachtree Street, known as the "Crystal Palace," featured crystal chandeliers, marble fixtures, and mirror-lined walls, catering to Atlanta’s elite white clientele. Herndon channeled his earnings into Atlanta real estate, amassing more than one hundred residential and commercial properties across the city.

In 1905, approached by local ministers, Herndon invested $140 to acquire a failing mutual aid association, reorganizing it as the Atlanta Mutual Insurance Association. Navigating strict state capital regulations, Herndon personally deposited the necessary cash reserves, transforming the venture into the Atlanta Life Insurance Company in 1922. Atlanta Life provided vital life, sickness, and burial insurance to African Americans systematically denied coverage by white firms, while providing professional careers for college-educated Black youth. Herndon also co-founded the Niagara Movement with W.E.B. Du Bois in 1905. Survived by his wife Adrienne and son Norris, Herndon passed away on July 21, 1927, as Atlanta’s wealthiest Black citizen.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Alonzo Herndon lived in Atlanta for forty-four years, building his landmark Herndon Home mansion in the University Center and establishing Atlanta Life Insurance Company on Sweet Auburn. When he died in July 1927, his funeral was attended by thousands of civic leaders and citizens. Herndon was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in an ornate family mausoleum that remains one of the cemetery’s most iconic historic landmarks (Henderson 5–6; Merritt 85–86). His resting place at South-View represents the pinnacle of Black corporate resilience in Atlanta.

Name: Annie L. McPheeters
Body:
Overview:
Annie L. McPheeters was a pioneering librarian, educator, and civil rights advocate who expanded literacy, integrated public library services, and preserved African American history in Atlanta. As head librarian of the Auburn Avenue branch and later Georgia State University's first Black faculty appointee, she safeguarded Black literary collections and dismantled institutional segregation.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 22, 1908, in Berwin, Floyd County, Georgia, Annie Lucille McPheeters was dedicated to academic excellence from childhood. She earned her bachelor’s degree from Clark College in 1929 and pursued graduate library science studies at Hampton Institute in Virginia, earning her professional degree in 1933. She later completed a master’s degree in library science from Columbia University in 1957.

In 1934, McPheeters returned to Atlanta to begin an illustrious career with the Atlanta Public Library system, serving as head librarian of the historic Auburn Avenue Branch Library. Under her direction, the branch became a vibrant cultural haven and research depot for Black Atlantans during legal segregation. McPheeters recognized that African American literature, manuscripts, and civic histories were in jeopardy of being lost or neglected; she meticulously established the Negro History Collection, gathering rare books, manuscripts, and archival photographs.

McPheeters also led adult literacy campaigns, community bookmobiles, and public lecture series. In the 1950s, she partnered with civil rights organizations, including Irene Dobbs Jackson and the NAACP, to challenge segregated library policies, successfully securing the desegregation of the city's central library system in 1959. In 1966, McPheeters broke another institutional barrier when she was hired as a reference librarian and instructor at Georgia State College (now Georgia State University), becoming its first African American faculty member. Her seminal archival efforts laid the foundation for the Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History. She passed away in December 1994.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Annie L. McPheeters spent six decades in Atlanta transforming the intellectual landscape of Sweet Auburn and higher education at Georgia State University. Following her death in December 1994, she was interred at South-View Cemetery, where many of Atlanta’s foremost educators, civic trailblazers, and civil rights icons rest (Henderson 228; [Connection to South-View](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/aarl_afpc_mcpheetersanniel19941229)). Her grave at South-View connects the historic cemetery to the generations of librarians who safeguarded Black heritage and secured equal access to public knowledge.

Name: Annie Shepard
Body:
Overview:
Annie Shepard was an African American woman who was murdered during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, an eruption of white mob terror that left dozens of Black citizens dead or displaced. Her tragic killing underscores how Jim Crow violence targeted Black women and residential communities indiscriminately, shattering families and destabilizing neighborhoods across the city.

Life and Contributions:
Annie Shepard was born in Georgia during the late nineteenth century and lived as an African American resident in Atlanta at the beginning of the twentieth century. Like thousands of Black citizens during this period, Shepard sought to build an independent life and support her household despite the severe social, economic, and political restrictions imposed by Jim Crow segregation. During the early 1900s, Atlanta's Black population established vibrant communities, neighborhood churches, and local mutual aid societies.

In late September 1906, political demagoguery and sensationalized, false news reports in local white newspapers ignited severe racial hostilities across Atlanta. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, a violent mob of thousands of white men and boys swarmed downtown streets, attacking Black laborers, passengers, and passersby. Over the subsequent seventy-two hours, the mob expanded outward into residential neighborhoods, breaking into homes and firing weapons into Black households.

During the outbreak of violent terror, Annie Shepard was violently assaulted and suffered fatal injuries. Her death, documented in contemporary records and municipal fatality lists, reflected the tragic reality that the mob spared neither women nor children. Her tragic loss was officially memorialized over a century later through the research and commemorative projects of the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project, which restored the names and dignity of victims whose deaths had long been obscured in official civic histories.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Annie Shepard was an Atlanta resident whose life was brutally cut short by mob violence during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the immediate aftermath of the violence, South-View Cemetery served as the primary sanctuary and sacred burial ground for African American massacre victims (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)).

Name: Asa G. Yancey Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Asa Greenwood Yancey Sr. was a renowned surgeon, medical educator, and civic leader who revolutionized healthcare equity and surgical training in Georgia. As chief of surgery at Grady Memorial Hospital's Hughes Spalding Pavilion and the first Black faculty member at Emory University School of Medicine, he established Georgia's first accredited surgical training for Black physicians.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, on August 18, 1916, Asa Greenwood Yancey Sr. was the son of prominent educator Arthur H. Yancey. He attended Morehouse College, graduating with honors in 1937 with a bachelor of science degree. Pursuing medicine, Yancey earned his medical degree from the University of Michigan Medical School in 1941. He then completed advanced surgical residencies, training under the renowned pioneer Dr. Charles Drew at Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, D.C.

During the late 1940s and 1950s, Dr. Yancey developed groundbreaking surgical techniques. He authored pioneering medical papers on surgical modifications, inventing the "Yancey modification" of the Swenson abdominoperineal pull-through procedure for congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease), which gained international recognition. In 1958, Dr. Yancey was recruited back to Atlanta to become Chief of Surgery at Grady Memorial Hospital’s Hughes Spalding Pavilion, the segregated hospital facility serving Black Atlantans.

At Hughes Spalding, Dr. Yancey established Georgia's first accredited surgical residency program for African American doctors, training generations of minority surgeons who had previously been excluded from southern medical institutions. In 1964, he made history as the first African American appointed to the faculty of Emory University School of Medicine, serving as professor of surgery and later as Medical Director of Grady Memorial Hospital from 1972 until 1989. Beyond the hospital, Yancey was elected to the Atlanta Board of Education in 1967, serving for five years to advance educational equity. He passed away in 2013 at the age of ninety-six.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr. lived and practiced in Atlanta for over five decades, desegregating medical faculty at Emory University, directing surgical care at Grady Hospital, and serving on the Atlanta Board of Education. Following his death in March 2013, a memorial service honoring his monumental contributions was held in Atlanta. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery alongside his wife Carolyn Dunbar Yancey and generations of civic leaders (Henderson 257–58). His resting place at South-View marks an extraordinary legacy of medical justice.

Name: Bazoline E. Usher
Body:
Overview:
Bazoline Estelle Usher was an influential educator, school administrator, and youth organizer who dedicated over four decades to advancing public education for African Americans in Atlanta. Serving as principal of David T. Howard High School and later Supervisor of Negro Schools during legal segregation, she broke administrative barriers and founded the city's first Black Girl Scout troops.

Life and Contributions:
Born on December 26, 1885, in Walnut Grove, Georgia, Bazoline Estelle Usher moved to Atlanta to pursue higher education at Atlanta University. She earned her normal school teaching credential in 1906, followed by a bachelor of arts degree in 1911 and a master of arts degree in education in 1937. Usher began teaching in 1906 at Atlanta University’s laboratory school and later joined the faculty of Booker T. Washington High School.

In 1929, Usher made history when she was appointed principal of David T. Howard Junior High School (later David T. Howard High School), guiding faculty and students with distinction during challenging economic years. In 1943, she was named Supervisor of Negro Schools for the Atlanta Public School System, the highest administrative post held by an African American woman in the district at the time. For eleven years, Usher oversaw curriculum standards, mentored hundreds of Black teachers, and fought for improved facilities across Atlanta's segregated schools until her retirement in 1954.

Usher was also an ardent champion of youth empowerment. In 1943, when African American girls were excluded from mainstream scouting, she organized the first Girl Scout troops for Black girls in Atlanta, founding District V of the Northwest Georgia Girl Scout Council and serving as its commissioner for nearly a decade. She was an active member of First Congregational Church and numerous civic associations. Living to the extraordinary age of 106, Usher passed away on February 8, 1992, honored statewide as a pioneer of Georgia education.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Bazoline E. Usher spent over eight decades in Atlanta shaping public instruction, supervising the city's Black schools, and establishing Girl Scout troops for Black youth. When she passed away in Atlanta in February 1992 at age 106, civic leaders across Georgia commemorated her monumental service. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests among her fellow educators and community builders (Henderson 247; Georgia Women of Achievement). Her grave at South-View honors more than a century of educational leadership and youth advocacy.

Name: Benjamin Elijah Mays
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Benjamin Elijah Mays was an internationally renowned educator, theologian, author, and civil rights visionary who served as the sixth president of Morehouse College. Revered as the intellectual and spiritual mentor to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Mays articulated the philosophical foundations of nonviolent resistance, elevating Morehouse into a world-class center of African American leadership and academic excellence.

Life and Contributions:
Born into poverty on August 1, 1894, in Epworth, South Carolina, to formerly enslaved parents Hezekiah and Louvenia Mays, Benjamin Elijah Mays pursued higher education with fierce resolve. He graduated as valedictorian from Bates College in Maine in 1920, earned a master's degree in 1925, and completed his doctorate in religion from the University of Chicago in 1935. After serving as dean of the Howard University School of Religion, Mays was appointed president of Morehouse College in Atlanta on August 1, 1940.

Over his twenty-seven-year tenure until 1967, Mays transformed Morehouse College. He upgraded institutional finances, recruited top-tier scholars, and established rigorous intellectual standards. In his Tuesday morning chapel addresses, Mays challenged students to attain excellence and confront racial injustice without hatred. He formed a profound, life-shaping mentorship with young Martin Luther King Jr., who arrived at Morehouse in 1944. Mays's theological integration of Christian ethics and nonviolent direct action directly molded King's philosophy.

Following King's assassination in April 1968, Mays delivered the eulogy at King's funeral in Atlanta, honoring his student's prophetic leadership before more than 100,000 mourners. In 1969, Mays was elected to the Atlanta Board of Education, serving as its first African American president from 1970 to 1981, guiding the district through difficult school desegregation compromises. Mays authored foundational texts, including *The Negro's God as Reflected in His Literature* and his autobiography *Born to Rebel*, before passing away on March 28, 1984.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. Benjamin Elijah Mays lived in Atlanta for more than four decades, shaping higher education at Morehouse College and leading the Atlanta Board of Education through court-ordered desegregation. When Mays passed away on March 28, 1984, he was initially laid to rest at historic South-View Cemetery, resting alongside fellow educators and civil rights colleagues (Henderson 6; [Royster and Mehta](https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/)). In 1995, his remains were reinterred on the Morehouse College campus alongside his wife Sadie, permanently honoring his institutional legacy.

Name: Benjamin J. Davis Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Benjamin Jefferson Davis Sr. was an influential newspaper publisher, fraternal leader, and Republican national committeeman who helped build Sweet Auburn into a center of Black economic self-determination. As Grand Secretary of the Odd Fellows of Georgia, he founded the *Atlanta Independent* and oversaw construction of the historic Odd Fellows Building and Auditorium in 1912–1913.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on May 27, 1870, in Dawson, Terrell County, Georgia, Benjamin J. Davis Sr. attended Atlanta University. At age seventeen, he joined the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, quickly demonstrating exceptional organizational and financial acumen. Rising to the post of District Grand Secretary, Davis spearheaded a period of unprecedented expansion, guiding the Georgia Odd Fellows to become the wealthiest and largest Black fraternal order in the United States, with tens of thousands of members and over $1 million in assets.

In 1903, Davis established the *Atlanta Independent*, an influential weekly newspaper that served as the official voice of the Odd Fellows and a major platform for Black political debate across the South. Davis utilized the paper to condemn lynching, demand voting rights, and champion commercial enterprise. Under his leadership, the Odd Fellows established mandatory death benefit funds ($300 to $500) to ensure financial protection for surviving widows and orphans.

In 1912, Davis led the construction of the six-story Odd Fellows Building on Auburn Avenue, followed in 1913 by an adjacent 1,300-seat auditorium and roof garden. The complex provided professional suites for Black physicians, lawyers, and business owners, anchoring Sweet Auburn. A close political ally of Booker T. Washington, Davis served as a Georgia delegate and committeeman in the Republican National Committee. He continued his publishing and fraternal work until his death on October 22, 1945.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Benjamin J. Davis Sr. spent over forty years in Atlanta building the commercial and physical landscape of Sweet Auburn, constructing the Odd Fellows Building and publishing the *Atlanta Independent*. When Davis died on October 22, 1945, civic leaders and fraternal lodges across Georgia paid him tribute. Davis was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow Odd Fellows and business pioneers (Henderson 104, 193). His resting place at South-View commemorates a towering architect of Black business enterprise.

Name: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner
Body:
Overview:
Bishop Henry McNeal Turner was a towering African Methodist Episcopal prelate, Union Army chaplain, Georgia Reconstruction legislator, orator, and civil rights activist. After helping draft Georgia's 1868 constitution and resisting illegal legislative expulsion, Turner organized Black churches and schools across the state, advocated for armed self-defense during the escalating racial crises of 1906, and championed institutional self-reliance and Black citizenship.

Life and Contributions:
Born free on February 1, 1834, near Newberry, South Carolina, Henry McNeal Turner overcame antebellum barriers by teaching himself to read and write and independently studying theology, law, and history. Licensed to preach in the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1853, he later transferred to the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church and gained national prominence in Washington, D.C. In 1863, President Abraham Lincoln appointed Turner chaplain of the 1st United States Colored Troops, making him the first Black chaplain in U.S. military history.

Assigned to Georgia by the AME Church in 1865, Turner mobilized freedpeople across the state, establishing dozens of churches and schools that served as community centers and civic forums. In 1867, he helped organize the Georgia Republican Party and was elected as a delegate to the 1868 state constitutional convention, securing provisions for Black male suffrage and public education. Elected to the Georgia House of Representatives that same year, Turner and thirty-two fellow Black legislators were unconstitutionally expelled by white politicians in September 1868. Turner delivered an immortal address on the legislative floor, proclaiming: "Am I a man? If I am such, I claim the rights of a man." The legislators were reinstated in 1870.

Elected the twelfth bishop of the AME Church in 1880, Turner oversaw church expansion, established conferences across West and South Africa, and published influential religious periodicals. Facing Jim Crow disenfranchisement and mob terror, Turner rejected racial appeasement, championing Black nationalism, emigration to Africa, and armed self-defense. In 1906, as racial violence escalated in Atlanta, Turner advised African Americans to obtain firearms to protect their homes and families. He continued his theological writing and public advocacy in Atlanta until his death on May 8, 1915, remembered as one of the most prophetic figures in American religious and political history.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Bishop Henry McNeal Turner made Atlanta the center of his ministerial, publishing, and political leadership for decades, expanding the AME Church, mobilizing Black political participation, and confronting white supremacy. When Turner died in May 1915, more than 25,000 mourners participated in his funeral cortege through the streets of Atlanta. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where an impressive monument marks his gravesite (Henderson 134–35). His resting place connects South-View directly to Georgia's Reconstruction legislature, early civil rights struggles, and the enduring fight for African American liberation.

Name: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey
Body:
Overview:
Carolyn Dunbar Yancey was an educator, civic leader, and public servant who broke historic barriers in Georgia’s educational governance. A dedicated advocate for urban instruction and community welfare, she served on the Atlanta Board of Education before becoming the first African American woman appointed to the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia in 1985.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Detroit, Michigan, in 1921, Carolyn Dunbar was the daughter of Henry Steward Dunbar, a prominent executive with the YMCA, and Annie Louise Dunbar. Raised in a household deeply committed to education, community service, and Christian fellowship, she pursued higher education, earning a bachelor’s degree in education and launching her career as a classroom teacher. In 1944, she married Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr., a talented young surgeon who trained under Dr. Charles Drew.

In 1958, the Yancey family relocated to Atlanta when Dr. Yancey was appointed Chief of Surgery at Grady Memorial Hospital's Hughes Spalding Pavilion. In Atlanta, Yancey quickly immersed herself in civic advancement, child welfare, and educational equity. She served on numerous community boards, including the Atlanta Urban League, the Links, and the YWCA, advocating tirelessly for enhanced resources in underserved Black schools.

In 1982, Yancey was elected to the Atlanta Board of Education, where she worked to improve educational standards, support teachers, and modernize classroom facilities across the city. Her exceptional administrative competence and civic leadership led Georgia Governor Joe Frank Harris to appoint her in 1985 to the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, marking a historic breakthrough as she became the first Black woman to serve on the statewide governing body. She served on the Board of Regents with distinction for seven years, championing access to higher education for minority students until her passing on December 23, 2010.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Carolyn Dunbar Yancey spent over five decades in Atlanta advancing public education on the Atlanta Board of Education and statewide higher education through the Board of Regents. Following her death on December 23, 2010, at the age of eighty-nine, her civic contributions were celebrated across Georgia. Yancey was interred at South-View Cemetery beside her husband, Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr. (Henderson 257–58; [Atlanta History Center](https://album.atlantahistorycenter.com/digital/collection/p17222coll55)). Her grave at South-View honors a pioneer who transformed educational opportunities across the state.

Name: Carrie Cunningham
Body:
Overview:
Carrie Cunningham, affectionately known throughout the city as "Mama" Cunningham, was a pioneering entrepreneur, club owner, and hospitality leader on Sweet Auburn. By establishing the legendary Royal Peacock nightclub and the Royal Hotel, Cunningham created premier, dignified spaces for African American musicians, celebrities, and travelers during the height of Jim Crow segregation.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Georgia in 1890, Carrie Cunningham emerged during the early twentieth century as one of Atlanta's most shrewd and daring businesswomen. In an era when Black entrepreneurs—particularly women—faced immense financial barriers and racial segregation, Cunningham accumulated capital through tireless enterprise, initially operating rooming houses, restaurants, and small hospitality establishments that served the Black community.

In 1948, Cunningham made a transformative commercial investment by acquiring the Top Hat Club on Auburn Avenue, which had been founded in the late 1930s. She completely renovated and rebranded the venue as the Royal Peacock, outfitting it with elegant velvet draperies, tiered booths, and a polished dance floor. Under her management, the Royal Peacock became known as the "Club Beautiful of the South." It served as an indispensable venue on the national "Chitlin' Circuit," hosting legendary performers including Ray Charles, Aretha Franklin, James Brown, Sam Cooke, Little Richard, and B.B. King.

Recognizing that Black entertainers and tourists were barred from downtown Atlanta’s white-owned hotels, Cunningham expanded her commercial holdings in 1949 by purchasing the McKay Hotel on Auburn Avenue, renovating it into the Royal Hotel. The hotel provided luxurious, safe, and dignified accommodations for visiting performers, civil rights leaders, and travelers. Cunningham operated her enterprises with motherly care and firm discipline, mentoring young employees and investing profits back into Sweet Auburn until her passing in 1973.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Carrie Cunningham spent decades anchoring the nightlife, hospitality, and commercial vibrancy of Sweet Auburn in Atlanta. Her Royal Peacock and Royal Hotel provided vital sanctuary and prestige for Black travelers and artists during Jim Crow. When Cunningham passed away in Atlanta in 1973, she was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests among the business pioneers who built Sweet Auburn into a national cultural landmark (Henderson 200). Her resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary businesswoman of the jazz and rhythm-and-blues era.

Name: Charles H. Morgan
Body:
Overview:
Charles H. Morgan was an artisan carriage trimmer, grocer, church founder, and founding board member of South-View Cemetery. Born into slavery, Morgan achieved acclaim for his craftsmanship, built a thriving grocery on Wheat Street, and purchased South-View’s very first capital shares in 1886, becoming the first founder laid to rest on the cemetery’s grounds.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in South Carolina, Charles H. Morgan’s exact birth date was not preserved in nineteenth-century census records. Following the Civil War and the abolition of slavery, Morgan migrated to Atlanta, applying his specialized artisan training as a master carriage trimmer. Morgan’s exceptional leathercraft, upholstery, and fine detail work for high-end horse-drawn carriages earned him widespread respect across Atlanta, allowing him to accumulate independent savings.

By 1881, Morgan had channeled his artisan savings into independent commerce, opening a prosperous grocery store on Wheat Street (later renamed Auburn Avenue). Morgan was also a devoted religious and civic leader. In the late 1860s, he helped organize First Congregational Church of Atlanta, which became an intellectual and social anchor for educated African Americans. Morgan served on First Congregational’s Board of Deacons and was appointed to the Board of Trustees of Atlanta University.

Morgan’s prominence in Atlanta society was celebrated in April 1883, when his only daughter, Rebecca, married master tailor John C. "Jack" Huggins in a lavish wedding reported in the *Atlanta Constitution* as a milestone of elite Black society. In early 1886, Morgan joined five fellow Black leaders to petition the city council for a cemetery charter to combat municipal grave desecrations. Demonstrating supreme confidence in the venture, Morgan purchased South-View's first three capital shares. Tragically, just three days after buying the stock, Morgan died suddenly in December 1886.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Charles H. Morgan lived and operated his businesses in Atlanta, co-founding First Congregational Church, supporting Atlanta University, and organizing South-View Cemetery. When Morgan passed away unexpectedly in December 1886, three days after purchasing South-View's very first shares, he was buried at South-View Cemetery on December 17, 1886 (Henderson 18). He holds the historic distinction of being the first founder laid to rest on the cemetery grounds, consecrating the sanctuary he helped establish.

Name: Clara A. Howard
Body:
Overview:
Clara A. Howard was a missionary, educator, and leader who graduated in Spelman Baptist Seminary’s historic first class of 1887. For nine years, she served as a missionary and educator in the Congo before returning to Atlanta, where she served for decades as a beloved housemother and administrator at Spelman College.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Greenville, Georgia, on January 23, 1866, Clara Ann Howard relocated to Atlanta as a child following emancipation. In 1881, when Sophia B. Packard and Harriet E. Giles opened the Atlanta Baptist Female Seminary (later Spelman College) in the basement of Friendship Baptist Church, Howard enrolled as one of its earliest pupils. Demonstrating intellectual excellence, she graduated in 1887 in Spelman’s historic first graduating class.

Deeply committed to international Christian service, Howard felt a calling to African missionary work. In 1890, sponsored by the Woman's American Baptist Home Mission Society, Howard joined her Spelman classmate Nora Gordon at the Lukunga mission station in the Congo Free State. For nine years, Howard ran a school for more than one hundred Congolese children, teaching literacy, hygiene, and domestic sciences, while training local teachers. Her missionary dedication was cut short by repeated bouts of severe malaria, forcing her return to the United States in 1899 accompanied by a young Congolese student, Flora Zeto Malekebu, whom she raised and educated at Spelman.

Upon returning to Atlanta, Howard served Spelman College for nearly three decades as a residence hall director, advisor, and alumni secretary. Her gentle guidance and high standards shaped generations of young Black women. In recognition of her service, Spelman College named Howard-Harreld Hall partly in her honor. She passed away in Atlanta on October 9, 1935.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Clara A. Howard was a foundational figure in Atlanta’s educational history, graduating in Spelman College’s first class of 1887 and serving on its staff for decades. When Howard died on October 9, 1935, Spelman faculty, students, and alumnae gathered to honor her lifetime of service. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests near her fellow Congo missionary Nora Gordon and adopted daughter Flora Zeto Malekebu (Henderson 213; Historic South-View Preservation Foundation). Her resting place at South-View preserves Spelman's global missionary legacy.

Name: Clayton R. Yates
Body:
Overview:
Clayton Russell Yates Sr. was a prominent business executive, chairman of Citizens Trust Bank, co-founder of the Yates & Milton drugstore chain, and president of the South-View Cemetery Association. A trailblazer in corporate and hospital governance, Yates modernized Black commercial enterprise along Sweet Auburn and directed South-View’s diamond jubilee.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Sparta, Georgia, Clayton Russell Yates Sr. relocated to Atlanta to attend Morehouse College, where he excelled in business administration and economics. After graduating, Yates established himself as one of Black Atlanta’s most versatile commercial organizers. In the 1920s, partnering with fellow Morehouse alumnus and economist Lorimer D. Milton, Yates opened the first Yates & Milton drugstore on Auburn Avenue, which expanded into a renowned chain of retail pharmacies.

The Yates & Milton pharmacies served as vital commercial and social hubs for Sweet Auburn. During the student sit-ins of the 1960s, the basement of their flagship drugstore served as a secure, clandestine meeting headquarters for student organizers of the Atlanta Student Movement. Beyond retail pharmacology, Yates was an influential financial executive. He served for decades as chairman of the Board of Directors of Citizens Trust Bank, guiding the bank to become the first Black-owned financial institution in the nation to join the Federal Reserve System.

Yates also broke racial barriers in public service, becoming the first African American appointed to the Fulton-DeKalb Hospital Authority, which governed Grady Memorial Hospital. Additionally, he held executive directorships with Southeastern Fidelity Fire Insurance Company and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan. In 1961, when South-View Cemetery celebrated its 75th anniversary, Yates was serving as president of the South-View Cemetery Association, directing corporate modernization and establishing its perpetual care trust fund at Citizens Trust Bank. Yates passed away in 1977.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Clayton R. Yates spent his entire career building commerce and civic institutions in Atlanta, leading Citizens Trust Bank and serving as president of the South-View Cemetery Association during its diamond jubilee in 1961. Following his death in 1977, Yates was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among his fellow banking partners and civic associates (Henderson 4, 33, 258). His grave at South-View honors a commercial giant who stewarded the cemetery's corporate and physical legacy.

Name: Clem Rhodes
Body:
Overview:
Clem Rhodes was an African American citizen of Atlanta who was murdered by armed white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal assault reflects the catastrophic violence inflicted on Black residents during four days of mob terror, an atrocity that left dozens dead and traumatized Black communities across the South.

Life and Contributions:
Clem Rhodes was born in Georgia during the late nineteenth century and lived in Atlanta at the turn of the twentieth century. Earning his livelihood through daily industry in the city's expanding urban economy, Rhodes was part of Atlanta's hardworking African American community that sought economic self-reliance and community stability in the face of Jim Crow restrictions.

During the late summer of 1906, sensationalized newspaper reports in local white publications maliciously alleged a wave of assaults by Black men on white women. On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, white mobs numbering in the thousands gathered in downtown Atlanta, launching violent assaults against Black laborers, pedestrians, and passengers on streetcars. The mob violence quickly escalated from downtown thoroughfares into residential neighborhoods, continuing across multiple days.

Rhodes was caught in the path of the mob during the height of the violence on September 22. Armed rioters attacked him with blunt weapons and firearms, inflicting catastrophic injuries from which he died. For decades, the identities of many victims were excluded from public civic memory until historical investigations by organizations like the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition documented Rhodes’s death, ensuring his name and tragic fate were recovered for history.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Clem Rhodes lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the immediate aftermath of the tragedy, municipal undertakers and community families brought the bodies of African American victims to South-View Cemetery for dignified Christian burial, as municipal facilities often neglected Black victims (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View served as an indispensable sanctuary of honor and remembrance for the community.

Name: Curtis Walker
Body:
Overview:
Curtis Walker was an industrious thirteen-year-old African American youth from Atlanta who was abducted and murdered in February 1981 during the Atlanta Child Murders crisis. His heartbreaking death intensified the grief and vulnerability felt by working-class families across the city, spurring community mobilizations to protect neighborhood youth from racial and criminal terror.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1967 in Atlanta, Georgia, Curtis Walker was raised by his family in a working-class neighborhood. Known for his mature work ethic and devotion to his relatives, thirteen-year-old Curtis took on odd jobs after school and on weekends, running errands, helping neighbors, and washing cars to contribute to his family's household income. In early 1981, fear hung heavily over Black neighborhoods across Atlanta, as dozens of young boys and teenagers had vanished over the preceding eighteen months.

On February 19, 1981, Curtis left home in southwest Atlanta to look for odd jobs and run an errand. He never returned. His sudden disappearance sent his family into frantic searches across neighborhood streets and vacant lots. Tragically, on March 6, 1981, searchers discovered Curtis’s body in the South River near the DeKalb-Rockdale county line. Medical examiners determined that he had suffered fatal asphyxiation.

Curtis’s death dealt an agonizing blow to a city already overwhelmed with grief. Local mothers and civic organizers, including the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP), mobilized national support, organizing prayer vigils, neighborhood youth patrols, and rallies demanding aggressive action from city officials. Curtis’s case became a central priority for the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force and federal investigators, remaining an enduring symbol of a tragic era in Atlanta's modern history.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Curtis Walker lived in Atlanta and lost his life in the metropolitan area during the harrowing 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Following the discovery of his remains, his grieving family and Atlanta community members held memorial services to honor his young life. Curtis was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where multiple youth victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were provided sacred, permanent resting places (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His grave at South-View connects the cemetery to Atlanta's collective period of communal mourning and remembrance.

Name: David T. Howard
Body:
Overview:
David Tobias Howard was a pioneer mortician, bank founder, philanthropist, and one of Atlanta’s first African American millionaires. Born into slavery, Howard built a premier funeral home under the motto "Treat Everyone Right," co-founded Citizens Trust Bank, and donated prime real estate to build public schools for Black children. Renowned for his compassionate service during Atlanta's darkest crises, Howard provided dignified burials during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre and restored sanctity to graves following the 1922 casket scandal.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on December 10, 1849, on a plantation in Knoxville, Crawford County, Georgia, David Tobias Howard was emancipated following the Civil War. Moving to Atlanta, he taught himself to read and write while working in the railroad repair shops of R. C. Robson and later as a Pullman porter. Practicing disciplined thrift, Howard saved over $1,000, which he combined with a $200 legacy from Robson in 1882 to establish an undertaking business in Atlanta in 1883.

Howard attended Cincinnati’s Clarke School of Embalming, graduating in 1890 as Georgia's first formally trained Black mortician. Operating under the golden rule of "Treat Everyone Right," Howard's funeral business flourished into one of the largest in the South, gaining a reputation for flawless professionalism, integrity, and charitable generosity. In 1930, he opened a state-of-the-art mortuary complex at 71 Piedmont Avenue featuring the first pipe organ installed in a Georgia funeral home. Howard was renowned for conducting pauper burials with the same dignity and fine carriages afforded the wealthiest patrons.

Howard served Atlanta through some of its most harrowing historical trials. During the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, when white mobs roamed the streets attacking Black citizens, Howard was summoned to south Atlanta to recover the body of a riot casualty; upon examination, Howard discovered the deceased man was actually white, his face intentionally blackened with polish to incite anti-Black hysteria. During the 1922 South-View casket theft scandal, when dishonest undertaker Samuel F. Ware was arrested for disinterring coffins, the cemetery association and community entrusted Howard with the solemn task of reinterring the desecrated remains in new caskets with full Christian dignity.

Howard invested his mortuary profits into banking and community welfare. In 1921, he co-founded Citizens Trust Bank on Auburn Avenue, serving on its board of directors. A passionate civic builder and advocate for Black youth, Howard funded church construction and donated land on Houston Street in the Old Fourth Ward to the city of Atlanta to construct an elementary and high school for African American children. The David T. Howard School opened in 1923, educating generations of leaders including Martin Luther King Jr., Maynard Jackson, and Walt Frazier. He remained active in community charities, fraternal organizations, and the Atlanta Negro Voters League until his passing on April 19, 1935, revered as a founding father of Sweet Auburn.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
David T. Howard made Atlanta the lifelong center of his groundbreaking mortuary and philanthropic enterprises for over fifty years. At South-View Cemetery, Howard conducted thousands of funeral processions over five decades, securing dignified burials for leaders and paupers alike (Henderson 45–46, 50). He also intervened in times of crisis, personally overseeing the reinterment of desecrated graves following the 1922 casket scandal (Henderson 45, 51). When Howard died in April 1935, his massive funeral concluded at South-View Cemetery, where he was interred in his prominent family mausoleum. His resting place at South-View honors a founding titan of Black Atlanta commerce and education, permanently linking his name to the cemetery’s history of honor and community service.

Name: Dennis Taylor Hubert
Body:
Overview:
Dennis Taylor Hubert was an eighteen-year-old divinity student at Morehouse College whose brutal murder by white vigilantes on an Atlanta playground in June 1930 sparked historic Black resistance. The courageous organizing of Atlanta's Black community resulted in the rare conviction of white perpetrators, transforming tragedy into a watershed civil rights victory.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1911 into one of Georgia’s most distinguished African American families, Dennis Taylor Hubert was the son of Rev. Giles J. Hubert, a prominent Baptist minister, and Pearl Parks Hubert, principal of Crogman School in Atlanta's Pittsburgh neighborhood. His uncle, Rev. Dr. Charles D. Hubert, served as director of Morehouse College’s School of Religion and later as acting president of Morehouse. Dennis attended local schools and enrolled at Morehouse College as a sophomore divinity student, working part-time as a personal driver for Morehouse president John Hope.

On Sunday afternoon, June 15, 1930, while playing with friends on the grounds of Crogman School, Hubert was confronted by seven white men who falsely claimed he had made an insulting remark to a white woman. One of the men shot Hubert dead on the playground. When authorities denied bail to the suspects, white racists retaliated by burning the Hubert family home to the ground and tear-gassing a fundraising service at a local Black church.

Refusing to be intimidated, Black Atlantans united under the leadership of A.T. Walden and the NAACP, demanding vigorous prosecution. In an extraordinary legal triumph during Jim Crow, juries convicted the shooter of voluntary manslaughter and six companions as accessories. In 2025, Morehouse College honored his legacy by conferring upon him a posthumous Bachelor of Arts degree.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dennis Taylor Hubert was born, raised, and educated in Atlanta, where his murder on the Crogman School playground galvanized the entire city against racial terror. Following his death in June 1930, Hubert was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in his family plot. In 2022, a memorial marker was erected at South-View in his honor through the efforts of Morehouse College and the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition (Henderson 214; [Killing of Dennis Hubert](https://crrjarchive.org/incidents/196); [Morehouse College Student Given Degree](https://www.ajc.com/education/morehouse-college-student-given-degree-95-years-after-his-lynching/LA7YEFCXTBF5FDEH4AAGEW52UQ/)). His resting place at South-View commemorates a pivotal turning point in Georgia civil rights history.

Name: Dinah Watts Pace
Body:
Overview:
Dinah Watts Pace was an educator, humanitarian, and pioneer child advocate who established one of Georgia's earliest orphanages and industrial schools for African American children. Born into slavery, Pace overcame poverty to graduate from Atlanta University and dedicate forty-three years to providing shelter, education, and vocational training to over 700 vulnerable youth.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Athens, Georgia, in January 1853, Dinah Watts Pace moved to Atlanta with her family following the Civil War. Demonstrating an intense thirst for knowledge, Pace enrolled at Storrs School and subsequently entered Atlanta University, graduating from its normal course in 1883. She began her career teaching in rural Georgia public schools, witnessing firsthand the destitution of orphaned and neglected Black children who had no social safety net under Jim Crow.

In 1884, while teaching in Covington, Georgia, Pace took two neglected orphan girls into her own home, providing food, clothing, and schooling out of her modest teacher's salary. In 1890, she secured a formal state charter for the Covington Colored Orphans Home, later renamed the Reed Home and School in honor of benefactor L. O. Reed. Pace expanded the home into a self-sustaining farm and industrial school spanning more than fifty acres.

Under Pace's compassionate and disciplined direction, the school educated, housed, and trained more than seven hundred African American boys and girls over four decades. Students learned academic curricula alongside farming, carpentry, blacksmithing, sewing, and culinary arts, equipping them with essential skills for self-sufficiency. Pace traveled extensively, speaking before church conferences and civic clubs to raise operating funds. She continued directing the institution until her death on January 25, 1933, revered throughout Georgia as "Mother Pace."

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dinah Watts Pace was educated in Atlanta at Atlanta University, and her humanitarian school maintained vital fundraising and institutional partnerships with Atlanta churches and civic societies. Following her death on January 25, 1933, in Covington, her remains were brought to Atlanta for memorial services. Pace was interred at South-View Cemetery, where she rests alongside generations of educators, missionaries, and child welfare advocates (Henderson 233). Her grave at South-View honors an extraordinary life of selfless service to Georgia’s children.

Name: Essie Whitman
Body:
Overview:
Essie Whitman was an acclaimed contralto vocalist, comedic performer, and costume designer who starred in the legendary Whitman Sisters vaudeville troupe. Alongside her sisters, she headlined the nation's premier African American theatrical circuits for nearly three decades, designing dazzling stage costumes and creating enduring musical entertainment that captivated audiences from coast to coast.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1882 in Kansas, Essie Whitman was the daughter of Rev. Albery Allson Whitman, an esteemed African Methodist Episcopal minister and poet, and Caddie Whitman. Raised in an intellectually stimulating and musical family, Essie began performing sacred hymns and traditional spirituals with her sisters—Mabel, Alberta, and Alice—at church revivals and Chautauqua programs throughout the American Midwest during the late 1890s.

Around 1899, Essie and her elder sister Mabel launched their secular stage career as the Danzette Sisters, performing songs and dances that quickly gained regional acclaim. As the other sisters joined them, they incorporated the company as the Whitman Sisters Revue. Within the troupe, Essie distinguished herself as a versatile performer with a rich, powerful contralto singing voice and impeccable comedic timing. She frequently performed comic routines and vocal duets that served as major highlights of the show.

In addition to her stage performances, Essie served as the principal costume designer and wardrobe mistress for the company. She designed and tailored elaborate, sophisticated gowns, dance costumes, and tuxedos for a troupe that expanded to include more than forty dancers, musicians, and comedians. Her striking sartorial designs set fashion standards across Black vaudeville. Essie retired from the touring stage in 1926, shifting her focus to church music, civic endeavors, and supporting the family's business investments until her passing in 1963.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Essie Whitman and the Whitman Sisters established deep institutional and personal ties to Atlanta, using the city as their central touring hub, rehearsal base, and eventual retirement residence. When Essie passed away in 1963, she was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in the Whitman family plot, where her sisters Mabel, Alberta, and Alice are also interred (Henderson 252). Her burial at South-View connects the historic grounds to the pioneering golden age of African American theater and stage craft.
