Name: Eula Benning
Body:
Overview:
Eula Benning was a pioneering public health nursing supervisor, healthcare educator, and professional organizer who transformed nursing in Atlanta and Georgia. Serving as a clinical supervisor in Fulton County, she founded the Atlanta School for Practical Nurse Education in 1963 and led the historic integration of Georgia’s professional nursing associations.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Georgia, Eula Benning dedicated her life to expanding community healthcare, clinical training, and professional recognition for African American nurses. She earned her nursing diploma from the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses and completed advanced academic degrees in public health and nursing education at New York University.

Returning to Atlanta, Benning joined the Fulton County Department of Public Health, rising to become one of the city's foremost public health nursing supervisors. She directed field clinics, maternal and infant health programs, and disease prevention initiatives across Atlanta’s segregated Black neighborhoods. Benning recognized that severe shortages of trained nurses and racial exclusion from white vocational schools limited healthcare delivery and economic advancement for Black women.

In 1963, Benning addressed this critical need by founding the Atlanta School for Practical Nurse Education, establishing an accredited clinical and classroom curriculum that trained hundreds of licensed practical nurses. Concurrently, Benning was a courageous leader in professional civil rights. During the early 1960s, she spearheaded the difficult negotiations that united Georgia's segregated Black and white nurses' associations, successfully dissolving the color barrier in the state's professional nursing body. Honored by her peers through the establishment of the Eula Benning Club, she continued mentoring public health professionals until her death in 1964.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Eula Benning spent her career serving the healthcare needs of Atlanta and Fulton County, supervising public health clinics, training practical nurses, and integrating professional nursing statewide. Following her death in 1964, community leaders and colleagues celebrated her pioneering service. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests alongside her mentor Ludie Clay Andrews and fellow healthcare trailblazers (Henderson 174). Her resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary champion of public health and professional equality.

Name: Frank Fambro
Body:
Overview:
Frank Fambro was an African American laborer from Atlanta who was murdered by armed white mobs during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His violent death illustrates the indiscriminate brutality unleashed against working-class Black citizens during seventy-two hours of mob violence that devastated Black neighborhoods and damaged the city’s national standing.

Life and Contributions:
Frank Fambro was an African American laborer living and working in Atlanta at the turn of the twentieth century. Like thousands of Black citizens during this period, Fambro earned his livelihood through manual labor in Atlanta's expanding commercial and industrial centers, seeking to provide for his family within the strictures of legal segregation.

In late September 1906, political demagoguery surrounding the Georgia gubernatorial campaign, combined with sensationalized, irresponsible headlines in local white daily newspapers, whipped racial hostility into hysteria. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys took control of downtown Atlanta, launching savage assaults against Black workers, streetcar patrons, and pedestrians. Over the next three days, roving armed vigilantes invaded residential Black communities and commercial districts.

Fambro was ambushed and killed by mob members during the height of the violent outbreak. His death certificate and contemporary reports documented that he succumbed to severe traumatic injuries. For over a century, Fambro’s death remained largely unacknowledged in official city histories until rigorous archival research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project restored his memory, identifying him as an innocent victim of racial violence.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Frank Fambro was an Atlanta laborer whose life was violently taken during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the violence, when city facilities and municipal cemeteries neglected Black casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds as a sacred haven, providing solemn Christian burials for the massacre victims (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Frank Smith
Body:
Overview:
Frank Smith was a nineteen-year-old African American commercial bicycle messenger for Western Union whose brutal murder by a white mob on September 22, 1906, became one of the most widely documented tragedies of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His grave at South-View Cemetery features one of only two inscribed headstones marking victims identified immediately following the 1906 violence, standing as a permanent, sacred monument to the victims of southern racial terror.

Life and Contributions:
Born around 1887 in Georgia, Frank Smith grew up in Atlanta during the rise of legal segregation. As a young man of nineteen, Smith secured employment as a commercial bicycle courier for the Western Union Telegraph Company in downtown Atlanta. In this essential role, Smith delivered time-sensitive commercial telegrams and personal messages across the central business district, known for his promptness, reliability, and diligence as he cycled along the busy streets of Peachtree, Pryor, and Decatur.

On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, Smith was diligently carrying out his courier deliveries when an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, incited by fabricated newspaper reports. As violence erupted near Five Points, rioters began attacking any African American in sight. While crossing the Forsyth Street bridge above the downtown railway tracks, Smith was surrounded by mob members. Despite having no involvement in any dispute, he was beaten with stones, stabbed repeatedly, and hurled over the bridge railing onto the railroad tracks below, succumbing to catastrophic injuries.

Eyewitnesses and friends lamented that Smith was an innocent, hardworking youth targeted solely because of his race. His family recovered his body from the county morgue, arranging a solemn funeral that moved the community. Over a century later, Smith’s story was revitalized through the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights, providing historical truth and dignity to his memory.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Frank Smith lived and labored in downtown Atlanta until his murder on the Forsyth Street bridge on September 22, 1906. Following the massacre, his family secured a plot and interred his remains at South-View Cemetery. His headstone—inscribed with his name, age, and date of death—remains one of only two marked headstones erected for 1906 massacre victims, serving as a solemn focal point for annual community pilgrimages, historical tours, and civil rights education (Henderson 118–19; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). His grave at South-View preserves the memory of youth lost to racial violence.

Name: Fred C. Bennette Jr.
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr. was an influential civil rights strategist, youth organizer, and trusted aide to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Known as the "Commandante," Bennette led student sit-ins during the Atlanta Student Movement, directed voter registration and Operation Breadbasket for the SCLC, and advised civic leaders across Georgia.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, on September 15, 1928, Fred C. Bennette Jr. was educated in the city's public schools and attended Morris Brown College, graduating with a bachelor's degree in 1953. An ordained minister, Bennette brought fierce strategic acumen, charisma, and discipline to the freedom movement.

In 1960, when the Atlanta Student Movement launched citywide lunch counter sit-ins, Bennette served as a principal adult advisor and frontline organizer, directing the pivotal demonstrations at Rich’s Department Store that challenged downtown commercial segregation. Impressed by his organizational prowess, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. recruited Bennette to the senior executive staff of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). Bennette directed the SCLC's voter registration campaigns across the Deep South, registering tens of thousands of Black voters. He also directed the Atlanta chapter of Operation Breadbasket, utilizing targeted consumer boycotts to compel corporations to hire Black workers and stock products from Black-owned businesses.

Bennette was a trusted confidant and security coordinator for Dr. King, accompanying him on major civil rights marches. Following Dr. King's assassination in 1968, Bennette served as director of security and physical facilities for the King Center. He also served as a senior advisor to Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter and Atlanta Mayor Andrew Young, assisting with urban development and community relations until his passing on May 24, 1994.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr. lived and organized in Atlanta throughout his distinguished career, directing the Rich's sit-ins, leading SCLC operations, and counseling Atlanta mayors. Following his death in May 1994, he was interred at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 174). His gravestone at South-View carries the title "Commandante," accompanied by Ambassador Andrew Young’s heartfelt epitaph: "You were always there when Martin needed you." His resting place connects South-View directly to the inner circle of the modern civil rights movement.

Name: Freddye Scarborough Henderson
Body:
Overview:
Freddye Scarborough Henderson was a pioneer educator, fashion designer, travel industry executive, and international cultural ambassador. In 1955, she co-founded Henderson Travel Service in Atlanta, establishing the first fully accredited African American-owned travel agency in the United States and opening groundbreaking global travel and tourism pathways to the African continent during segregation.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 18, 1917, in Pensacola, Florida, Freddye Scarborough pursued higher education at Hampton Institute in Virginia, graduating with a bachelor of science degree in home economics and fashion design in 1937. She subsequently completed a master’s degree in fashion merchandising and design from New York University. Henderson joined the faculty of Spelman College and later Clark College in Atlanta, teaching textiles, fashion design, and merchandising. She also authored widely read syndicated fashion columns for the *Atlanta Daily World*.

Recognizing the severe racial barriers, indignities, and physical hazards African Americans faced when attempting to travel under Jim Crow laws, Henderson and her husband James established Henderson Travel Service in Atlanta in 1955. Operating from Sweet Auburn, the agency was the first African American-owned travel agency to secure full accreditation from the Air Traffic Conference of America and the International Air Transport Association.

Henderson Travel achieved historic international acclaim by pioneering leisure and educational tourism to the African continent. In March 1957, the agency organized the historic delegation of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Coretta Scott King, and civil rights leaders to attend the independence celebrations of Ghana. Throughout her career, Henderson advised international tourism ministries, founded professional tourism associations, and introduced thousands of Black travelers to global cultural heritage. She passed away in Atlanta in 2007, celebrated as a visionary entrepreneur and cultural pioneer.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Freddye Scarborough Henderson lived in Atlanta for over six decades, teaching at Spelman and Clark colleges and building Henderson Travel Service on Sweet Auburn into an internationally acclaimed enterprise. Following her death in 2007 at age ninety, her monumental contributions to Black business and international diplomacy were honored across the city. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests alongside Atlanta’s leading entrepreneurs, educators, and civil rights pioneers (Henderson 207). Her grave at South-View honors an extraordinary global visionary.

Name: Frederick and Bennie McLendon
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Frederick Earl McLendon and Bennie Bell McLendon were prominent medical, civic, and cultural pioneers in Atlanta. For thirty-five years, they operated the McLendon Medical Clinic, providing vital healthcare to Black Atlantans, funding the Selma civil rights marchers, and courageously desegregating the Biltmore Hotel and the Fox Theatre.

Life and Contributions:
Dr. Frederick Earl McLendon and Bennie Bell McLendon formed a powerful, transformative partnership in healthcare, civil rights activism, and community philanthropy in Atlanta. Dr. McLendon earned his medical degree from Meharry Medical College, while Bennie completed her education at Spelman College and Atlanta University, mastering business and healthcare administration.

In 1946, the McLendons opened the McLendon Medical Clinic on Simpson Street in northwest Atlanta. For thirty-five years, the clinic served as a beacon of affordable, compassionate medical care for thousands of Black citizens excluded from segregated municipal facilities. Dr. McLendon provided expert clinical medicine, while Bennie McLendon served as the chief administrative director, managing medical records, pharmacy supplies, and patient finances with remarkable skill.

The McLendons were equally fearless in the civil rights struggle. During the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery voting rights march, Dr. McLendon traveled to Alabama to provide emergency medical treatment and medical supplies to wounded marchers. In Atlanta, Dr. McLendon was arrested during a direct-action demonstration challenging racial exclusion at the segregated Biltmore Hotel. Concurrently, Bennie McLendon co-founded the Atlanta Chapter of The Links, Incorporated, in 1953, and led the campaign that desegregated Metropolitan Opera performances at the historic Fox Theatre. Dr. McLendon passed away in 1981, and Bennie continued her community leadership until her death in 1995.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
The McLendons spent their entire adult lives in Atlanta, transforming community health on Simpson Street and desegregating elite cultural and commercial institutions across the city. Following Dr. McLendon's passing in 1981 and Bennie McLendon's death in 1995, both were interred at historic South-View Cemetery in their family plot (Henderson 170, 227–28, 231). Their resting places at South-View commemorate a husband-and-wife team whose combined medical and civic courage permanently dismantled segregation in Atlanta.

Name: Geneva Moton Haugabrooks
Body:
Overview:
Geneva Moton Haugabrooks was a pioneer educator, mortician, entrepreneur, and civic philanthropist who founded Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue in 1929. Defying severe economic depression and gender barriers, she built one of Atlanta’s foremost Black-owned mortuary enterprises, providing compassionate burials, emergency ambulance services, and vital philanthropic support to the Sweet Auburn community.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1887 in Georgia, Geneva Moton Haugabrooks began her professional life as an educator, teaching in rural Georgia schools and mentoring young students. Recognizing that Jim Crow laws denied African Americans equal treatment in life and dignity in death—and observing that white funeral homes refused Black decedents—she decided to enter the mortuary profession.

In 1929, with approximately $300 in personal savings during the onset of the Great Depression, Haugabrooks founded the Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue. As one of the few African American women licensed as a mortician and funeral director in Georgia, she established an enterprise renowned for exceptional elegance, compassion, and community service. During decades of municipal neglect, Haugabrooks Funeral Home maintained a 24-hour private ambulance service that transported injured and sick Black citizens when municipal ambulances refused to enter Black neighborhoods.

Beyond her funeral enterprise, Haugabrooks was an influential civic leader and benefactor. She served on the board of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home, was an active officer in the National Funeral Directors and Morticians Association, and generously financed voter registration drives led by the Atlanta Negro Voters League. She also provided financial aid and scholarships for students attending the Atlanta University Center. She directed the mortuary until her passing in 1977 at age ninety.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Geneva Moton Haugabrooks spent nearly fifty years in Atlanta anchoring the commercial, civic, and philanthropic life of Sweet Auburn. Her mortuary conducted thousands of dignified funeral processions to South-View Cemetery for Black families across the city. When Haugabrooks passed away in 1977, she was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where many of the community leaders and families she faithfully served are also interred (Henderson 208; [Digital Library of Georgia](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/geh_byd_3914)). Her resting place at South-View honors an extraordinary businesswoman and community matriarch.

Name: George Union Wilder
Body:
Overview:
George Union Wilder was a Union Army Civil War veteran, Odd Fellow, and seventy-year-old elder of south Atlanta's Brownsville community who was murdered by white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Wilder's marked grave at South-View Cemetery stands as an enduring monument to Black veterans who fought for freedom and faced racial violence.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Georgia around 1836, George Union Wilder escaped chattel bondage during the American Civil War to enlist in the United States Colored Troops (USCT). Wilder served honorably in Union blue, risking his life on the battlefield to defeat the Confederacy and secure universal emancipation. Following the war, he adopted the symbolic middle name "Union" to permanently commemorate his military service and loyalty to the nation.

Settling in Atlanta during Reconstruction, Wilder established his home in the middle-class African American community of Brownsville in south Atlanta, near Clark University and Gammon Theological Seminary. Wilder was an active fraternal leader in the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, participating in the lodge’s mutual benefit and community uplift programs. By September 1906, Wilder was seventy years old and revered as a patriarch in Brownsville.

On the night of September 24, 1906, following two days of mob violence in downtown Atlanta, armed county police and white vigilantes invaded Brownsville under the pretext of disarming Black residents. As gunfire erupted near a neighborhood store, Wilder took up his antique muzzle-loading musket to defend his home and neighbors from the invading mob. Responding officers shot Wilder down in a shed behind the store, killing him instantly. Four decades after fighting for freedom in the Civil War, Wilder was killed in his old age in a city that denied Black veterans equal protection.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
George Union Wilder lived in Atlanta's Brownsville neighborhood and was murdered during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre on September 24, 1906. Following the tragedy, he was buried at South-View Cemetery. His gravestone—inscribed "A soldier of the Civil War, was killed in the riot"—bears the three linked rings of the Odd Fellows and remains one of the few contemporary stone markers honoring a 1906 massacre victim (Bauerlein 198; Henderson 119). His resting place at South-View preserves the memory of Black military valor and civil sacrifice.

Name: George W. Graham
Body:
Overview:
George W. Graham was a Reconstruction politician, entrepreneur, master carpenter, and co-founder of South-View Cemetery. Born into slavery, Graham broke political barriers in 1871 by becoming one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council, dedicating his career to securing municipal infrastructure and dignified burial grounds for Black Atlantans.

Life and Contributions:
Born enslaved in Georgia in 1833, George W. Graham was denied formal schooling under the slave regime but acquired rigorous vocational expertise as a master carpenter. Following the Civil War and emancipation, Graham emerged as a courageous political organizer during Reconstruction. In December 1870, running as a Black Republican representing the working-class Third Ward, Graham won election to the Atlanta City Council, taking office in January 1871 alongside William Finch as the first Black aldermen in Atlanta history.

Despite intense racial hostility and public ridicule from conservative newspapers, Graham served on the city council with exceptional diligence. Assigned to the Printing and the Wells, Pumps, and Cisterns committees, he successfully secured vital municipal water lines, public pumps, and sanitation improvements for Black neighborhoods along Martin and Richmond streets. Following his council term, Graham expanded into independent enterprise, establishing a successful drayage freight service and operating a prosperous grocery business.

By 1890, his net worth approached $3,000, which included $525 in capital stock in South-View Cemetery. In early 1886, Graham joined five fellow Black leaders to petition the city council for a cemetery charter to provide dignified burials free from racial segregation. He served on South-View's founding board until his passing on September 5, 1894, honored as a true pioneer of Black Atlanta.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
George W. Graham was a trailblazing Atlanta civic leader, serving on the Atlanta City Council in 1871 and co-founding South-View Cemetery in 1886. Graham invested $525 in capital shares to ensure dignified burials for Black Atlantans excluded from equal treatment in city cemeteries. Graham lived and operated his businesses in Atlanta until his death on September 5, 1894, when he was honorably interred in South-View Cemetery (Henderson 19–20). His resting place at South-View connects the cemetery directly to the birth of Black municipal governance in Atlanta.

Name: George Washington
Body:
Overview:
George Washington was Atlanta's most respected and prolific nineteenth-century African American funeral carriage driver. Working for more than twenty years with Miller & Brady Livery, Washington drove in more Atlanta funeral processions than anyone in the city, ensuring dignified transportation to cemetery grounds for thousands of families across racial lines.

Life and Contributions:
While details of his birth and early life in enslavement remain unrecorded, George Washington became a central figure in Atlanta’s post-Civil War mortuary community. Following emancipation in 1865, Washington secured employment with Miller & Brady, one of Atlanta’s oldest and largest commercial livery stables. Over twenty years of dedicated service, Washington operated the firm's finest horse-drawn funeral coaches and carriage hacks.

Washington possessed exceptional horsemanship and quiet dignity, navigating unpaved and treacherous city roads in all weather conditions. Historical accounts documented that Washington drove in more Atlanta funeral processions than any other individual in the city, frequently conducting cortege processions across Oakland, Westview, and South-View cemeteries. Living on Wheat Street (later Auburn Avenue), Washington was an active member of Big Bethel AME Church and a trusted neighbor in the Old Fourth Ward.

When Washington passed away in 1890, his life of humble yet essential service was honored across racial lines. Liverymen throughout Atlanta donated their carriages and hearses free of charge for his funeral cortege, and prominent white funeral director H. M. Patterson donated a luxury casket, declaring that Washington’s family should not pay a single cent in recognition of his faithful service. He was mourned across the entire municipality as a beloved civic figure.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
George Washington provided essential funeral cortege transportation to South-View Cemetery from its inception in 1886 until his death in 1890, regularly escorting Black families through Atlanta's streets to their loved ones' final resting place. Following a large funeral service at Big Bethel AME Church on Auburn Avenue, Washington was interred at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 50). His resting place at South-View honors a humble artisan who faithfully conducted thousands of Atlanta citizens to their final rest.

Name: Grace Towns Hamilton
Body:
Overview:
Grace Towns Hamilton was an influential civic leader, sociologist, and legislator who shattered barriers in 1965 as the first African American woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly. Serving nineteen years in the House and seventeen years as executive director of the Atlanta Urban League, she was a principal architect of Atlanta's 1973 City Charter.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 10, 1907, in Atlanta, Georgia, Grace Towns was the daughter of Atlanta University professor George A. Towns. She graduated from Atlanta University in 1927 and earned a master’s degree in psychology from Ohio State University in 1929. In 1943, Hamilton was appointed executive director of the Atlanta Urban League, leading the agency for seventeen years until 1961.

Under Hamilton's strategic leadership, the Urban League conducted rigorous sociological studies that documented severe disparities in housing, healthcare, and education for Black Atlantans. She used these empirical data to compel city officials to build new public schools, improve sanitation in Black neighborhoods, and desegregate healthcare facilities. Hamilton was also a brilliant political strategist, co-founding the Atlanta Negro Voters League in 1949 and mobilizing historic voter registration campaigns.

In 1965, following federal court-ordered reapportionment, Hamilton made history by winning election to the Georgia House of Representatives, taking her seat in January 1966 as the first Black woman in the state legislature. Over a distinguished nineteen-year legislative career until 1984, Hamilton championed education, reapportionment, and municipal reform. She served as a principal architect of Atlanta's 1973 City Charter, which modernized municipal governance and created the modern City Council structure. She continued public service on the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights until her passing on June 17, 1992.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Grace Towns Hamilton spent her entire adult life shaping Atlanta’s civic, educational, and political institutions through the Atlanta Urban League, the Georgia General Assembly, and the 1973 City Charter. When she died on June 17, 1992, at age eighty-five, she was honored as a Georgia Woman of Achievement. Hamilton was interred at South-View Cemetery, where generations of her family and civil rights colleagues rest (Henderson 204–5, 245). Her resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary pioneer of southern legislative history.

Name: Graham Washington Jackson Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Graham Washington Jackson Sr. was an internationally acclaimed musician, organist, choral conductor, and educator whose musical mastery made him a cultural icon in Atlanta and performer for six U.S. presidents. Known as the "Ambassador of Good Will," his accordion performance of "Goin' Home" at President Franklin D. Roosevelt's funeral train became an iconic national symbol.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 22, 1903, in Portsmouth, Virginia, Graham Washington Jackson Sr. displayed prodigal talent from childhood, mastering piano, pipe organ, and accordion. In 1924, Jackson moved to Atlanta to attend Morehouse College. That same year, he organized the Seminole Syncopators, who became one of the first African American musical ensembles to broadcast on WSB radio and record popular jazz sides.

Jackson became a central fixture in Atlanta's musical life. A resident of the historic Washington Park neighborhood, he served as house organist at Bailey’s 81 Theatre and the Royal Theatre on Auburn Avenue, performed on the Fox Theatre's mighty Möller pipe organ, and served as music director at First Congregational Church. From 1928 to 1940, Jackson served as director of music at Booker T. Washington High School, training and inspiring a generation of young Atlanta musicians.

During the 1930s and 1940s, Jackson developed a close friendship with President Franklin D. Roosevelt, performing for him dozens of times at the Little White House in Warm Springs, Georgia. On April 13, 1945, as Roosevelt’s funeral train departed Warm Springs, Jackson stood by the tracks playing "Goin' Home" on his accordion with tears streaming down his face, a moment immortalized in *Life* magazine. During World War II, Jackson served in the U.S. Navy, raising millions in war bonds. He continued performing and composing until his passing on January 15, 1983.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Graham Washington Jackson Sr. lived in Atlanta for nearly sixty years, enriching its cultural landscape through Booker T. Washington High School, First Congregational Church, and radio broadcasts across the city. When Jackson died in Atlanta on January 15, 1983, civic and musical leaders commemorated his immense contributions. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among Atlanta's prominent artists, educators, and community pioneers (Henderson 215; [New Georgia Encyclopedia](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/graham-jackson-sr/)). His resting place at South-View celebrates an indelible musical legacy.

Name: Hank Aaron
Body:
Overview:
Henry Louis "Hank" Aaron was a legendary Major League Baseball Hall of Famer, civil rights champion, and humanitarian who became one of Atlanta's most celebrated cultural icons. Breaking Babe Ruth's all-time career home run record in Atlanta on April 8, 1974, Aaron integrated major professional sports in the Deep South with the Braves' 1966 arrival, overcame relentless racism with extraordinary dignity, and dedicated his post-playing career to civic philanthropy and corporate leadership.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 5, 1934, in Mobile, Alabama, Henry Louis Aaron overcame childhood poverty and Jim Crow discrimination, honing his hitting skills before joining the Negro American League's Indianapolis Clowns in 1951. In 1952, he signed with the Boston Braves, making his major league debut with the Milwaukee Braves in 1954 and winning the National League MVP award in 1957.

When the Braves franchise relocated to Atlanta in April 1966, Aaron became the premier athletic star of the Deep South, taking the field on April 12, 1966, for the Braves' inaugural home opener at Atlanta Stadium and symbolizing a new era of desegregation. In the early 1970s, as Aaron closed in on Babe Ruth's hallowed record of 714 home runs, he was targeted with hundreds of thousands of pieces of racist hate mail, vitriol, and death threats. Displaying monumental poise and moral courage, Aaron shattered the record on April 8, 1974, hitting his 715th home run into the Atlanta bullpen before a national television audience.

Aaron finished his playing career with 755 home runs, 3,771 hits, and 2,297 runs batted in, records that stood for decades. Retiring as an active player, Aaron returned to Atlanta as senior vice president for the Braves, directing player development and minor league operations as one of baseball's earliest Black corporate executives. Beyond sports, he invested extensively in Atlanta real estate, automotive dealerships, and charitable initiatives, establishing the Hank Aaron Chasing the Dream Foundation to fund collegiate scholarships and youth education. In 1973, he married civil rights leader Billye Suber Williams. In 2002, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Aaron passed away in Atlanta on January 22, 2021.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Hank Aaron made Atlanta his permanent home and civic base for more than fifty-five years, hitting his historic 715th home run at Atlanta Stadium, expanding executive opportunities for African Americans, and investing millions in youth education. Following his passing on January 22, 2021, at age eighty-six, funeral services were held at Friendship Baptist Church. Aaron was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in an elegant private mausoleum, joining generations of civil rights pioneers and civic leaders who shaped the city (Henderson 254; [AJC 2021](https://ajc.com/sports/hank-aarons-funeral-a-tribute-to-more-than-a-baseball-great/NTMY77KPAFCWFHKNE4LJRBSGS4/); [City of Atlanta Promised Land](https://citydesign.atlantaga.gov/blog/2022/7/28/promised-land-a-tour-of-atlantas-historically-african-american-cemeteries-and-the-graves-of-civil-rights-pioneers)). His resting place at South-View permanently links the cemetery to Atlanta’s greatest athletic, cultural, and civil rights milestones.

Name: Harold I. Bearden
Body:
Overview:
Bishop Harold I. Bearden was an influential clergyman, civil rights leader, and the 83rd bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church. As pastor of historic Big Bethel AME Church on Auburn Avenue and president of the Atlanta NAACP, Bearden utilized weekly radio broadcasts to mobilize resistance against racial segregation.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1910, Harold I. Bearden dedicated his life to Christian ministry, institutional advancement, and civil rights leadership across the South. After completing his theological education and pastoral training, Bearden served as pastor of several prominent AME congregations before assuming the pulpit of historic Big Bethel AME Church on Auburn Avenue during the 1950s and 1960s.

Under Bearden’s leadership, Big Bethel served as a pivotal command center for the civil rights movement in Atlanta. Bearden recognized the power of mass media, instituting weekly radio broadcasts from Big Bethel that reached tens of thousands of listeners across Georgia. Through his broadcasts, Bearden fearlessly condemned Jim Crow laws, demanded equal public accommodations, and urged the Black community to engage in voter registration drives.

Concurrently, Bearden served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP, coordinating legal strategies and community rallies in support of school desegregation and fair employment. In 1964, Bearden achieved the highest ecclesiastical office in the denomination when he was elected the 83rd bishop of the AME Church, overseeing episcopal districts across North America and Africa. A committed champion of Black higher education, Bishop Bearden served as chairman of the Board of Trustees of Morris Brown College in Atlanta, providing crucial leadership that helped the institution maintain its academic accreditation and financial stability until his passing in 1990.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Bishop Harold I. Bearden lived and ministered on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta for decades, pastoring Big Bethel AME Church, presiding over the Atlanta NAACP, and chairing the Morris Brown College Board of Trustees. Following his death in 1990, his lifelong ministry was commemorated across the city. Bearden was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow AME prelates, educators, and civil rights advocates (Henderson 173). His resting place at South-View preserves the memory of prophetic pastoral leadership in Atlanta.

Name: Henry Hugh Proctor
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Dr. Henry Hugh Proctor was an influential theologian, author, and pastor of Atlanta's historic First Congregational Church. A leading national proponent of the institutional church model, Proctor responded to the devastating 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre by establishing the Atlanta Interracial Committee and organizing community civic leagues to restore peace, social welfare, and mutual respect.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on December 8, 1868, in Fayetteville, Tennessee, Henry Hugh Proctor supported himself through school, graduating from Fisk University in 1891 and earning a Bachelor of Divinity degree from Yale Divinity School in 1894. That same year, Proctor accepted the pastorate of First Congregational Church in Atlanta, an African American congregation founded during Reconstruction.

Influenced by the Social Gospel, Proctor transformed First Congregational into an institutional church that served the holistic needs of Black Atlantans under Jim Crow. Under his direction, the church established Atlanta’s first Black public library branch, a water plant, a gymnasium, a kindergarten, a music school, and counseling programs. In 1908, he commissioned master contractor Robert E. Pharrow to build an impressive brick sanctuary on Houston Street (now John Wesley Dobbs Avenue).

Following the catastrophic devastation of the September 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, Proctor partnered with white attorney Charles T. Hopkins to organize the Interracial Committee of Atlanta, convening twenty Black and twenty white civic leaders to ease tensions, investigate violence, and halt racial bloodshed. Proctor also established the Colored Co-operative Civic League, which mobilized over 1,500 members to foster community improvement and crime reduction. Proctor welcomed prominent national figures such as Theodore Roosevelt and Booker T. Washington to his pulpit before accepting a pastorate in Brooklyn, New York, in 1919. He passed away in 1933.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Dr. Henry Hugh Proctor served as pastor of First Congregational Church in downtown Atlanta for twenty-five years, leading relief and interracial peacemaking efforts following the 1906 massacre. When Proctor died in Brooklyn on May 12, 1933, his body was returned to Atlanta for an elaborate memorial service at First Congregational. He was interred at South-View Cemetery, where many of his congregants, deacons, and community partners rest (Henderson 237; [Bevington](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-hugh-proctor-1868-1933/)). His resting place at South-View honors a giant of the Social Gospel and racial reconciliation.

Last updated: November 2026

Name: Henry Ossian Flipper
Body:
Overview:
Henry Ossian Flipper was a military officer, engineer, author, and government advisor who made history in 1877 as the first African American graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point. Enduring relentless racial ostracism as a cadet and Buffalo Soldier, Flipper spent decades achieving engineering milestones and fighting for vindication.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on March 21, 1856, in Thomasville, Georgia, Henry Ossian Flipper moved to Atlanta following the Civil War to attend Atlanta University. In 1873, he received an appointment to the United States Military Academy at West Point. Enduring extreme racial hostility, verbal abuse, and total social isolation from fellow cadets, Flipper persevered through academic rigor, graduating in 1877 as the first Black commissioned officer in U.S. Army history.

Assigned to the 10th U.S. Cavalry, Flipper served with the Buffalo Soldiers across frontier posts in Texas and the Indian Territory. Demonstrating brilliant engineering expertise, he surveyed military supply roads and engineered a complex ditch and drainage system at Fort Sill to combat malaria, which became known as "Flipper's Ditch" and is now a National Historic Landmark. In 1881, while stationed at Fort Davis, Texas, Flipper was falsely accused of embezzling commissary funds. Although cleared of embezzlement during his court-martial, he was convicted of conduct unbecoming an officer and dismissed from service in 1882.

Refusing to accept the unjust verdict, Flipper spent the rest of his life fighting to clear his military record while building an illustrious civilian career. Over nearly five decades, he applied his talents as a civil and mining engineer, land surveyor, author, Spanish translator, and special assistant to the Secretary of the Interior. Flipper passed away in Atlanta on May 3, 1940. In 1976, the U.S. Army posthumously awarded him an honorable discharge.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Henry Ossian Flipper attended Atlanta University during Reconstruction and returned to Atlanta in his later years, residing in the city until his death on May 3, 1940. Following his passing, Flipper was initially laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, joining many of Atlanta’s prominent African American leaders and educators (Henderson 6; [Georgia Historical Society](https://www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/first-black-graduate-of-west-point/)). In 1978, following the official restoration of his honorable military status, his remains were reinterred with full military honors in his hometown of Thomasville, Georgia.

Name: Herman J. Russell
Body:
Overview:
Herman Jerome Russell was a master builder, real estate developer, and philanthropist whose enterprise, H. J. Russell & Company, helped construct Atlanta's modern skyline. Rising from shining shoes during the Depression, Russell built one of the nation's premier Black-owned construction firms, broke chamber business barriers, and quietly funded civil rights campaigns.

Life and Contributions:
Born on December 23, 1930, in Atlanta, Georgia, Herman Jerome Russell was the son of a plasterer. Growing up in the Summerhill neighborhood during the Great Depression, Russell learned plastering and brick masonry from his father. At age sixteen, using money saved from shining shoes and manual labor, he purchased his first vacant lot on Terry Street, constructing a duplex to fund his education at Tuskegee Institute, where he earned a degree in building construction in 1952.

Returning to Atlanta, Russell founded H. J. Russell & Company, expanding from residential plastering into commercial development. Over five decades, Russell developed his enterprise into one of the largest African American-owned construction and development firms in the United States. His company helped construct iconic landmark projects across metropolitan Atlanta, including the Georgia Dome, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Turner Field, Philips Arena, and Coca-Cola headquarters.

Russell paired his business success with civic and civil rights leadership. In the early 1960s, he became the first Black member of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, later serving as its president. A close confidant of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Russell provided crucial financial backing to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), quietly posting bail bonds for jailed protesters and hosting movement strategists in his home. He also funded the mayoral campaigns of Maynard Jackson and Andrew Young. Russell passed away on November 15, 2014.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Herman J. Russell was a lifelong Atlanta native whose construction projects shaped the city’s architectural skyline from Hartsfield-Jackson Airport to the Georgia Dome. He was a major benefactor to the SCLC and Atlanta civil rights leaders. Following his passing in November 2014 at age eighty-three, thousands gathered for his funeral in Atlanta. Russell was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among Atlanta's foremost business giants and civil rights colleagues (Henderson 6, 239). His grave at South-View honors a master builder of Atlanta.

Name: Horace A. Bohannon
Body:
Overview:
Horace Augustus Bohannon was a decorated Tuskegee Airman, veteran reintegration advocate, educator, and federal postal executive. Born in Atlanta, Bohannon earned his military wings in 1944, directed GI Bill services for thousands of returning Black veterans across Georgia, integrated regional postal management, and co-founded the Atlanta Chapter of Tuskegee Airmen, Inc.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta on August 15, 1922, Horace Augustus Bohannon grew up in poverty during the Great Depression, taking his first job at age eight to assist his family. As a young boy, Bohannon spent hours watching airplanes take off at Candler Field (now Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport), developing a lifelong passion for aviation. After completing civilian pilot training at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, Bohannon worked at Tuskegee Army Air Field before earning his military wings as a flight officer in December 1944.

Bohannon served with the 332nd Fighter Group at Godman Field, Kentucky, during the final stages of World War II. Following the war, Bohannon completed his degree at Lincoln University in 1948 and returned to Georgia to serve as director of the Southern Regional Council's Georgia Veterans Service Project. In this vital role, he assisted thousands of returning Black veterans in securing GI Bill educational benefits, mortgages, and vocational employment despite widespread bureaucratic discrimination.

Bohannon taught for fifteen years in the Fulton County public school system, mentoring youth in science and mathematics. In the 1960s, he broke federal administrative barriers as the first African American Regional Management Training Officer for the U.S. Postal Service. A dedicated civic preservationist, Bohannon helped establish commemorative statues for Black educators and co-founded the Atlanta Chapter of Tuskegee Airmen, Inc., to preserve the history of Black military aviation. Bohannon died in Atlanta on January 8, 2003.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Horace A. Bohannon was a lifelong Atlanta native who directed veteran assistance programs across Georgia, taught in Fulton County schools, and founded the Atlanta Chapter of Tuskegee Airmen. When Bohannon passed away in Atlanta on January 8, 2003, his military valor and civic leadership were honored across the city. He was interred at South-View Cemetery, where his service as a Tuskegee Airman is commemorated with military honors (Henderson 176; [Bohannon Oral History Interview](https://sclfind.libs.uga.edu/catalog/ms2854)). His grave at South-View preserves the legacy of Atlanta's Red Tail aviators.

Name: Horace Mann Bond
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Horace Mann Bond was an eminent historian, sociologist, college president, and dean of education at Atlanta University. A pioneer in documenting racial inequalities in southern education, Bond’s historical research for Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund provided the foundational Fourteenth Amendment arguments that overturned school segregation in *Brown v. Board of Education*.

Life and Contributions:
Born on April 24, 1904, in Nashville, Tennessee, Horace Mann Bond was the son of James Bond, an educator and former slave, and Jane Browne. Bond graduated with honors from Lincoln University in Pennsylvania in 1923, completed his master's degree in 1926, and earned his doctorate in education from the University of Chicago in 1936.

Throughout the 1930s, Bond produced groundbreaking scholarship, most notably his 1934 book *The Education of the Negro in the American Social Order* and *Negro Education in Alabama* (1939). His rigorous research demonstrated that academic disparities in segregated schools resulted from chronic economic deprivation and institutional discrimination rather than innate intellectual differences. In 1939, Bond was appointed the founding president of Fort Valley State College in Georgia, guiding its transition into a four-year institution. In 1945, he became the first Black president of Lincoln University, serving twelve years.

In 1953, Bond joined historians John Hope Franklin and C. Vann Woodward in conducting crucial research for Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, demonstrating that the framers of the Fourteenth Amendment intended to eliminate racial caste systems, which proved pivotal in the Supreme Court’s unanimous *Brown v. Board of Education* ruling. In 1957, Bond moved to Atlanta to become dean of the School of Education at Atlanta University, directing graduate research until 1971. His son Julian Bond became a prominent civil rights leader and Georgia legislator. Bond passed away on December 21, 1972.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. Horace Mann Bond spent fifteen years leading graduate educational research as dean at Atlanta University and advising civic leaders throughout the civil rights movement. When Bond passed away in Atlanta on December 21, 1972, academic and civil rights communities paid tribute to his scholarly legacy. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside his wife Julia and near his son Julian Bond (Henderson 177). His resting place at South-View honors a scholar whose research helped dismantle American school segregation.

Name: Irene Dobbs Jackson
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson was a professor of French at Spelman College and a courageous civil rights pioneer who desegregated the Atlanta Public Library system. In 1959, as the lead plaintiff in a federal desegregation challenge, she became the first African American to receive a library card from Atlanta’s central public library.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1908 in Atlanta, Georgia, Irene Dobbs was the eldest of six daughters of prominent civic and political leader John Wesley Dobbs and Irene Thompson Dobbs. Raised in a household dedicated to education, classical culture, and community uplift along Auburn Avenue, Jackson completed her education at Spelman College, graduating with honors in 1929.

Jackson pursued graduate studies in French literature, earning a master's degree from Atlanta University and later completing her doctorate in French literature at the University of Toulouse in France in 1958, becoming one of the earliest African American women to earn a French doctorate abroad. Returning to Atlanta, Dr. Jackson served for decades as a distinguished professor and chair of the French department at Spelman College, inspiring generations of students.

In 1959, Jackson took a courageous stand against municipal Jim Crow segregation. With support from Spelman professor Howard Zinn, Whitney Young, and the NAACP, Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss served as plaintiffs in a planned federal lawsuit challenging the racial exclusion of Black citizens from the central branch of the Atlanta Public Library. Rather than fight the suit, the library board capitulated. In 1959, Dr. Jackson walked into the Carnegie central library and was issued the first library card granted to a Black citizen in Atlanta's history, despite receiving threatening phone calls and harassment. Her son, Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr., later became Atlanta's first Black mayor. She died in 1999.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson lived and taught in Atlanta for seven decades, anchoring Spelman College and courageously desegregating the Atlanta Public Library system in 1959. Following her passing in 1999 at age ninety-one, she was interred at South-View Cemetery in the Dobbs family lot (Henderson 129, 216). Her gravestone at South-View features an epitaph from Kahlil Gibran: "You have walked among us as a spirit." Her resting place at South-View honors an intellectual trailblazer who opened public learning to all Atlantans.

Name: Jacob McKinley
Body:
Overview:
Jacob McKinley was a master carpenter, brick manufacturer, real estate investor, and founding trustee of South-View Cemetery. Overcoming chattel slavery, McKinley established an expansive commercial empire that employed over one hundred workers, becoming post-Civil War Atlanta's wealthiest Black businessman and providing vital capital to charter South-View Cemetery in 1886.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Newnan, Coweta County, Georgia, around 1830, Jacob McKinley displayed exceptional talent in building and woodworking from an early age. At age sixteen, he entered formal training as a carpenter, developing craftsmanship of such extraordinary skill that by 1853 he was purchased for the substantial price of $1,550.

When emancipation arrived in 1865 at the close of the Civil War, McKinley immediately mobilized his artisan expertise to build independent economic enterprise in Atlanta. During Reconstruction, he established a diverse commercial empire. He operated a major brickyard, a successful grocery store, and worked as a prosperous wholesale dealer in wood, coal, and building materials. McKinley employed between 100 and 150 Black and white workers, a rare feat in the postbellum South that established him among the city’s premier builders.

McKinley strategically invested his earnings into prime Atlanta real estate. By 1886, municipal tax digests recorded his taxable personal and real estate holdings at $6,800 (equivalent to approximately $250,000 today), establishing him as the wealthiest African American businessman among South-View’s organizers. McKinley used his capital to fund Black civic organizations and provide employment that protected Black laborers from discriminatory practices. In February 1886, McKinley joined Albert Watts and four other leaders to petition for the charter of South-View Cemetery, providing vital startup financial backing. McKinley managed his properties until his death in Atlanta in 1896.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Jacob McKinley was an indispensable financial organizer and founding trustee of South-View Cemetery in 1886, investing his substantial commercial capital to establish a dignified, non-segregated cemetery for Black Atlantans. Although McKinley was a pivotal co-founder of South-View, he is one of the few founders who does not rest on its grounds; upon his death in 1896, he was interred in his family's private burial plot at Oakland Cemetery (Henderson 18). His foundational role at South-View remains permanently honored in the cemetery's historical charter.

Name: James Fletcher
Body:
Overview:
James Fletcher was an African American citizen of Atlanta who was murdered by armed white rioters during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal shooting reflects the catastrophic human toll of four days of unchecked racial terror, during which white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods, killed dozens, and displaced hundreds.

Life and Contributions:
James Fletcher lived and worked in Atlanta during the opening years of the twentieth century. Like many African American residents of the era, Fletcher participated in the city's expanding industrial and service economy, seeking to earn an honest living and build community stability despite the harsh realities of legal Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, a bitter gubernatorial campaign focused on Black disenfranchisement, combined with sensational, false newspaper reports of attacks on white women, inflamed white racial animosity. On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, thousands of white men and boys flooded downtown Atlanta, attacking Black pedestrians, barbers, and streetcar passengers. Over the following two days, the mob violence spread into residential Black communities.

Fletcher was caught in the path of the mob violence between September 22 and September 24. Armed white vigilantes ambushed and shot him, inflicting catastrophic wounds from which he died. Official municipal death records and subsequent cold-case investigations verified his death as a direct fatality of the massacre. For decades, Fletcher’s name was omitted from general public history until modern research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition documented his fate, ensuring that the community remembered his life and tragedy.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
James Fletcher was an Atlanta resident whose life was brutally cut short by mob violence during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Following the unrest, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions failed to provide equal care for deceased Black victims, South-View Cemetery provided solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre casualties brought to its grounds (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: James Harrison
Body:
Overview:
James Harrison was an African American resident of south Atlanta who was murdered by an armed white mob during the 1902 Pittsburgh Riot. An innocent bystander walking along railroad tracks to escape gunfire, Harrison was pursued and shot hundreds of times, exemplifying the indiscriminate terror inflicted on Black citizens during racial unrest.

Life and Contributions:
James Harrison was a peaceful resident of southwest Atlanta who resided near the Pittsburgh and Summerhill communities, earning his livelihood through daily industry. In the early morning hours of May 17, 1902, violence erupted across the working-class Pittsburgh neighborhood when former police officer Samuel Kerlin led police and armed white civilians in a siege against Will Richardson’s grocery store on McDaniel Street.

As gunfire echoed across the district, a crowd of approximately three thousand people—more than two thousand of them armed—swarmed into Pittsburgh. While Richardson and his companions remained barricaded inside the store, roving vigilantes began pursuing and attacking innocent Black pedestrians throughout the area. Harrison was walking quietly along the nearby railroad tracks, attempting to avoid the spreading gunfire and reach safety.

When the mob spotted Harrison on the tracks, hundreds of armed men and boys gave chase. Desperately trying to escape the murderous crowd, Harrison ran toward a drainage culvert and railway embankment. The mob cornered him and opened fire with shotguns and rifles, shooting him hundreds of times before leaving his body on the tracks. Harrison had no connection to the dispute between Richardson and the police, yet became one of nine people killed in the violence. His murder shocked Black Atlantans, who called for state militia intervention to restore order.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
James Harrison was an innocent Atlanta resident murdered on May 17, 1902, along railroad tracks in the Pittsburgh community during mob violence. Following the deployment of state militia to quell the unrest, municipal authorities and undertakers recovered Harrison's body. He was provided a solemn, dignified burial at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 116–17). His resting place at South-View connects the grounds to the tragic events of the 1902 Pittsburgh Riot and stands as a memorial to innocent victims of racial violence.

Name: Jean Childs Young
Body:
Overview:
Jean Childs Young was an educator, civil rights activist, child welfare advocate, and civic leader who championed educational equality locally and globally. As First Lady of Atlanta and chair of the U.S. Commission for the International Year of the Child, Young established public school task forces and spearheaded global youth initiatives through UNICEF.

Life and Contributions:
Born on July 1, 1933, in Marion, Alabama, Jean Childs was educated in local schools and graduated from Manchester College in Indiana in 1954 with a bachelor's degree in elementary education. She later earned a master's degree in education from Queens College in New York. In 1954, she married civil rights leader Andrew Young.

Throughout the civil rights movement, Young was an active grassroots participant, helping organize citizenship education schools, coordinating voter registration campaigns for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), and mentoring student activists in SNCC. Settling in Atlanta, Young taught in the Atlanta Public Schools system for decades, developing innovative elementary curricula and advocating for integrated classrooms.

In 1977, President Jimmy Carter appointed Young chair of the U.S. National Commission on the International Year of the Child, elevating her advocacy for children's health, literacy, and legal protection to the international stage. She subsequently served as chair of the U.S. Committee for UNICEF from 1981 until her death in 1994. As First Lady of Atlanta from 1982 to 1990 during Andrew Young's mayoral administration, she established the Mayor's Task Force on Public Education and co-founded the Atlanta Parents and Teachers Together project. She passed away on September 16, 1994.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Jean Childs Young lived in Atlanta for over thirty years, teaching in Atlanta Public Schools, leading civic education task forces, and serving as First Lady of Atlanta. Following her passing from cancer on September 16, 1994, an outpouring of community tributes culminated in a massive memorial service at Atlanta’s Civic Center. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests among Atlanta’s preeminent civil rights leaders and educators (Henderson 259). Her grave at South-View commemorates an extraordinary champion of the world’s children.

Name: Jesse B. Blayton Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Jesse Bee Blayton Sr. was an accountant, radio broadcasting pioneer, banking executive, and educator who broke historic racial barriers across Georgia. In 1928, Blayton became Georgia's first African American Certified Public Accountant, and in 1949, he purchased Atlanta's WERD, making it the first Black-owned and operated radio station in the United States.

Life and Contributions:
Born on December 6, 1897, in Fallis, Oklahoma, Jesse Bee Blayton Sr. served in the U.S. Army during World War I before completing his education at the Walton School of Commerce in Chicago. In 1928, Blayton passed the state examination to become the first Black Certified Public Accountant (CPA) in Georgia and only the fourth in the nation, establishing an accounting firm on Auburn Avenue.

In 1930, Blayton joined the faculty of Morehouse College and later Atlanta University, serving as professor of business administration and accounting for over thirty years. Concurrently, Blayton was a central figure in Sweet Auburn finance, serving as vice president of Citizens Trust Bank and co-founding Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association in 1925 to provide home mortgages to Black families.

In October 1949, Blayton achieved broadcasting history when he purchased radio station WERD in Atlanta for $50,000, establishing the nation's first Black-owned radio station. Operating from the Prince Hall Masonic Temple on Auburn Avenue, WERD revolutionized radio by featuring Black announcers, gospel, rhythm and blues, and civil rights news. Blayton offered studio facilities to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, allowing Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to broadcast announcements directly to the city. Blayton was inducted into the National Radio Hall of Fame in 1995. He passed away on September 7, 1977.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Jesse B. Blayton Sr. anchored the commercial, academic, and media life of Sweet Auburn in Atlanta for nearly fifty years through WERD, Citizens Trust Bank, and Morehouse College. Following his death on September 7, 1977, civic and business leaders commemorated his historic breakthroughs. Blayton was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow banking and civic associates (Henderson 175–76, 192). His resting place at South-View permanently honors the pioneer of Black radio broadcasting and accountancy in Georgia.

Name: Jesse Hill Jr.
Body:
Overview:
Jesse Hill Jr. was a prominent business executive, civil rights leader, and publisher who served as president and CEO of Atlanta Life Insurance Company. As the first African American president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce and chairman of the Georgia Board of Regents, Hill forged crucial biracial coalitions that guided modern Atlanta.

Life and Contributions:
Born on May 30, 1926, in St. Louis, Missouri, Jesse Hill Jr. attended Lincoln University in Missouri, graduating with a bachelor of science degree in 1947. He subsequently earned an MBA in actuarial science from the University of Michigan in 1949, becoming one of the nation's few professionally trained Black actuaries.

In 1949, Hill moved to Atlanta to join the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, rising through executive ranks to become the company's president and chief executive officer in 1973, succeeding Norris B. Herndon. Under Hill's leadership, Atlanta Life expanded its assets and operations across multiple states, financing Black commercial development. In 1960, Hill co-founded the *Atlanta Inquirer*, an independent weekly newspaper that provided crucial, truthful coverage of the student sit-ins and the civil rights movement.

Hill was a brilliant political strategist and mediator. He served as a trusted economic and civil rights advisor to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Mayor Maynard Jackson, Mayor Andrew Young, and Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter. In 1973, Hill was appointed the first Black member of the Georgia Board of Regents, later serving as its chairman. In 1977, he made history as the first African American elected president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, promoting business growth and civic inclusion. Hill passed away on December 17, 2012.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Jesse Hill Jr. spent over six decades in Atlanta leading Atlanta Life Insurance Company, co-founding the *Atlanta Inquirer*, and serving as president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce. Following his death in December 2012, Atlanta leaders renamed a major portion of Butler Street as "Jesse Hill Jr. Drive" in his honor. Hill was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, resting alongside Alonzo Herndon and Norris Herndon (Henderson 6, 210–12). His grave at South-View commemorates an iconic architect of Atlanta's business and civic triumph.

Name: John and Billie Harden
Body:
Overview:
John Harden and Willie Lee "Billie" Harden were pioneer Atlanta entrepreneurs and sports executives who owned the Atlanta Black Crackers baseball team and operated the city's first African American-owned 24-hour service stations. Listed in Victor Green's *Negro Motorist Green Book*, their stations provided vital hospitality, safety, and automotive services to travelers during Jim Crow.

Life and Contributions:
John Harden and Willie Lee "Billie" Harden established themselves during the 1930s and 1940s as two of Atlanta’s most innovative and respected business leaders. Operating during an era when African Americans faced severe economic restrictions and municipal segregation, the Hardens recognized that the rapid expansion of automobile travel created urgent commercial opportunities and safety needs for Black travelers.

In the mid-1930s, the Hardens opened modern 24-hour service stations on Hunter Street (now Martin Luther King Jr. Drive) and Auburn Avenue. Their service stations were among the first Black-owned full-service filling stations in the South, offering gasoline, oil, mechanic repairs, clean restrooms, and dining options. Because Black motorists faced refusal and hostility at white service stations, the Hardens' stations were prominently featured in *The Negro Motorist Green Book* as trusted, welcoming stops.

In addition to their automotive business, the Hardens were passionate sports promoters. In 1937, they acquired ownership and management of the Atlanta Black Crackers, a professional baseball club in the Negro American League. Under their ownership, the team captured the second-half championship of the Negro American League in 1938, providing top-tier athletic entertainment to thousands of Black Atlantans at Ponce de Leon Park. John Harden passed away in 1979, and Billie Harden continued their philanthropic endeavors until her death in 1991.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
John and Billie Harden spent four decades in Atlanta anchoring commercial enterprise on Hunter Street and Auburn Avenue and providing sports entertainment through the Atlanta Black Crackers. Following John Harden’s death in 1979 and Billie Harden’s passing in 1991, both were interred at South-View Cemetery in an elegant family mausoleum (Henderson 206; Historic South-View Preservation Foundation). Their resting place at South-View connects the cemetery to the history of Black entrepreneurship, the Green Book, and Negro League baseball in Atlanta.

Name: John Glover
Body:
Overview:
John Glover was a trailblazing federal law enforcement official who broke historic ground as the first African American appointed to lead an FBI field office. Directing the Atlanta field division during the harrowing Atlanta Child Murders crisis, Glover managed unprecedented interagency operations and brought federal strategic resources to the investigation.

Life and Contributions:
Born in the mid-twentieth century, John Glover pursued higher education and law enforcement training before embarking on a distinguished career with the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Joining the Bureau during an era when African Americans were severely underrepresented in federal law enforcement, Glover excelled in criminal investigations, counterintelligence, and tactical operations. His demonstrated leadership, analytical rigor, and command presence earned him steady promotions through the ranks of supervisory management.

In 1979, FBI Director William H. Webster appointed Glover as Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Atlanta Field Office, making him the first African American in the history of the Bureau to head a field division. His historic appointment coincided with the onset of the Atlanta Child Murders, an unprecedented crisis involving the abduction and murder of dozens of Black youths across the metropolitan area.

Under immense national scrutiny and local community anxiety, Glover spearheaded federal involvement in the investigation. He coordinated the deployment of federal behavioral profilers, forensic analysts, and hundreds of special agents to support the joint Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force. Working closely with Atlanta Public Safety Commissioner Lee P. Brown and Mayor Maynard Jackson, Glover managed complex interagency logistics that culminated in the 1981 stakeout operations and subsequent prosecution of Wayne Williams. Glover's barrier-breaking leadership established new standards for federal law enforcement administration and community engagement.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
John Glover was stationed in Atlanta as head of the FBI’s Atlanta Field Office, leading federal investigative support for the city during the 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Because Glover was a federal official stationed in Atlanta rather than a permanent cemetery interree, his direct institutional connection to the city is established through FBI records and task force proceedings ([FBI Serial Killers Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)).

Name: John H. Calhoun Jr.
Body:
Overview:
John Henry Calhoun Jr. was an influential civil rights organizer, businessman, and politician who dedicated sixty years to expanding Black political power in Atlanta. As president of the Atlanta NAACP, co-founder of the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and City Council member, Calhoun empowered grassroots neighborhood governance and created Atlanta's Neighborhood Planning Units.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1899 in Georgia, John Henry Calhoun Jr. completed his higher education at Morehouse College and Atlanta University. Entering commercial real estate and business administration, Calhoun recognized early that political enfranchisement was essential for African American economic advancement under Jim Crow.

In 1949, Calhoun joined John Wesley Dobbs and A.T. Walden to co-found the Atlanta Negro Voters League (ANVL). The ANVL coordinated nonpartisan voter registration drives and leveraged bloc voting to compel municipal candidates to address the needs of Black citizens. Calhoun served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP during the turbulent 1950s. In 1956, when state officials launched investigations to suppress civil rights organizing, Calhoun was arrested and jailed for contempt after courageously refusing to surrender the confidential membership lists and financial records of the NAACP.

Calhoun was also a stalwart supporter of the Atlanta Student Movement in 1960, advising student leaders and coordinating legal defense funds. In 1974, at the age of seventy-four, Calhoun was elected to the Atlanta City Council, serving under Mayor Maynard Jackson. As councilman, Calhoun was a primary architect of the Neighborhood Planning Unit (NPU) system, establishing a citizen advisory structure that decentralized municipal decision-making and gave neighborhood residents direct influence over zoning and urban development. Calhoun passed away in 1988.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
John H. Calhoun Jr. spent six decades in Atlanta organizing voters, defending the NAACP, and serving on the Atlanta City Council. When he died in 1988 at age eighty-nine, his civic contributions were commemorated across the city. Calhoun was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow ANVL founders and civil rights colleagues (Henderson 185; [John H. Calhoun Papers](https://findingaids.auctr.edu/repositories/2/resources/91)). His resting place at South-View honors a patriarch of Atlanta municipal democracy and grassroots civic empowerment.

Name: John Lewis
Body:
Overview:
John Robert Lewis was a towering civil rights icon, SNCC chairman, and longtime U.S. Congressman who represented Atlanta for thirty-three years. A leader of the Nashville sit-ins, Freedom Rides, March on Washington, and "Bloody Sunday" in Selma, Lewis served as the "conscience of the Congress," tirelessly advocating for voting rights and equality.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 21, 1940, in Troy, Alabama, to sharecroppers Eddie and Willie Mae Lewis, John Lewis was inspired as a teenager by the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the radio sermons of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He attended American Baptist Theological Seminary and graduated from Fisk University in Nashville, Tennessee.

As a student, Lewis organized lunch counter sit-ins across Nashville and was beaten and arrested during the 1961 Freedom Rides. From 1963 to 1966, Lewis served as chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), becoming one of the "Big Six" leaders of the civil rights movement. At age twenty-three, he was the youngest keynote speaker at the historic 1963 March on Washington. On March 7, 1965, Lewis co-led more than 600 marchers across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, where state troopers attacked peaceful demonstrators on "Bloody Sunday," fracturing Lewis's skull; televised images of the brutality galvanized national passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Moving to Atlanta, Lewis directed the Voter Education Project, registering over four million minority voters. In 1981, he was elected to the Atlanta City Council, and in 1986, he won election to the U.S. House of Representatives representing Georgia’s Fifth Congressional District. Serving seventeen terms in Congress until his death on July 17, 2020, Lewis championed universal health care, civil liberties, and the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
John Lewis lived in Atlanta for over fifty years, anchoring his public service, civil rights organizing, and congressional representation in the city. Following his death on July 17, 2020, his funeral was held at historic Ebenezer Baptist Church on July 30. Lewis was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery beside his beloved wife, Lillian Miles Lewis (Henderson 223; [John Lewis: A Founding Father](https://www.ajc.com/john-lewis/john-lewis-a-founding-father-of-a-better-america/2PYQEPHYIRH7NE4R6B5SS2JPZU/)). His burial at South-View connects the cemetery directly to the epic triumphs and moral victories of the modern civil rights movement.

Name: John Render
Body:
Overview:
Rev. John Render was an African Methodist Episcopal minister, commercial drayman, civic leader, and founding investor of South-View Cemetery. Born into slavery, Render dedicated five decades to establishing durable economic, religious, and educational institutions for Black Georgians, serving as a trustee of Morris Brown College and founding shareholder of South-View.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Meriwether County, Georgia, in 1845 to Daniel and Anne Render, John Render endured forced agricultural labor before gaining freedom at the close of the Civil War. Moving to Atlanta during Reconstruction, Render established himself as an industrious commercial drayman, hauling freight across Atlanta's rapidly expanding railway and warehouse districts.

Render felt a deep calling to Christian ministry and was ordained in the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church, pastoring congregations throughout metropolitan Atlanta and rural Georgia. Render married Laura Herenton, and together they became central figures in Atlanta's faith and civic communities. In 1886, Render joined fellow Black entrepreneurs to incorporate South-View Cemetery, purchasing two founding shares to create a non-segregated burial ground.

That same year, Render helped charter the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company, designed to assist Black families in securing residential mortgages and accumulating generational wealth. In 1890, Render entered electoral politics, running for Second Ward city councilman to demand fair municipal allocations. He served as long-term treasurer of the AME Church Ministers Union and was an essential financial trustee of Morris Brown College, providing vital fiscal oversight during the institution’s formative decades. Render continued his ministerial and community uplift work until his passing in 1923.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. John Render spent over fifty years in Atlanta serving Second Ward civic causes, pastoring AME congregations, and stewarding Morris Brown College. In 1886, Render co-founded South-View Cemetery, purchasing founding capital shares to secure an African American-governed burial ground free from racial indignities. Upon his death in 1923, Render was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where his wife Laura was later interred beside him in 1945 (Henderson 20). His resting place at South-View honors a founding father who invested his life in Black institutional independence.
