Name: John Wesley Dobbs
Body:
Overview:
John Wesley Dobbs was a postal employee, civic organizer, orator, and Grand Master of the Prince Hall Masons who was affectionately crowned the "Unofficial Mayor of Sweet Auburn." Dobbs spearheaded mass voter registration, constructed the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, and co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League, transforming Black political participation in Georgia.

Life and Contributions:
Born on March 26, 1882, in Marietta, Cobb County, Georgia, John Wesley Dobbs was raised by his mother and grandparents following his father's early death. Moving to Atlanta, Dobbs worked odd jobs and studied at Atlanta Baptist College (later Morehouse College). In 1903, he passed the civil service examination and was appointed a railway postal clerk for the U.S. Post Office, a position he held for thirty-two years.

During the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, Dobbs stood armed guard through terrifying nights to protect his household on Auburn Avenue. The ordeal forged his lifelong determination to fight for civil dignity and political empowerment. In 1911, Dobbs joined the Prince Hall Masons, rising in 1932 to become Grand Master of the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Georgia, a post he held until his death. In 1937, Dobbs oversaw construction of the iconic Prince Hall Masonic Temple on Auburn Avenue, which became a commercial powerhouse and headquarters for WERD radio and the SCLC.

Dobbs was an electrifying orator who championed the motto "Voters, Books, and Bucks." In 1936, he founded the Atlanta Civic and Political League, and in 1949, alongside A.T. Walden, he co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League, registering over 20,000 Black voters. His grandson, Maynard Jackson Jr., was elected Atlanta's first Black mayor in 1973. Dobbs died on August 30, 1961.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
John Wesley Dobbs lived and organized in Atlanta for over six decades, building the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, leading the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and defining Sweet Auburn. When Dobbs died on August 30, 1961, thousands marched in his funeral procession along Auburn Avenue. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in the Dobbs family lot (Henderson 129, 216). In 1994, Atlanta renamed Houston Street as "John Wesley Dobbs Avenue" in his honor, permanently celebrating his civic leadership.

Name: John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Dr. John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr. was a nationally prominent theologian, educator, editor, and the third president of Gammon Theological Seminary. One of the first African Americans in the nation to earn a Ph.D., Bowen transformed Gammon into a center of theological scholarship and courageously sheltered community members during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre.

Life and Contributions:
Born in New Orleans, Louisiana, on September 3, 1855, to an enslaved carpenter who purchased his freedom and fought for the Union Army, John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr. pursued education with extraordinary diligence during Reconstruction. He graduated from New Orleans University in 1878, completed a Bachelor of Sacred Theology at Boston University in 1885, and in 1887 earned his Ph.D. in historical theology from Boston University, becoming only the second African American in the nation to receive a doctorate.

In 1893, Bowen relocated to Atlanta to become the first full-time Black professor at Gammon Theological Seminary, teaching historical theology and systematic theology for forty years. In 1895, he achieved national prominence at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition with his address "An Appeal to the King," articulating the moral imperatives of racial equality. In 1904, Bowen co-founded *The Voice of the Negro*, the premier national monthly journal of Black thought in the South, reaching 15,000 subscribers.

In 1906, Bowen was elected president of Gammon Theological Seminary. During the September 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, when white mobs invaded south Atlanta, Bowen opened Gammon's campus as an armed sanctuary for hundreds of fleeing Black families. When police and armed vigilantes arrived in Brownsville on September 24, officers pistol-whipped Bowen and arrested him alongside 250 residents. Bowen survived the attack, retired from Gammon in 1932, and passed away on July 20, 1933.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr. lived in south Atlanta for forty years as professor and president of Gammon Theological Seminary in Brownsville, heroically protecting citizens during the 1906 massacre. Following his death on July 20, 1933, his funeral was held at Gammon Theological Seminary. Bowen was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside his family and faculty colleagues (Henderson 119; South-View Brochure). His grave at South-View commemorates an intellectual titan and courageous defender of Atlanta’s Black community.

Name: Julian Bond
Body:
Overview:
Julian Bond was a charismatic civil rights leader, co-founder of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), poet, author, Georgia state senator, and national chairman of the NAACP. For over five decades, Bond stood at the forefront of the struggle for racial, political, and economic equality, leaving an indelible imprint on American democracy.

Life and Contributions:
Born on January 14, 1940, in Nashville, Tennessee, Horace Julian Bond was the son of eminent educator Dr. Horace Mann Bond and Julia Washington Bond. In 1957, Bond moved to Atlanta when his father became dean of education at Atlanta University. Enrolling at Morehouse College, Bond excelled in writing, editing the campus newspaper and studying under poet Robert Frost.

In early 1960, inspired by the Greensboro sit-ins, Bond co-founded the Committee on Appeal for Human Rights (COAHR) and helped draft *An Appeal for Human Rights*, launching the Atlanta Student Movement. Later that year, Bond helped organize the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) and served as its communications director from 1961 to 1966, publicizing voter drives and protests across the nation.

In 1965, Bond was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives. However, on January 10, 1966, white state representatives unconstitutionally barred him from taking his seat due to his outspoken opposition to the Vietnam War. Bond challenged the exclusion, and on December 5, 1966, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in *Bond v. Floyd* that the Georgia legislature had violated his First Amendment rights. Bond was sworn into office in January 1967, serving twenty years in the Georgia House and Senate. He co-founded and served as first president of the Southern Poverty Law Center and chaired the national NAACP from 1998 to 2010 before passing away on August 15, 2015.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Julian Bond spent his foundational activist and legislative career in Atlanta, organizing the student movement at Morehouse College and representing the city in the Georgia General Assembly for two decades. Following his death in 2015, a portion of his cremated remains was interred at South-View Cemetery beside his parents, Dr. Horace Mann Bond and Julia Bond (Henderson 177; [Canopy Atlanta](https://canopyatlanta.org/2023/11/17/atlantans-share-their-familial-connections-to-south-view-cemetery/)). His memorial marker at South-View bears his self-chosen epitaph, "Easily Amused Race Man," permanently celebrating his wit, grace, and civil rights legacy.

Name: Katie McBride
Body:
Overview:
Katie McBride was an African American entrepreneur and hospitality proprietor in Atlanta whose dining and lodging accommodations provided essential refuge and dignified service to Black travelers during Jim Crow segregation. Operating during an era of rigid municipal exclusion, McBride created welcoming commercial spaces that formed vital mutual aid and hospitality networks.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Georgia around 1895, Katie McBride emerged during the early decades of the twentieth century as an enterprising businesswoman in Atlanta. In an era when municipal Jim Crow statutes and social customs barred African Americans from downtown hotels, restaurants, and public facilities, independent Black entrepreneurs stepped forward to establish vital accommodation networks.

McBride established and operated a prominent boarding house and dining parlor in Atlanta. Her establishment offered clean, dignified, and safe overnight lodging, nourishing home-cooked meals, and community fellowship for Black visitors, touring musicians, traveling ministers, and business professionals. Her hospitality business formed part of the vital commercial ecosystem documented in travel directories like Victor Green's *The Negro Motorist Green Book*, which directed Black motorists to safe havens across the segregated South.

Operating a hospitality business required great resilience, resourcefulness, and diplomatic skill in navigating local licensing regulations and racial tensions. McBride ran her enterprise with warmth and high standards, serving as a trusted community matriarch who offered comfort and security to strangers far from home. Her business flourished for decades as a community gathering space, contributing to the economic self-reliance of Atlanta's Black neighborhoods until her retirement. McBride passed away in Atlanta around 1970, leaving behind a legacy of hospitality and communal care.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Katie McBride lived and operated her hospitality business in Atlanta for decades, providing safe shelter and nourishment for travelers barred from white hotels downtown. Following her passing around 1970, community members gathered to honor her entrepreneurial and charitable legacy. She was laid to rest at historic South-View Cemetery, where many of Atlanta’s pioneer hospitality proprietors, merchants, and civic figures rest (Henderson 226). Her grave at South-View honors the unsung women whose commercial enterprise sustained Black dignity under Jim Crow.

Byline: LMC 3403, Fall 2026
Last updated: November 2026
Tags: Hospitality, Green Book, Women Entrepreneurs, Black Enterprise
See also: Carrie Cunningham, John and Billie Harden, South-View founded

Name: Leola Maddox
Body:
Overview:
Leola Maddox was an African American woman who was murdered by a white mob in Atlanta during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Her killing demonstrated that white mobs targeted Black women and families in their own neighborhoods indiscriminately, shattering families and destabilizing residential communities across the city.

Life and Contributions:
Leola Maddox was born in Georgia during the late nineteenth century and lived in Atlanta at the turn of the twentieth century. She was married and maintained a home with her family, participating in the civic, spiritual, and community life of Atlanta's industrious African American population during the early Jim Crow era.

In late September 1906, inflammatory political rhetoric during the Georgia gubernatorial race, amplified by reckless newspaper reports, unleashed racial hostility across the municipality. On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, thousands of armed white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, attacking Black laborers, streetcar passengers, and passersby. By Sunday and Monday, armed vigilante mobs invaded residential Black neighborhoods, firing weapons into private residences and terrorizing families.

Maddox was assaulted and killed in her neighborhood as white mobs swept through residential streets. Her violent death stands out among the documented female casualties of the massacre, demonstrating that the mob's brutality extended far beyond downtown commercial areas into private homes. Maddox’s tragic fate was officially commemorated through archival research conducted by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project, which restored the names and dignity of victims whose deaths had long been omitted from mainstream Atlanta histories.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Leola Maddox lived, maintained her family home, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic days following the violence, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions failed to provide equal care for deceased Black victims, South-View Cemetery provided solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre casualties brought to its grounds (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital sanctuary of annual remembrance for the massacre.

Name: Lillian Miles Lewis
Body:
Overview:
Lillian Miles Lewis was an accomplished librarian, university administrator, and educator who directed special collections at Atlanta University and Clark Atlanta University. As the wife and trusted political adviser to civil rights icon John Lewis, she supported his historic campaigns and public service while safeguarding vital African American cultural records.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1939 in Los Angeles, California, Lillian Miles was educated in California schools before earning a bachelor’s degree from California State University, Los Angeles. Pursuing advanced studies in library science and literature, she completed a master’s degree in library science from the University of Southern California.

In 1965, Miles relocated to Atlanta, Georgia, to join the library faculty at Atlanta University. She served with distinction as director of special collections in the Trevor Arnett Library, where she meticulously organized, preserved, and expanded the university’s world-renowned archives of African American literature, manuscripts, and historical records. Later, she continued her academic leadership as director of international affairs and external programs at Clark Atlanta University, expanding global study opportunities for students.

In 1967, at a New Year’s Eve party hosted by civil rights activist Xernona Clayton, Miles met young civil rights leader John Robert Lewis. The couple married in 1968 at Ebenezer Baptist Church. Throughout their forty-four-year marriage, Lillian was John’s closest confidante, intellectual partner, and political strategist. She encouraged his run for the Atlanta City Council in 1981 and served as a central advisor in his historic 1986 campaign for the U.S. House of Representatives. Lillian managed congressional district initiatives and supported educational causes until her death on December 31, 2012.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Lillian Miles Lewis spent nearly fifty years in Atlanta preserving African American archival heritage at Atlanta University and Clark Atlanta University while advising her husband Congressman John Lewis. Following her death on December 31, 2012, a memorial service was held at Ebenezer Baptist Church on January 7, 2013. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery ([Auburn Avenue Research Library](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/aarl_afpc_lewislillianmiles20130107); [City of Atlanta Promised Land](https://citydesign.atlantaga.gov/blog/2022/7/28/promised-land-a-tour-of-atlantas-historically-african-american-cemeteries-and-the-graves-of-civil-rights-pioneers)). Her resting place at South-View connects the historic grounds to Atlanta’s distinguished community of academic archivists and civil rights partners.

Name: Lorimer D. Milton
Body:
Overview:
Lorimer Douglas Milton was a prominent economist, Morehouse College professor, president of Citizens Trust Bank, and co-founder of the Yates & Milton drugstore chain. A key business leader and chairman of the Howard University Board of Trustees, Milton financed Black businesses and served on the executive board of South-View Cemetery.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1898 in Washington, D.C., Lorimer Douglas Milton was an exceptionally brilliant student, earning both his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in economics from Brown University, where he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. In 1920, at the personal invitation of Morehouse College president John Hope, Milton relocated to Atlanta to teach economics and banking.

Milton served as professor of economics at Morehouse and Atlanta University for three decades, training a generation of African American business leaders and economists. Concurrently, Milton applied his financial theories to commercial enterprise on Sweet Auburn. In the 1920s, partnering with Clayton R. Yates, Milton established the Yates & Milton drugstore chain, opening retail locations that anchored Black Atlanta’s commercial life. During the 1960s, the basement of their Auburn Avenue pharmacy served as a clandestine meeting site for student sit-in organizers.

In 1927, Milton became cashier of Citizens Trust Bank, later serving as its president for twenty-seven years until his retirement in 1971. Under his leadership, Citizens Trust became the first Black-owned bank insured by the FDIC and the first to join the Federal Reserve System. Milton also co-founded Southeastern Fidelity Fire Insurance Company and served as chairman of the Board of Trustees of Howard University in Washington, D.C., from 1940 to 1966. He passed away on August 2, 1986.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Lorimer D. Milton lived in Atlanta for over sixty-five years, shaping the financial, commercial, and academic landscape of Sweet Auburn through Morehouse College and Citizens Trust Bank. Milton served as first vice president on the board of the South-View Cemetery Association in 1976. When Milton died on August 2, 1986, he was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery alongside Clayton R. Yates and business associates (Henderson 33–34, 229). His resting place at South-View honors a giant of twentieth-century African American finance.

Name: Lucius Henry Holsey
Body:
Overview:
Bishop Lucius Henry Holsey was an eminent theologian, orator, author, and senior bishop of the Christian Methodist Episcopal (CME) Church. Born into slavery, Holsey taught himself to read, helped found the CME Church in 1870, and established Paine College in Augusta, Georgia, in 1882 to educate African American youth.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery on July 3, 1842, near Columbus in Muscogee County, Georgia, to an enslaved woman and her white enslaver, Lucius Henry Holsey was entirely denied formal schooling. Determined to learn, Holsey secretly gathered discarded newspapers and Bible fragments, teaching himself to read by candlelight.

Licensed to preach in 1868, Holsey played a pivotal role in organizing the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church in America (now Christian Methodist Episcopal) in 1870, ensuring Black Methodists possessed institutional and ecclesiastical independence following emancipation. In 1873, at just thirty years of age, Holsey was elected bishop. Holsey was a passionate champion of higher education, leading the founding of Paine College in Augusta, Georgia, in 1882 to provide collegiate education for Black youth with interracial faculty support.

Holsey moved to Atlanta, establishing his residence on Auburn Avenue. Over several decades, he published numerous influential theological works and essays, including *Autobiography, Sermons, Addresses and Essays* (1898) and *Racial Problems in the United States*. Holsey served as senior bishop of the CME Church, directing its national expansion, until his passing in Atlanta on August 3, 1920. On November 17, 1927, approximately five hundred church delegates and civic leaders gathered at South-View Cemetery to unveil a magnificent marble monument honoring him as a "bishop, orator, lecturer and eloquent preacher of the gospel."

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Bishop Lucius Henry Holsey resided on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta for decades, directing CME church affairs, educational initiatives, and theological publications across Georgia. Following his passing in Atlanta on August 3, 1920, Holsey was interred at South-View Cemetery. In 1927, hundreds of delegates gathered at South-View to dedicate an elaborate memorial monument celebrating his life and ecclesiastical leadership (Henderson 132–33, 213; [Eskew](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/lucius-holsey-1842-1920/)). His monument at South-View remains a prominent landmark honoring nineteenth-century Black religious independence.

Name: Lucius L. Lee
Body:
Overview:
Lucius L. Lee was a prominent Atlanta undertaker, fraternal officer, and founding shareholder of South-View Cemetery who operated L. L. Lee & Son on Decatur Street for nearly thirty years. Born into slavery, Lee secured municipal pauper burial contracts and fought for equitable compensation for Black burials, earning deep community respect.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Covington, Newton County, Georgia, in 1854, Lucius L. Lee relocated to Atlanta following the Civil War. At age fifteen, Lee gained employment at O. H. Jones' livery stable, where he developed expert skills in carriage driving and horse management. He subsequently apprenticed in mortuary science under white undertaker Charles H. Swift, acquiring rigorous technical training in embalming and funeral administration.

In the 1880s, Lee established his own independent undertaking firm on Decatur Street. He operated the business for nearly three decades, eventually partnering with his son William to form "L. L. Lee & Son." In 1904, Lee was awarded the municipal pauper burial contract at $1.40 per body, providing a shroud, coffin, and carriage transport—a stark contrast to the $10 the city paid white undertakers for white paupers. When Lee raised his bid to $2.50 in 1905 to demand fair compensation, the city council awarded the contract to a lower bidder.

Lee was an influential civic and fraternal leader, holding high offices in the Prince Hall Masons, Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias, and the Knights and Daughters of Tabor. When Lee died in 1915 after a prolonged illness, his funeral was delayed so state Tabor officials returning from Savannah could attend his massive service at Big Bethel AME Church.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Lucius L. Lee lived and operated his mortuary business in Atlanta for four decades, conducting hundreds of funerals to South-View Cemetery. In 1886, Lee purchased an original burial lot at South-View Cemetery and became a shareholder, actively supporting the cemetery's mission of providing dignified Christian burials. Lee passed away in 1915 and was buried at South-View Cemetery beside his wife Julia, who had died in 1912 (Henderson 46, 48–49). His resting place at South-View honors a pioneer of Atlanta's mortuary profession.

Name: Ludie Clay Andrews
Body:
Overview:
Ludie Clay Andrews was a visionary healthcare pioneer, hospital administrator, and civil rights advocate who became Georgia's first licensed African American registered nurse in 1920. As the founder of the Grady Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses and superintendent of MacVicar Hospital, Andrews waged a relentless decade-long legal campaign against the state nursing board that dismantled racial barriers and established professional equity in southern medicine.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1875 in Baldwin County near Milledgeville, Georgia, Ludie Clay Andrews dedicated her life to nursing and healthcare equity. She graduated from the nurse training program at Spelman Seminary’s MacVicar Hospital in 1906, quickly distinguishing herself as an exceptional clinician, instructor, and supervisor.

In 1914, Andrews organized the Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses at Grady Memorial Hospital, establishing a rigorous curriculum to prepare Black women for professional healthcare careers. When discriminatory state regulations barred Black graduates from taking the state licensing examination, Andrews launched an unyielding ten-year legal and legislative battle at her own expense. When state officials offered to grant Andrews an individual license as a special compromise, she resolutely refused to abandon her students, insisting on equal examination rights for all qualified Black nurses.

In 1920, Andrews won a landmark legal victory, forcing the state of Georgia to open the licensing exam to Black nurses and becoming Georgia's first licensed Black registered nurse. From 1928 to 1948, Andrews served as superintendent of MacVicar Hospital and director of student health services across the Atlanta University Center. She was also an active civic reformer in the Neighborhood Union alongside Lugenia Burns Hope. In 1943, Andrews received the prestigious Mary Mahoney Award from the National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses, and she was posthumously inducted into Georgia Women of Achievement. She passed away in Atlanta on January 13, 1969.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Ludie Clay Andrews spent over six decades in Atlanta transforming nursing education at Grady Hospital, directing student medical services at Spelman College, and advancing community welfare. Following her death in January 1969 at age ninety-three, she was celebrated statewide as the "Dean of Black Nurses." Andrews was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where she rests among Atlanta's preeminent healthcare trailblazers, educators, and civic reformers (Henderson 6, 171). Her resting place at South-View commemorates a courageous pioneer who opened southern medical professions to generations of Black women.

Name: Luther Judson Price
Body:
Overview:
Luther Judson Price was a prominent merchant, postmaster, real estate investor, and civic leader who anchored south Atlanta’s Brownsville community for over five decades. As Brownsville’s federal postmaster and general store proprietor, Price organized neighborhood defense during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre and donated land and funds to build public schools for Black youth.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1856 in rural Georgia, Luther Judson Price relocated to Atlanta as a young man to pursue commercial opportunities. In the 1880s, Price settled in the developing south Atlanta neighborhood of Brownsville, adjacent to Clark University and Gammon Theological Seminary. At the bustling crossroads of Jonesboro and McDonough roads, Price constructed and opened a substantial general merchandise store.

Price's store quickly became the economic and civic anchor of Brownsville. When the federal government appointed Price as Brownsville's postmaster, he became one of the few African American postmasters in the region, managing mail distribution for thousands of Black families, educators, and seminary students. Price expanded his investments into residential real estate, constructing rental housing for working-class families and providing credit to community members during economic hardships.

In late September 1906, when white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods across Atlanta, Price courageously helped organize community defense and relief committees in Brownsville. When county police and armed vigilantes raided Brownsville on September 24, Price was falsely accused of supplying firearms and ammunition to Black citizens defending their homes. He was arrested and held in the Fulton County jail before all unfounded charges were dismissed. Continuing his successful business for decades, Price donated real estate and funding for local education. Today, Luther J. Price Middle School stands as a tribute to his legacy. He passed away in 1936.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Luther Judson Price spent over fifty years in Atlanta anchoring Brownsville as postmaster, merchant, and defender of civil rights. Following his death in Atlanta in 1936, community members and educators honored his lifelong dedication to south Atlanta. Price was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among his fellow Brownsville neighbors and civic trailblazers (Henderson 236; [Celebration of Life Honoring Watts](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/aarl_afpc_wattsalberthawes20011126)). His resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary business leader who defended his community with courage.

Name: Mabel Whitman
Body:
Overview:
Mabel Whitman was an entertainer, theatrical producer, and the eldest of the acclaimed Whitman Sisters, directing one of the longest-running, highest-earning, and most influential Black vaudeville troupes in American history. From 1909 until the 1940s, Whitman managed the company's touring productions, broke theatrical segregation barriers, and launched the careers of legendary performers.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1880 in Kansas, Mabel Whitman was the eldest daughter of Rev. Albery Allson Whitman, a noted African Methodist Episcopal minister and epic poet, and Caddie Whitman. Raised in an environment steeped in music and elocution, Mabel began touring with her sisters—Essie, Alberta, and Alice—singing religious hymns and jubilee spirituals at church conventions across the Midwest.

Around 1899, Mabel and her sister Essie launched their professional stage careers as the Danzette Sisters. In 1904, the sisters staged an early act of civil rights resistance by refusing to perform at a theater in Birmingham, Alabama, unless Black patrons were granted integrated main-floor seating. Following her mother's death in 1909, Mabel assumed full executive and creative management of the company, officially founding the Whitman Sisters Comedy Company.

Under Mabel's shrewd management, the revue expanded into a national theatrical powerhouse featuring more than forty dancers, musicians, and comedians. Mabel was widely recognized as one of the few women—and one of the only African American women—to maintain absolute executive control over a major touring theatrical troupe on the TOBA and Keith vaudeville circuits. She personally booked itineraries, negotiated contracts with white theater owners, and trained emerging young Black talent, including Count Basie and Bill "Bojangles" Robinson. Mabel directed the company until her passing in Atlanta in 1942.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Mabel Whitman maintained deep, enduring ties to Atlanta, using the city as the primary winter rehearsing base and management headquarters for the Whitman Sisters Revue. When Mabel retired and passed away in Atlanta in 1942, her theatrical peers and community gathered to celebrate her pioneering career. She was interred at South-View Cemetery in the Whitman family plot, where her sisters Essie, Alberta, and Alice were later laid to rest beside her (Henderson 252). Her resting place at South-View honors a pioneer of American theater.

Name: Marshall Carter
Body:
Overview:
Marshall Carter was a thirteen-year-old African American schoolboy who was murdered by a white mob on the opening night of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Recorded for more than a century as an anonymous casualty, historical research in 2023 restored his identity and documented his final resting place at South-View Cemetery.

Life and Contributions:
Marshall Carter was born around 1893 in Atlanta, Georgia. He resided with his family on Love Street in the historic Summerhill neighborhood, just south of downtown Atlanta. As a thirteen-year-old youth, Carter attended local public elementary schools, growing up in a working-class African American community during the rise of Jim Crow segregation.

On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, white mobs numbering in the thousands invaded downtown Atlanta, attacking Black laborers and pedestrians along Peachtree, Pryor, and Decatur streets. While walking home from downtown, thirteen-year-old Carter was surrounded and savagely assaulted by an armed mob of white men and boys. Carter suffered a catastrophic skull fracture inflicted by blunt force trauma from stones, wooden clubs, or gun butts.

Bystanders rushed the gravely injured youth to Grady Memorial Hospital, which operated segregated wards for Black patients. Despite emergency medical attention, Carter succumbed to his severe head injuries later that night on September 22, 1906, becoming one of the youngest documented fatalities of the massacre. For over 117 years, Carter's name was omitted from general public records until archival research in September 2023 by the National Center for Civil and Human Rights uncovered his original Fulton County death certificate, officially restoring his identity and documenting his tragic murder for history.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Marshall Carter lived in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood and was killed at age thirteen during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Following his death at Grady Hospital, his family brought his body to South-View Cemetery, where he was interred in an unmarked plot. In September 2023, archival historians from the National Center for Civil and Human Rights confirmed his burial at South-View Cemetery ([Palmore](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/); [WSB-TV 2023](https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/two-victims-1906-atlanta-race-massacre-identified-nearly-120-years-later/5LVMJY55DFBPZP76CKLWA57T5Y/)). His presence at South-View stands as a solemn memorial to young lives stolen by southern racial terror.

Last updated: November 2026

Name: Martin Luther King Jr.
Body:
Overview:
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was an Atlanta-born Baptist minister, Nobel Peace Prize laureate, and the foremost moral leader of the modern Civil Rights Movement. Leading the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Birmingham campaign, the March on Washington, and the Selma march, King dedicated his life to nonviolent resistance, civil rights, economic justice, and international peace.

Life and Contributions:
Born on January 15, 1929, at 501 Auburn Avenue in Atlanta, Georgia, Martin Luther King Jr. was the son of Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King. Growing up immersed in Ebenezer Baptist Church, King entered Morehouse College at age fifteen, graduating in 1948 before earning a divinity degree from Crozer Theological Seminary and a Ph.D. in systematic theology from Boston University in 1955.

While pastoring Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama, King was chosen to lead the 1955–1956 Montgomery Bus Boycott, which successfully desegregated public transit and launched him into global prominence. In 1957, King co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), establishing its national headquarters on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta. King returned to Atlanta in 1960 to co-pastor Ebenezer with his father, joining the student sit-ins at Rich’s Department Store.

Throughout the 1960s, King orchestrated monumental direct-action campaigns that captured the world’s conscience. In 1963, his "Letter from Birmingham Jail" and his "I Have a Dream" address at the March on Washington catalyzed passage of the historic Civil Rights Act of 1964. That year, King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, becoming its youngest recipient. In 1965, he led the Selma-to-Montgomery voting rights marches, securing the Voting Rights Act of 1965. In his final years, King launched the Poor People’s Campaign and spoke out forcefully against poverty and the Vietnam War. On April 4, 1968, King was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born, educated, and lived in Atlanta, directing the national civil rights struggle from his SCLC headquarters on Auburn Avenue. Following his assassination, his funeral was held in Atlanta on April 9, 1968, followed by a procession of 100,000 mourners to Morehouse College. King was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he remained until 1970 when his crypt was moved to the King Center (Henderson 114–15). His parents were later interred in his original South-View crypt, permanently linking the cemetery to his legacy.

Name: Martin Luther King Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Martin Luther King Sr., affectionately revered as "Daddy King," was a stalwart civil rights leader, civic organizer, and pastor of Atlanta's historic Ebenezer Baptist Church for forty-four years. King Sr. championed voting rights, desegregated Atlanta teacher pay, and nurtured the moral courage of his son, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Life and Contributions:
Born Michael King on December 19, 1899, in Stockbridge, Henry County, Georgia, into a family of impoverished sharecroppers, King Sr. experienced the brutal realities of southern racism firsthand. Determined to escape agricultural peonage and pursue Christian ministry, he moved to Atlanta during World War I, working manual jobs while attending Bryant Preparatory School. In 1926, he married Alberta Christine Williams, daughter of Ebenezer Baptist Church's pastor, Rev. A.D. Williams. In 1930, King Sr. graduated with a bachelor’s degree in theology from Morehouse College.

In 1931, following the death of Rev. Williams, King Sr. assumed the pastorate of Ebenezer Baptist Church, serving until 1975. Over four decades, King Sr. built Ebenezer into one of the South’s most influential institutional churches. He was equally active in civic battles for racial equity. In 1935, he led a historic voting rights march of hundreds of Black citizens to Atlanta City Hall, demanding equal registration access. In the 1940s, working alongside the NAACP, King Sr. filed lawsuits that successfully equalized salaries for Black public school teachers in Atlanta.

King Sr. served as a trustee of Morehouse College and Atlanta University and was an executive leader in the Atlanta Negro Voters League. He endured unimaginable personal grief—losing his son Martin to assassination in 1968, his son A.D. to drowning in 1969, and his wife Alberta to murder at the Ebenezer organ in 1974—yet continued preaching love and reconciliation until his death on November 11, 1984.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. lived and organized in Atlanta for over six decades, leading Ebenezer Baptist Church and guiding the Atlanta NAACP. When King Sr. passed away on November 11, 1984, he was buried at South-View Cemetery in the very crypt where his son Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. had initially rested from 1968 to 1970, beside his wife Alberta (Henderson 115, 220). His resting place at South-View honors a fearless patriarch of Atlanta’s religious and civil rights struggles.

Name: Mattiwilda Dobbs
Body:
Overview:
Mattiwilda Dobbs was an internationally acclaimed coloratura soprano, recitalist, and vocal pedagogue who shattered major racial barriers in classical music and opera. Born in Atlanta, Dobbs made history in 1953 as the first African American singer to perform a principal role at La Scala in Milan and in 1956 debuted at the Metropolitan Opera.

Life and Contributions:
Born on July 11, 1925, in Atlanta, Georgia, Mattiwilda Dobbs was one of six daughters of prominent civic organizer John Wesley Dobbs and Irene Thompson Dobbs. Immersed in music and scholarship on Sweet Auburn, Dobbs began studying piano at age seven and sang in the choir at First Congregational Church. She attended Spelman College, graduating as class valedictorian in 1946 with a degree in music and Spanish.

Dobbs moved to New York to study under renowned vocal coaches, earning a master's degree in Spanish from Columbia University in 1948. Awarded Marian Anderson and John Hay Whitney fellowships, Dobbs traveled to Europe to refine her operatic training. In 1951, she won the prestigious International Music Competition in Geneva, Switzerland, launching an extraordinary international opera career.

In 1953, Dobbs achieved an operatic milestone by becoming the first African American singer to perform a principal role at the historic Teatro alla Scala in Milan, singing Elvira in Rossini’s *L'Italiana in Algeri*. In 1956, she made her historic debut at the Metropolitan Opera in New York as Gilda in Verdi’s *Rigoletto*, becoming only the third Black artist to perform there. Refusing to sing before segregated audiences, Dobbs declined all invitations to perform in her hometown until 1962, when she performed before Atlanta's first integrated municipal audience at the Municipal Auditorium. She later taught voice at Howard University and Spelman College before passing away on December 8, 2015.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Mattiwilda Dobbs was born, raised, and educated in Atlanta at Spelman College, using her international stature to challenge municipal segregation in Atlanta’s concert halls. Following her passing on December 8, 2015, at age ninety, her life was commemorated across the cultural world. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery in the Dobbs family lot, where her parents John Wesley and Irene Dobbs and sister Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson rest (Henderson 194). Her grave at South-View honors a trailblazer of the world operatic stage.

Name: Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr.
Body:
Overview:
Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr. was a transformative political leader, attorney, and orator who made history in 1973 when he was elected Atlanta's first African American mayor, becoming the first Black mayor of a major Southern city. Serving three impactful terms, Jackson pioneered affirmative action in municipal contracting and expanded Atlanta's international airport.

Life and Contributions:
Born on March 23, 1938, in Dallas, Texas, Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr. moved to Atlanta as a child when his father, Rev. Maynard H. Jackson Sr., became pastor of Friendship Baptist Church. His maternal grandfather was civic titan John Wesley Dobbs. An intellectual prodigy, Jackson entered Morehouse College at age fourteen as a Ford Foundation early-entry scholar, graduating in 1956. He earned his law degree cum laude from North Carolina Central University in 1964.

In 1968, Jackson launched a courageous challenge against incumbent U.S. Senator Herman Talmadge, winning widespread support in Atlanta's Black precincts. In 1969, he was elected Vice Mayor of Atlanta, and in October 1973, at age thirty-five, Jackson made history by being elected Mayor of Atlanta, inaugurating a new era of Black municipal leadership in the South.

During his three terms (1974–1982 and 1990–1994), Jackson revolutionized city governance. He established groundbreaking affirmative action joint-venture policies, ensuring that minority- and women-owned businesses received over 25 percent of municipal contracts, up from less than one percent. His administration oversaw the construction of the massive midfield passenger terminal complex at Atlanta’s international airport, completing the multi-million-dollar project on time and within budget. Jackson also expanded MARTA rail transit, reformed the police department, and co-led Atlanta's successful bid to host the 1996 Olympic Games. Jackson passed away on June 23, 2003.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Maynard Holbrook Jackson Jr. shaped the modern economic, political, and physical landscape of Atlanta as its historic first Black mayor. Following his death in June 2003, his funeral was held at the Atlanta Civic Center, and the city honored his legacy by renaming the facility Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. He was laid to rest at Oakland Cemetery in his family lot (Henderson 216; [Maynard Jackson Elected](https://www.todayingeorgiahistory.org/tih-georgia-day/maynard-jackson-elected/)). His profound political legacy remains inextricably intertwined with his grandfather John Wesley Dobbs and mother Irene Dobbs Jackson, who rest at South-View Cemetery.

Name: Miles G. Amos
Body:
Overview:
Miles G. Amos was a prominent pharmacist, healthcare entrepreneur, and civic leader who operated Amos' Drugstore as a trusted healthcare anchor on Atlanta's West Side for over four decades. Continuing a pioneering family tradition established by his uncle Moses Amos, Miles broke municipal political barriers by winning election to the City Executive Committee in 1953.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, into one of the city’s foremost African American medical and business families, Miles G. Amos was the nephew of Moses Amos, Georgia's first licensed Black pharmacist. Inspired by his family’s enterprise, Amos pursued professional pharmaceutical education, graduating with a degree in pharmacy and earning his state license as a registered pharmacist.

In 1928, Amos took over the management of the West Side Drug Store on Ashby Street (now Joseph E. Lowery Boulevard) in northwest Atlanta, renaming it Amos' Drugstore. For forty-one years until his retirement in 1969, Amos' Drugstore served as a cornerstone of healthcare and community life for Black Atlantans who faced segregation at white-owned pharmacies. Amos filled hundreds of thousands of prescriptions, provided medical supplies, and created employment opportunities for young African Americans entering healthcare.

In addition to his business success, Amos was an active and courageous civic leader. In 1953, Amos challenged racial exclusion in municipal Democratic Party primary politics. Winning a landmark legal decision, Amos secured election to the Atlanta City Executive Committee from the Third Ward, becoming one of the first African Americans elected to city party governance since Reconstruction. He supported voter registration drives, church initiatives, and collegiate scholarships throughout his life before passing away in 1995.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Miles G. Amos lived and conducted business on Atlanta's West Side for more than forty years, providing vital pharmaceutical healthcare and winning historic political office in 1953. Following his passing in 1995, community leaders and pharmacists honored his decades of community service. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside his uncle Moses Amos and generations of Sweet Auburn business leaders (Henderson 170). His grave at South-View commemorates an essential healthcare provider and political trailblazer.

Name: Milton Brown
Body:
Overview:
Milton Brown was an African American laborer from Atlanta who was murdered by white rioters during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal assault reflects the catastrophic human toll of four days of unchecked racial terror, during which white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods, killed dozens, and displaced hundreds.

Life and Contributions:
Milton Brown was an African American resident who lived and worked in Atlanta during the turn of the twentieth century. Like thousands of Black citizens during this period, Brown earned his livelihood through manual labor in Atlanta's expanding commercial economy, seeking to provide for his family within the strictures of legal Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, inflammatory political speeches by candidates for governor, combined with fabricated, sensational headlines in local white daily newspapers, whipped racial tensions into violence. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys took control of downtown Atlanta, launching violent assaults against Black laborers, streetcar passengers, and pedestrians. Over the next three days, roving armed mobs attacked Black homes and business districts.

Brown was caught in the path of the mob violence on September 22 and was violently assaulted, sustaining fatal injuries. Municipal death records and subsequent research confirmed that Brown died as a direct victim of the massacre. For over a century, Brown’s death was omitted from mainstream city histories until rigorous archival research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project restored his memory, identifying him as an innocent casualty of racial violence.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Milton Brown lived, labored, and was murdered in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the tragedy, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions neglected deceased African American casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds to provide solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre victims brought to its care (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Milton Harvey
Body:
Overview:
Milton Harvey was a fourteen-year-old African American youth from Atlanta whose abduction and death in September 1979 marked one of the earliest tragedies of the Atlanta Child Murders crisis. His disappearance while running an errand on his bicycle ignited widespread dread and catalyzed community organizing to protect Black children across metropolitan Atlanta.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1965 in Atlanta, Georgia, Milton Harvey was raised by his family in a close-knit working-class neighborhood. Known as a lively, helpful, and dependable teenager, fourteen-year-old Milton enjoyed outdoor activities, sports, and assisting his family with everyday household chores. In the late summer of 1979, an alarming pattern of youth disappearances had begun to emerge across Atlanta, creating anxiety among local parents.

On the afternoon of September 4, 1979, Milton left his home on his yellow bicycle to run an errand for his mother, riding toward a local bank and grocery store. He never arrived. His sudden disappearance sent shockwaves through his south Atlanta neighborhood, prompting family members, neighbors, and volunteers to organize search parties across wooded areas and vacant lots. Weeks turned into months with no sign of the missing youth.

In November 1979, Milton’s remains were discovered in a wooded area off Redwine Road in Fulton County. Medical examiners determined that he had been murdered, becoming one of the earliest recognized victims of the serial crisis that became known as the Atlanta Child Murders. Milton's tragic loss deeply affected Black Atlantans, contributing directly to the mobilization of community mothers who demanded aggressive federal and municipal task force intervention to solve the killings.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Milton Harvey spent his childhood in Atlanta, and his tragic abduction and murder occurred within Fulton County during the onset of the 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Following the discovery of his remains, his grieving family held memorial services in Atlanta. Milton was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where multiple victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were provided solemn, sacred resting places (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His grave at South-View connects the cemetery to the city’s collective sorrow and enduring remembrance of innocent children.

Name: Milton Risdon
Body:
Overview:
Milton Risdon was an African American Atlanta resident who survived the intense gunfire and firestorm of the 1902 Pittsburgh Riot. Barricaded inside Will Richardson’s grocery store during a multi-hour armed siege, Risdon escaped through a hail of bullets as the building collapsed, survived his wounds, and was later interred at South-View Cemetery.

Life and Contributions:
While details of his birth and early life are unrecorded in census records, Milton Risdon lived and worked in Atlanta's Pittsburgh neighborhood at the turn of the twentieth century. On the evening of May 16, 1902, Risdon joined store owner Will Richardson at his grocery at the corner of McDaniel and Amy streets. In the early morning hours of May 17, when former police officer Samuel Kerlin returned with police and armed vigilantes, Risdon remained inside as the posse launched an armed assault.

During the multi-hour siege, thousands of rounds penetrated the wooden storefront. When the mob ignited the building to force the occupants out, smoke and flames engulfed the structure. As the roof began collapsing, Risdon made a desperate dash for survival through the rear exit. A hail of gunfire struck him multiple times as he fled into surrounding alleyways. Despite sustaining severe bullet wounds, Risdon survived the barrage and was captured by police cordons.

Risdon was transported under heavy armed guard to the Fulton County jail, where he was formally charged with complicity in the shootout. Risdon was among several Black men detained in the riot's aftermath, enduring incarceration and physical trauma from the attack. After surviving his wounds and navigating legal persecution following the siege, Risdon lived out his remaining days in Atlanta before his death.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Milton Risdon was a central figure and direct survivor of the 1902 Pittsburgh Riot in southwest Atlanta. After surviving multiple bullet wounds during the siege and enduring subsequent legal trials, Risdon lived out his remaining days in the city of Atlanta. Following his passing, he was provided a dignified burial at South-View Cemetery near the resting places of fellow riot victims and neighbors (Henderson 116). His resting place at South-View connects the cemetery to the dramatic historical record of Black resistance and survival during the 1902 Pittsburgh unrest.

Name: Mitchell Cargile
Body:
Overview:
Mitchell Cargile was Atlanta's first documented African American undertaker, a master carpenter, and a founding board member of South-View Cemetery. Born into slavery, Cargile purchased his own time before emancipation, built an extensive southern mortuary enterprise, and acquired substantial Atlanta real estate, paving the way for generations of Black funeral directors.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Monticello, Jasper County, Georgia, in 1811, Mitchell Cargile learned skilled carpentry and cabinetmaking as a young man. In the mid-1850s, Cargile negotiated an agreement to "purchase his own time" from his enslaver, paying regular fees to live and work independently in Atlanta. Following emancipation in 1865, Cargile utilized his woodworking expertise to open an undertaking business.

By 1874, he was actively advertising his custom "burial cases" in the *Atlanta Constitution*, and the 1876 Atlanta City Directory listed him as a professional cabinetmaker and mortician. Cargile built a thriving enterprise that served clients throughout Georgia and neighboring southern states. He trained his sons in carpentry and mortuary arts, bringing his son Lewis into formal partnership. In 1881, after being falsely implicated in a grave-robbing scheme supplying medical colleges, Cargile published a vigorous "Correction" in the *Atlanta Constitution*, affirming that he had never violated a sacred trust.

During the 1880s, Cargile acquired extensive real estate holdings and served on the founding board and shareholder directory of South-View Cemetery. Although the Panic of 1893 caused severe financial hardship—forcing him to default on a mortgage for a horse-drawn hearse—Cargile maintained his business until his death in 1896.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Mitchell Cargile was Atlanta's pioneer Black undertaker and an original shareholder and director of the South-View Cemetery Association, directing many of the cemetery's earliest funeral processions. Cargile lived, purchased real estate, and conducted business in Atlanta for over four decades following emancipation. When he passed away in 1896, he was buried at South-View Cemetery, where his son Lewis continued the family mortuary business for decades (Henderson 47–48). His resting place at South-View honors the founding patriarch of Atlanta's African American funeral industry.

Name: Moses Amos
Body:
Overview:
Moses Amos was an entrepreneur and pharmaceutical pioneer who became Georgia's first licensed African American pharmacist in 1889. Operating the renowned Gate City Drug Store on Auburn Avenue for nearly forty years, Amos established Sweet Auburn's foremost healthcare anchor, filled over one million prescriptions, and mentored generations of Black medical professionals.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1866, Moses Amos began working at age eleven as an errand boy for Dr. J. C. Huss, a white physician and apothecary. Demonstrating extraordinary intelligence, discipline, and scientific aptitude, Amos served a rigorous twelve-year apprenticeship under Huss, mastering pharmacopeia, chemical compounding, and drug preparation. In 1889, Amos sat for the Georgia State Board of Pharmacy examination and passed with honors, becoming the first licensed African American pharmacist in Georgia.

In 1891, when physicians Dr. Henry Rutherford Butler and Dr. Thomas Heathe Slater acquired Huss's pharmacy, Amos was appointed general manager. Amos subsequently acquired full ownership of the business, renaming it the Gate City Drug Store. In 1914, he relocated the pharmacy into the newly constructed Odd Fellows Building on Auburn Avenue, where it became the social, economic, and medical hub of Sweet Auburn.

Over a distinguished career spanning nearly five decades, Amos filled more than one million prescriptions and pioneered inclusive employment practices, including hiring African American women as store clerks. He trained and mentored at least ten young men who became licensed pharmacists and physicians, including his nephew Miles G. Amos. During the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, police warned Amos to close his drugstore immediately, admitting authorities could not protect him. Amos continued operating his pharmacy until his death in 1928.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Moses Amos spent his entire life in Atlanta, pioneering pharmaceutical licensing, managing Gate City Drug Store, and building Sweet Auburn commerce. Following his death in 1928, community members and health professionals honored his historic legacy. Amos was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow Sweet Auburn entrepreneurs and civic leaders (Henderson 170; [Georgia Pharmacy Association](https://www.gpha.org/mission-history)). His resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary pioneer who opened healthcare professions to generations of African Americans in Georgia.

Name: Nicodemus Holmes
Body:
Overview:
Nicodemus Holmes was a retail merchant, church leader, and the founding first president of the South-View Cemetery Association. Guiding the cemetery through the catastrophic national depression of the Panic of 1893, Holmes petitioned city council for tax relief and preserved corporate solvency, ensuring South-View’s survival as a sacred African American institution.

Life and Contributions:
Although his early life details and exact birth and death dates remain unrecorded in municipal census files, Nicodemus Holmes emerged in post-Civil War Atlanta as an accomplished commercial merchant and respected religious figure. Operating a prosperous retail boot and shoe store in downtown Atlanta, Holmes established a reputation for sound fiscal management, administrative discipline, and community integrity.

As an original stockholder in South-View Cemetery in 1886, Holmes recognized that the enterprise represented both an indispensable commercial corporation and a sacred sanctuary of dignity for Black Atlantans excluded from equal treatment in municipal cemeteries. Elected as South-View's first president, Holmes provided executive leadership during the cemetery's critical first decade.

When the Panic of 1893 devastated the national and local economy—triggering mass bank failures, prolonged unemployment, and business insolvencies—South-View faced acute financial distress while continuing to inter two-thirds of Atlanta's deceased African Americans. On August 7, 1893, Holmes and the board of directors submitted a formal petition to the Atlanta City Council requesting exemption from the city's $100 annual license fee, arguing that South-View's modest resources and charitable pauper burials warranted municipal relief. Although the council denied the request, Holmes maintained disciplined fiscal oversight, renegotiated burial contracts, and kept South-View solvent throughout the depression.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Nicodemus Holmes lived and operated his merchant business in downtown Atlanta, serving as the first president of the South-View Cemetery Association from its inception through the economic crisis of 1893. He petitioned the Atlanta City Council on August 7, 1893, to defend the cemetery's charitable work with Atlanta's impoverished Black population. Holmes was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, the historic institution he guided through economic peril (Henderson 27, 45). His resting place honors an essential executive founder of South-View.

Name: Norris B. Herndon
Body:
Overview:
Norris Bumstead Herndon was an executive and philanthropist who served as president and chief executive officer of Atlanta Life Insurance Company for over four decades. Succeeding his father Alonzo Herndon, he guided the company through the Great Depression, expanded operations across eleven states, and endowed the Herndon Foundation to support Atlanta University.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, on July 15, 1897, Norris Bumstead Herndon was the only child of Atlanta Life Insurance Company founder Alonzo Herndon and Adrienne McNeil Herndon, a renowned professor of elocution at Atlanta University. Reared in the University Center neighborhood, Herndon attended the 1905 founding meeting of the Niagara Movement in Fort Erie with his father.

Herndon attended Atlanta University, graduating in 1919 with a bachelor’s degree in business, and subsequently earned a Master of Business Administration from Harvard Business School in 1921, becoming one of the earliest African American Harvard MBA graduates. Returning to Atlanta, Herndon joined Atlanta Life as vice president and cashier. Following his father's passing in 1927, Norris assumed the presidency of Atlanta Life Insurance Company at age thirty.

Under Herndon's disciplined and conservative financial management, Atlanta Life navigated the severe shocks of the Great Depression without insolvency or defaulting on a single policy. Over his forty-six-year presidency until 1973, Herndon expanded the company's assets from $1 million to over $84 million, operating in eleven states. He established the Alonzo F. and Norris B. Herndon Foundation, which channeled millions of dollars in philanthropic support to Atlanta University, Morris Brown College, Morehouse College, the YMCA, and civil rights groups. Herndon passed away in Atlanta on June 7, 1977.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Norris B. Herndon lived in Atlanta his entire life, leading Atlanta Life Insurance Company on Sweet Auburn for forty-six years and residing in the historic Herndon Home mansion. Following his passing on June 7, 1977, civic and business leaders paid tribute to his corporate stewardship. Herndon was interred at South-View Cemetery in the magnificent Herndon family mausoleum beside his parents, Alonzo and Adrienne Herndon (Henderson 210). His resting place at South-View permanently honors a philanthropic titan of Black corporate America.

Name: Patrick Rogers
Body:
Overview:
Patrick Rogers was a vibrant sixteen-year-old African American teenager and aspiring musician from Atlanta who was abducted and murdered in November 1980 during the Atlanta Child Murders crisis. Known affectionately as "Pat Man," his heartbreaking death deepened the anguish of working-class neighborhoods and spurred community campaigns demanding justice for Atlanta’s missing children.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1964 in Atlanta, Georgia, Patrick Rogers grew up in a lively south Atlanta neighborhood near the Interstate 20 corridor. Known to friends and family by his nickname "Pat Man," Patrick was an outgoing, musically gifted teenager with an infectious smile and artistic ambition. He spent hours writing original songs, rapping, and creating musical beats with his close friend Joe Harper, dreaming of building a future in the emerging hip-hop and rhythm-and-blues scenes of Atlanta.

During late 1980, fear hung heavily over Black neighborhoods across Atlanta, as children and adolescents were being systematically targeted and abducted. On the evening of November 10, 1980, sixteen-year-old Patrick was hanging out near a familiar fast-food restaurant on Moreland Avenue near I-20. When he failed to return home, his family immediately sounded the alarm, contacting police and coordinating search parties across the surrounding community.

Tragically, on December 7, 1980, Patrick’s body was recovered from the Chattahoochee River in Cobb County. Medical examiners determined that he had died from blunt force head trauma. His murder shattered his family and sent shockwaves through local youth communities. Patrick's case was incorporated into the official investigations of the joint Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force and the FBI, galvanizing mothers in the STOP Committee to demand curfews and municipal protection.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Patrick Rogers spent his entire youth in Atlanta, and his tragic death in late 1980 occurred during the peak of the metropolitan missing and murdered crisis. Following the recovery of his remains, his grieving family and community held memorial services in Atlanta. Patrick was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where multiple youth victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were interred in sacred peace (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His resting place at South-View preserves the memory of an aspiring young artist taken by violence.

Name: Peter James Bryant
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Dr. Peter James Bryant was an influential Baptist minister, orator, author, and pastor of Atlanta's historic Wheat Street Baptist Church for thirty-one years. Bryant spearheaded church rebuilding following the Great Fire of 1917, co-founded the Christian Civic League after the 1906 Race Massacre, and helped establish the Atlanta Mutual Insurance Association.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1870 in rural Georgia, Peter James Bryant was educated in Baptist schools before graduating from Morehouse College (then Atlanta Baptist College) with high honors. Possessing an exceptional command of sacred literature and oratory, Bryant was called to the pastorate of Wheat Street Baptist Church on Auburn Avenue in 1898.

Over thirty-one years of transformative pastoral leadership until his death in 1929, Bryant elevated Wheat Street into one of the largest African American congregations in the United States, expanding membership to over 3,000 congregants. In 1905, recognizing the acute need for economic security among Black families, Bryant partnered with Rev. Joseph A. Carey to approach Alonzo Herndon, convincing him to purchase and reorganize the Atlanta Benevolent and Protective Association, which became Atlanta Life Insurance Company.

Following the horrific 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, Bryant hosted Black religious and civic leaders at Wheat Street to form the Christian Civic League, advocating for moral fortitude, legal protection, and community relief. In May 1917, when the devastating Great Atlanta Fire destroyed much of the Old Fourth Ward and burned Wheat Street’s sanctuary to the ground, Bryant mobilized his congregation and national donors to construct a magnificent Gothic-style stone sanctuary on Auburn Avenue, which was dedicated in 1921. Bryant was also a trustee of Morehouse College. He passed away in 1929.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Dr. Peter James Bryant lived and pastored on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta for over three decades, rebuilding Wheat Street Baptist Church after the 1917 fire and helping launch Atlanta Life Insurance Company. Following his death in 1929, thousands of mourners attended his funeral at Wheat Street. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow religious leaders and congregants (Henderson 182; South-View Brochure). His resting place at South-View honors a giant of Sweet Auburn faith and institutional development.

Name: Q.V. Williamson Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Quentin V. Williamson Sr. was a prominent real estate developer, broker, civic activist, and politician who broke a historic seventy-year color barrier in 1965 when he became the first African American elected to the Atlanta Board of Aldermen (now City Council) since Reconstruction. Williamson opened residential housing opportunities and championed voting rights.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1918 in Atlanta, Georgia, Quentin V. Williamson Sr. attended local public schools and graduated from Morehouse College. After serving his country in the military during World War II, Williamson entered the real estate profession, founding Q. V. Williamson & Company. His firm became one of the largest and most successful Black-owned real estate and mortgage brokerage enterprises in the South.

During legal segregation, white-controlled municipal zoning, restrictive covenants, and hostile redlining prevented Black families from purchasing homes outside overcrowded enclaves. Williamson fought tirelessly against housing discrimination. He served as president of the Empire Real Estate Board in Atlanta and later as president of the National Association of Real Estate Brokers. Williamson opened new subdivisions for Black homeowners in northwest and southwest Atlanta, providing modern housing and wealth accumulation for middle-class Black families.

Concurrently, Williamson was an indispensable civil rights organizer, serving as a key executive officer in the Atlanta Negro Voters League alongside A.T. Walden and John Wesley Dobbs. In 1965, Williamson achieved a historic political milestone by winning election to the Atlanta Board of Aldermen, becoming the city's first Black alderman since Reconstruction. He served on the city council for eight years, advocating for municipal employment integration and public improvements in Black neighborhoods until his passing in 1985.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Q.V. Williamson Sr. lived his entire life in Atlanta, pioneering real estate access for Black families and shattering political segregation as Atlanta's first post-Reconstruction Black alderman in 1965. When Williamson passed away in 1985 at age sixty-seven, city leaders and citizens commemorated his transformative civic leadership. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow civil rights and political trailblazers (Henderson 254–55, 275). His resting place at South-View honors an architect of Atlanta's political desegregation.

Name: Rheubin M. Taylor
Body:
Overview:
Rheubin Marcellus Taylor was a dedicated science educator, labor activist, and civil rights leader who served as president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association. In 1948, Taylor partnered with the NAACP and attorney Constance Baker Motley to sue the Atlanta Board of Education, winning equal pay for Black teachers.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Georgia, Rheubin Marcellus Taylor pursued higher education in science and education, earning advanced degrees before embarking on a distinguished career as a high school biology and general science teacher in the Atlanta Public Schools system. Deeply committed to professional standards, Taylor was elected president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association (GTEA), the statewide organization representing African American educators.

Under Jim Crow segregation, the Atlanta Board of Education enforced systemic salary discrimination, paying Black teachers and principals significantly less than their white colleagues with identical credentials and teaching duties. In 1948, Taylor took a courageous stand against municipal discrimination, serving as the lead plaintiff alongside fellow educators in *Davis v. Cook*, filed in federal district court with legal counsel from NAACP Legal Defense Fund attorney Constance Baker Motley.

The federal lawsuit triumphed, with the court ruling that paying Black teachers unequal salaries violated the Fourteenth Amendment and ordering Atlanta to equalize salary schedules. Following the landmark victory, Taylor faced persistent administrative retaliation and harassment from hostile municipal school officials. Refusing to compromise his integrity, Taylor transitioned into federal public service, serving for seventeen years with distinction as an investigator and supervisor for the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) until his retirement. Taylor passed away in 1991.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rheubin M. Taylor lived and taught in Atlanta for decades, courageously challenging the Atlanta Board of Education in federal court to establish salary equity for African American teachers. When Taylor passed away in 1991, his landmark civil rights victories were celebrated across Georgia. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where many of his fellow educators and NAACP colleagues rest (Henderson 218, 243–44). His grave at South-View commemorates an educator whose bravery secured dignity and fair wages for thousands of southern teachers.

Name: Robert E. Pharrow
Body:
Overview:
Robert Edward Pharrow was a master building contractor and self-taught civil engineer whose company constructed some of Black Atlanta’s most iconic architectural landmarks. Pharrow built the historic Odd Fellows Building and Auditorium on Auburn Avenue, Sale Hall at Morehouse College, and the sanctuary of First Congregational Church, establishing Sweet Auburn’s physical grandeur.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Virginia in the mid-nineteenth century, Robert Edward Pharrow possessed a brilliant technical mind and boundless ambition. Denied access to southern engineering schools because of his race, Pharrow taught himself advanced civil, structural, and mechanical engineering through disciplined private study and practical apprenticeship in carpentry and masonry.

Pharrow established a successful contracting firm in Birmingham, Alabama, before relocating his business to Atlanta in the early 1900s. In Atlanta, Pharrow quickly became the master contractor of choice for the city’s leading African American cultural, educational, and religious institutions. In 1908, under commission from Rev. Dr. Henry Hugh Proctor, Pharrow constructed the monumental stone and brick sanctuary of First Congregational Church in downtown Atlanta. In 1910, he constructed Sale Hall on the Morehouse College campus, followed by Flipper Hall at Morris Brown College.

In 1912, Grand Secretary Benjamin J. Davis Sr. and the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows selected Pharrow to build their six-story brick headquarters on Auburn Avenue. In 1913, Pharrow completed the adjoining 1,300-seat Odd Fellows Auditorium and roof garden, which became the cultural epicenter of Sweet Auburn. Pharrow was a prominent fraternal leader, holding memberships in the Odd Fellows, Masons, and Pythians, and served on the Board of Directors of Atlanta State Savings Bank until his passing in 1944.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Robert E. Pharrow literally built the physical architecture of Black Atlanta on Sweet Auburn and across the Atlanta University Center. His construction of the Odd Fellows Building, Morehouse’s Sale Hall, and First Congregational Church transformed the urban landscape. When Pharrow passed away in 1944, he was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among his fraternal brothers and civic collaborators (Henderson 104, 234–35). His resting place at South-View honors a master builder whose craftsmanship defines Atlanta’s historic fabric.

Name: Robert Grant
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Robert Grant was a master blacksmith, commercial drayman, founding pastor of historic Zion Hill Baptist Church, and co-founder of South-View Cemetery. Born into slavery, Grant taught himself to read, founded Zion Hill in 1872, and sacrificed two-thirds of his annual ministerial salary in 1886 to purchase founding stock in South-View.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Washington, Wilkes County, Georgia, in 1826, Robert Grant was entirely denied schooling under chattel bondage. Displaying fierce determination, Grant taught himself the alphabet with assistance from local white children. At age fourteen, his enslaver apprenticed him to a blacksmith; Grant labored at the anvil for twelve years, mastering metallurgy and metal fabrication. While enslaved, Grant experienced a religious conversion and began preaching from his master’s front porch.

Following the Civil War, Grant moved to Atlanta, gained ordination as a Baptist minister in 1869, and supported his family as an industrious commercial drayman. In 1870, he married his wife Eveline, raising two children. In 1872, Grant joined seven members of Friendship Baptist Church to establish Zion Hill Baptist Church, gathering worshippers under an outdoor brush arbor before raising funds to erect a permanent wooden sanctuary on Humphries Street in southwest Atlanta.

Grant served as Zion Hill's first pastor from 1872 to 1876, organizing its deacon board, choir, and Sunday school, expanding membership to over 400 congregants. In early 1886, Grant joined Albert Watts and four other leaders to petition the city council for a cemetery charter to protest municipal grave desecrations at Oakland Cemetery. Grant invested $300—two-thirds of his annual ministerial salary—into three founding shares of South-View stock, providing crucial startup capital. Grant passed away in Atlanta in 1896.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Robert Grant lived and ministered in Atlanta for three decades, founding Zion Hill Baptist Church and co-founding South-View Cemetery in 1886. Grant sacrificed the majority of his yearly ministerial salary to purchase founding shares in South-View, ensuring an African American-owned sanctuary free from municipal discrimination. When Grant died in 1896, he was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 21; [Zion Hill Baptist Church](https://www.zionhill.org/history/grant)). His resting place honors a spiritual father whose faith and sacrifice consecrated South-View’s founding.
