Name: Roscoe E. Thomas Jr.
Body:
Overview:
Roscoe Edwin Thomas Jr. was an influential civil rights attorney, president of the Gate City Bar Association, and corporate counsel to Citizens Trust Bank and Atlanta Life Insurance Company. As lead counsel in *Holmes v. Atlanta*, Thomas won a landmark 1955 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that desegregated Atlanta's public golf courses and recreational facilities.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, Roscoe Edwin Thomas Jr. was educated in the city's public schools and attended Morehouse College, graduating with honors. Choosing a career in the law, Thomas earned his Juris Doctor from the University of Michigan Law School, returning to Atlanta to establish an active civil rights and commercial legal practice.

During the 1950s, Thomas served as lead attorney in the historic desegregation case *Holmes v. Atlanta*. Representing Dr. Hamilton M. Holmes and his sons, who had been denied entry to the city's Bobby Jones Golf Course, Thomas argued that municipal segregation in recreational facilities violated the Equal Protection Clause. After fighting the case through lower federal courts, Thomas won a landmark per curiam decision from the U.S. Supreme Court in November 1955 ordering the immediate desegregation of Atlanta’s public golf courses. The victory opened municipal recreation across the South.

In addition to civil rights litigation, Thomas was a preeminent commercial attorney on Sweet Auburn. He served as corporate general counsel to Citizens Trust Bank and the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, guiding both institutions through regulatory expansion. Thomas also served as president of the Gate City Bar Association, mentoring generations of young African American attorneys and promoting judicial diversity across Georgia until his retirement. Thomas passed away in 1996.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Roscoe E. Thomas Jr. spent his legal career in Atlanta, winning the 1955 Supreme Court decision that desegregated the city's golf courses and advising Sweet Auburn’s premier financial corporations. Following his passing in 1996, members of the bench and bar celebrated his legal brilliance. Thomas was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow civil rights advocates and commercial leaders (Henderson 244; [Georgia Tech Holmes Exhibit](https://sites.gatech.edu/holmesvatlanta/about-the-case)). His grave at South-View commemorates an attorney who opened public recreation to all Atlantans.

Name: Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson
Body:
Overview:
Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson was a fearless civil rights organizer, Spelman student activist, and the first and only woman to serve as executive secretary of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). Organizing the Atlanta sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and "jail-no-bail" protests, she was the logistical engine and moral heartbeat of student direct action.

Life and Contributions:
Born on April 25, 1942, in Atlanta, Georgia, Ruby Doris Smith grew up in the historic Summerhill neighborhood. Inspired as a teenager by the 1955 Montgomery Bus Boycott, Smith entered Spelman College in 1959. In February 1960, when the Atlanta Student Movement launched citywide sit-ins at segregated lunch counters, Smith joined the frontline demonstrations, enduring repeated arrests.

Smith was a fierce advocate of the "jail-no-bail" philosophy. In February 1961, she traveled to Rock Hill, South Carolina, to join jailed protesters, serving thirty days of hard labor on a prison chain gang rather than paying a fine to a segregated court. Later that spring, she joined the Freedom Rides into Mississippi, enduring forty-five days of brutal imprisonment in Parchman State Penitentiary.

Operating from SNCC’s national headquarters on Raymond Street in Atlanta, Smith served as the organization’s executive administrator and logistical genius. She managed vehicle fleets, communication radios, payroll, and emergency medical bail funds, sustaining field organizers across Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia. In May 1966, SNCC delegates elected her as the first woman executive secretary of the organization. Her brilliant, tireless organizing was tragically cut short when she was diagnosed with terminal cancer, passing away on October 7, 1967, at the young age of twenty-five.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson was an Atlanta native who grew up in Summerhill, studied at Spelman College, and directed national civil rights campaigns from SNCC's Atlanta headquarters. Following her death on October 7, 1967, at age twenty-five, a funeral service was held in Atlanta. She was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 238; [SNCC Digital Gateway](https://snccdigital.org/people/ruby-doris-smith-robinson/)). Her gravestone at South-View carries her enduring words: "If you think free, you are free." Her resting place honors a fearless warrior of the Black student movement.

Name: Sam Magruder
Body:
Overview:
Sam Magruder was an African American Atlanta citizen who was murdered by white rioters during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal assault reflects the catastrophic violence inflicted on Black residents during four days of mob terror, an atrocity that left dozens dead and traumatized Black communities across the South.

Life and Contributions:
Sam Magruder lived and worked in Atlanta during the early twentieth century. Like thousands of African American residents of the period, Magruder participated in the city's bustling urban economy, seeking to earn a living and maintain community ties within the strictures of legal Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, political demagoguery surrounding the Georgia gubernatorial race, combined with sensational, false newspaper reports of assaults on white women, inflamed white racial animosity. On Saturday evening, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, attacking Black pedestrians, barbers, and streetcar passengers along Peachtree and Decatur streets. The mob violence quickly escalated from downtown thoroughfares into residential neighborhoods, continuing across multiple days.

Magruder was caught in the path of the mob violence during the height of the outbreak. Armed white rioters attacked him with blunt weapons and firearms, inflicting fatal injuries from which he died. For decades, Magruder’s death was omitted from mainstream civic history until archival investigations by organizations like the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition documented his fate, ensuring that his life and tragic death were recovered for historical memory.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Sam Magruder lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the violence, when city facilities and municipal cemeteries neglected Black casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds to provide solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre victims brought to its care (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Byline: LMC 3403, Fall 2026
Last updated: November 2026
Tags: 1906 Atlanta Massacre, Racial Terror, Jim Crow, Stories from the Soil
See also: Frank Smith, George Union Wilder, 1906 Atlanta Massacre

Name: Sam Robinson
Body:
Overview:
Sam Robinson was an African American laborer from Atlanta who was murdered by armed white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal assault reflects the catastrophic human toll of four days of unchecked racial terror, during which white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods, killed dozens, and displaced hundreds.

Life and Contributions:
Sam Robinson was an African American resident who lived and worked in Atlanta during the turn of the twentieth century. Like thousands of Black citizens during this period, Robinson earned his livelihood through manual labor in Atlanta's expanding commercial economy, seeking to provide for his family within the strictures of legal Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, inflammatory political speeches by candidates for governor, combined with fabricated, sensational headlines in local white daily newspapers, whipped racial tensions into violence. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys took control of downtown Atlanta, launching violent assaults against Black laborers, streetcar passengers, and pedestrians. Over the next three days, roving armed mobs attacked Black homes and business districts.

Robinson was caught in the path of the mob violence on September 22 and was violently assaulted, sustaining fatal injuries. Municipal death records and subsequent research confirmed that Robinson died as a direct victim of the massacre. For over a century, Robinson’s death was omitted from mainstream city histories until rigorous archival research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project restored his memory, identifying him as an innocent casualty of racial violence.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Sam Robinson lived, labored, and was murdered in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the tragedy, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions neglected deceased African American casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds to provide solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre victims brought to its care (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Samuel W. Williams
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Dr. Samuel Woodrow Williams was an esteemed theologian, philosopher, Morehouse College professor, civil rights leader, and pastor of Atlanta's historic Friendship Baptist Church. Chairing philosophy and religion at Morehouse for over thirty years, Williams mentored Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., presided over the Atlanta NAACP, and led the Triple L bus desegregation movement.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 12, 1912, in Sparkman, Dallas County, Arkansas, Samuel Woodrow Williams completed his education at Arkansas Baptist College and Morehouse College, graduating with a bachelor of arts degree in 1937. He subsequently earned a master's degree in religion and philosophy from the University of Chicago and pursued doctoral studies there, developing into one of Black America's foremost philosophical theologians.

In 1946, Williams returned to Morehouse College to chair the Department of Philosophy and Religion, serving with distinction for over thirty years. At Morehouse, Williams taught young Martin Luther King Jr., introducing him to social gospel ethics, personalism, and Henry David Thoreau's civil disobedience theories. In 1954, Williams was called to the pastorate of historic Friendship Baptist Church, the "mother church" of Black Baptists in Atlanta.

Williams was a stalwart civil rights militant. In January 1957, Williams joined Rev. William Holmes Borders in the Love, Law, and Liberation (Triple L) campaign to desegregate Atlanta's public transit, boarding buses and serving as lead plaintiff in the successful federal lawsuit that desegregated municipal transit in 1959. Williams served on the executive board of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) and presided over the Atlanta NAACP. His wife Billye later married baseball icon Hank Aaron. Williams passed away in October 1970.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. Dr. Samuel W. Williams lived and taught in Atlanta for over thirty-five years, shaping the intellectual and theological climate at Morehouse College, pastoring Friendship Baptist Church, and leading the Triple L transit desegregation campaign. When Williams died in October 1970 at age fifty-eight, civic leaders, scholars, and civil rights icons across Atlanta mourned his passing. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among his ministerial and academic colleagues (Henderson 254). His resting place at South-View honors a brilliant philosopher and prophetic civil rights warrior.

Name: Stinson Ferguson
Body:
Overview:
Stinson Ferguson was a twenty-five-year-old African American laborer and northwest Atlanta resident who was shot and killed by white rioters on September 22, 1906, during the Atlanta Race Massacre. Recorded as an unidentified casualty for over 117 years, cold-case research in 2023 officially verified his identity and burial at South-View Cemetery.

Life and Contributions:
Stinson Ferguson was born around 1881 in Georgia. As a young adult, he established his residence on Thurmond Street in northwest Atlanta, an active working-class African American neighborhood adjacent to downtown rail hubs and industrial yards. Employed as an industrious laborer in the city’s manufacturing and commercial sectors, Ferguson sought to build an independent livelihood despite the severe constraints of legal segregation.

On the warm Saturday evening of September 22, 1906, violent racial hysteria exploded across the city as white mobs gathered downtown and fanned outward into adjoining Black working-class neighborhoods. Ferguson was traversing neighborhood streets when rioters opened fire on African American pedestrians. Ferguson was struck in the abdomen by gunfire.

Law enforcement or medical transport brought him to Grady Memorial Hospital, which operated segregated wards. Despite medical intervention, Ferguson died shortly after arrival from severe internal hemorrhaging. Like many victims whose deaths were recorded hastily in segregated municipal logs, Ferguson's connection to the riot was obscured in mainstream historical narratives for over 117 years. In September 2023, researchers from the Georgia Civil Rights Cold Cases Project and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights analyzed Fulton County death certificates, confirming Ferguson was killed in the massacre.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Stinson Ferguson lived on Thurmond Street in northwest Atlanta and was murdered at age twenty-five during the outbreak of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. Archival records confirmed that following his autopsy at Grady Memorial Hospital, Ferguson was brought to South-View Cemetery for burial in late September 1906, resting alongside fellow victims of the racial violence ([Palmore](https://www.civilandhumanrights.org/unearthing-the-past-identifying-victims-of-the-1906-atlanta-race-massacre/); [WSB-TV 2023](https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/two-victims-1906-atlanta-race-massacre-identified-nearly-120-years-later/5LVMJY55DFBPZP76CKLWA57T5Y/)). His confirmed presence at South-View stands as a powerful testament to modern cold-case archival recovery, restoring names and sacred dignity to those lost to racial violence.

Name: T.M. Alexander Sr.
Body:
Overview:
Theodore Martin "T.M." Alexander Sr. was an insurance pioneer, civil rights strategist, and public servant who founded Alexander & Company in 1931, building one of the Southeast’s largest Black-owned insurance agencies. Alexander secured crucial Lloyd's of London insurance for the Montgomery Bus Boycott carpools and helped implement the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1909 in Montgomery, Alabama, Theodore Martin Alexander Sr. relocated to Atlanta to attend Morehouse College, graduating with honors in 1931. In the midst of the Great Depression, Alexander demonstrated daring entrepreneurial vision by establishing Alexander & Company, an independent general insurance and real estate agency on Auburn Avenue.

Alexander expanded his firm into one of the premier African American-owned insurance brokerage agencies in the United States, providing casualty, property, and business insurance to Black homeowners, churches, and businesses across the South. In late 1955, during the Montgomery Bus Boycott, when white insurance companies canceled liability policies on the church-owned station wagons and carpools transporting thousands of Black workers, Alexander utilized his international brokerage connections to secure comprehensive insurance coverage directly through Lloyd's of London, saving the boycott from collapse.

Alexander was an indispensable civil rights organizer. He served as president of the Empire Real Estate Board and was a key executive leader in the Atlanta NAACP and Atlanta Negro Voters League. In 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson's administration appointed Alexander to federal advisory committees to help implement the provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. He also co-founded the Atlanta Action Forum to bridge racial divides among business leaders. Alexander passed away on May 21, 2001, at the age of ninety-two.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
T.M. Alexander Sr. lived and conducted business in Atlanta for over seventy years, building Alexander & Company on Auburn Avenue and leading the Empire Real Estate Board. Following his passing in May 2001, his contributions to Black business and civil rights were honored across the nation. Alexander was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where he rests among his fellow Sweet Auburn pioneers and Morehouse alumni (Henderson 170). His resting place at South-View commemorates an extraordinary business builder and civil rights benefactor.

Name: Virgil W. Hodges
Body:
Overview:
Virgil Wendell Hodges was an educator, journalist, and civil rights leader who served as professor of sociology at Clark College and city editor of the *Atlanta Daily World*. As chairman of the Atlanta NAACP executive board during the 1940s and 1950s, Hodges courageously resisted judicial orders to disclose confidential membership lists.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Georgia, Virgil Wendell Hodges completed his higher education at Morehouse College and Atlanta University, earning advanced degrees in sociology and education. Hodges established an illustrious academic career in the Atlanta University Center, serving for decades as professor and chair of sociology at Clark College (now Clark Atlanta University), where he mentored generations of civil rights leaders.

Concurrently, Hodges was an accomplished journalist, serving as city editor of the *Atlanta Daily World*, the nation's premier Black daily newspaper. Hodges utilized his journalistic platform to expose police brutality, document racial disparities in municipal services, and cover the emerging direct-action campaigns of the freedom movement.

Hodges was a cornerstone of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP, serving as chairman of its executive and administrative boards. In the 1950s, when state officials attempted to suppress civil rights activism by demanding NAACP membership rolls, Hodges steadfastly refused to comply with court subpoenas, risking imprisonment to protect Black citizens from economic retaliation and vigilante violence. Into the 1980s, Hodges remained the branch’s top membership recruiter, building the Atlanta NAACP into one of the largest in the nation. His wife, Ruth Hodges, chaired the Department of Art at Morris Brown College. Hodges passed away in Atlanta in 1985.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Virgil W. Hodges spent more than fifty years in Atlanta enriching higher education at Clark College, editing the *Atlanta Daily World*, and guiding the executive leadership of the Atlanta NAACP. Following his death in 1985, educators, journalists, and civil rights colleagues gathered across the city to celebrate his enduring contributions. He was interred at South-View Cemetery alongside his wife Ruth and generations of NAACP leaders (Henderson 212–13). His resting place at South-View commemorates an educator and journalist who defended civil liberties with fearless integrity.

Name: W. F. Penn
Body:
Overview:
Dr. William Fletcher Penn was a pioneer physician, surgeon, and civic leader who became one of Atlanta’s most distinguished African American medical professionals. The first Black graduate of Yale Medical School, Dr. Penn passionately confronted white municipal leaders during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, demanding equal legal protection for Black citizens.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1872 in Lynchburg, Virginia, William Fletcher Penn was educated at Hampton Institute in Virginia before earning his undergraduate degree from Amherst College in Massachusetts. Pursuing medicine, Penn enrolled at Yale University School of Medicine, graduating with his medical degree in 1897 as the first African American in Yale Medical School's history.

Following medical training in New York, Dr. Penn relocated to Atlanta in 1898 to establish his surgical practice. He quickly became one of the city's foremost physicians, co-founding the Fair Haven Infirmary—one of the earliest private hospital facilities for Black Atlantans—and serving as chief surgeon. Dr. Penn served a prominent role in the National Medical Association and was a respected leader in sweet Auburn civic life.

During the horrific violence of the September 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre, Dr. Penn witnessed white mobs hunting Black citizens downtown. On September 25, 1906, at a tense interracial meeting convened at the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, Dr. Penn stood before white civic leaders and delivered an impassioned, courageous address: "If living a sober, industrious, upright life... is not the standard by which a colored man can live and be protected in the South, what is to become of him?... Shall I leave and go North?" His eloquent words shamed municipal leaders into deploying troops to halt the violence. Dr. Penn practiced medicine in Atlanta until his death on June 3, 1934.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Dr. W. F. Penn lived and practiced medicine in Atlanta for nearly four decades, operating Fair Haven Infirmary and courageously confronting city leaders at the Chamber of Commerce during the 1906 massacre. Following his death on June 3, 1934, at age sixty-two, medical colleagues and community leaders paid tribute to his heroic life. Dr. Penn was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery (Henderson 234; South-View Brochure). His resting place at South-View honors a pioneer physician who demanded equal protection for Black Atlantans.

Last updated: November 2026

Name: Walter D. Westmoreland
Body:
Overview:
First Lieutenant Walter Drake Westmoreland was a decorated Tuskegee Airman, fighter pilot in the 332nd Fighter Group, and Atlanta native who was killed in combat over Hungary during World War II. Flying long-range bomber escort missions in his P-51 Mustang, Westmoreland sacrificed his life fighting fascism abroad while breaking racial barriers at home.

Life and Contributions:
Born in Atlanta, Georgia, on May 2, 1920, Walter Drake Westmoreland was the son of William G. and Eula White Westmoreland, and the nephew of famed national NAACP executive secretary Walter White. Westmoreland was educated in Atlanta public schools, graduated from Morehouse College in 1941, and earned a master’s degree in mathematics from Atlanta University before enlisting in the U.S. Army Air Forces during World War II.

Selected for specialized military aviation training at Tuskegee Army Air Field in Alabama, Westmoreland earned his silver pilot's wings and officer's commission in July 1943. Assigned to the 302nd Fighter Squadron of the elite 332nd Fighter Group (the renowned "Red Tails"), Lieutenant Westmoreland deployed to the European Theater, flying combat bomber escort missions from Ramitelli Airfield in southern Italy in his P-51C Mustang fighter, affectionately nicknamed "Dopey."

On October 13, 1944, while returning from a critical escort mission over enemy oil refineries in Blechhammer, Germany, Westmoreland’s aircraft was hit by German anti-aircraft flak near Lake Balaton in Hungary, and he was killed in action at age twenty-four. In 1949, the U.S. government repatriated his remains to Atlanta. His father William passed away just days prior to his return, and the city honored father and son with a rare, massive double funeral service at First Congregational Church.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Walter D. Westmoreland was an Atlanta native who was raised in the city and graduated from Morehouse College and Atlanta University before serving his country as a Tuskegee Airman. In 1949, following a massive public memorial service attended by thousands at historic First Congregational Church, Westmoreland was laid to rest with full military honors at South-View Cemetery beside his father (Henderson 250; [CAF Rise Above](https://cafriseabove.org/walter-drake-westmoreland/)). His resting place at South-View permanently honors the extraordinary heroism and sacrifice of Atlanta's fallen Red Tail combat pilot.

Name: Washington W. King
Body:
Overview:
Washington W. King was a master architect, bridge engineer, and builder who designed and constructed covered wooden bridges across Georgia and Alabama. Carrying forward a distinguished family tradition of engineering craftsmanship following emancipation, King constructed enduring lattice truss bridges, including the historic covered bridge preserved at Stone Mountain Park.

Life and Contributions:
Born into slavery in Georgia in 1843, Washington W. King was the son of Horace King, the legendary African American architect, master builder, and legislator who was renowned throughout the antebellum South for constructing monumental town lattice truss covered bridges. Washington and his brothers John and Marshall apprenticed under their father, acquiring advanced technical mastery in structural geometry, timber framing, and civil engineering.

Following the Civil War, King joined his family to establish the King Brothers Bridge Company. Operating during Reconstruction, the firm contracted with southern municipal governments, county commissioners, and railway corporations to construct complex covered bridges, civic courthouses, and warehouses across Georgia and Alabama. Washington King demonstrated remarkable engineering prowess, designing bridges capable of spanning wide river channels and withstanding severe regional floods.

In 1891, King supervised the construction of a magnificent 150-foot Town lattice truss covered bridge over the North Oconee River in Athens, Georgia. Constructed with interlocking wooden lattices fastened with hardwood pegs (trunnels), King’s bridge stood for decades as a marvel of southern nineteenth-century civil engineering. In 1965, the historic structure was carefully dismantled, transported, and reassembled at Stone Mountain Park, where it remains a celebrated historic monument. King continued engineering and building structures across Georgia until his passing in 1910.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Washington W. King spent his post-Civil War career designing and constructing major infrastructure across Georgia, maintaining extensive commercial and family ties in the Atlanta metropolitan area. When King passed away in 1910, community members and master craftsmen gathered to celebrate his extraordinary engineering accomplishments. He was interred at South-View Cemetery, where his legacy as a master bridge builder is commemorated (Henderson 221). His resting place at South-View permanently connects the grounds to the historic King family dynasty of nineteenth-century African American structural architects and engineers.

Name: Wayne Williams
Body:
Overview:
Wayne Williams is a freelance photographer and music promoter who became the primary suspect in the Atlanta Child Murders investigation between 1979 and 1981. Convicted in 1982 of murdering two adult victims, law enforcement attributed the majority of the child homicide cases to him, effectively closing the task force investigation.

Life and Contributions:
Born on May 27, 1958, in Atlanta, Georgia, Wayne Bertram Williams was the only child of Homer and Faye Williams, both respected public school teachers. Raised in the Dixie Hills neighborhood of southwest Atlanta, Williams was an ambitious youth who developed an early fascination with electronics, radio broadcasting, and photography. As a teenager, he constructed a low-power radio station in his bedroom and worked as a freelance news photographer, capturing images of fires and accidents for local television stations.

By the late 1970s, Williams was attempting to establish himself as an independent music talent scout and promoter, auditioning local Black youths for musical groups. Between the summer of 1979 and May 1981, the city of Atlanta was terrorized by the serial abduction and murder of nearly thirty young African American boys and teenagers, prompting the creation of the joint Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force and extensive FBI involvement.

In the early morning hours of May 22, 1981, law enforcement officers monitoring the Jackson Parkway bridge over the Chattahoochee River heard a loud splash and observed Williams's vehicle crossing the bridge. Williams was stopped and questioned. Two days later, the body of twenty-seven-year-old Nathaniel Cater was pulled from the river downstream. In June 1981, Williams was arrested, and in February 1982, he was convicted in Fulton County Superior Court of murdering Cater and twenty-one-year-old Jimmy Ray Payne. Following the verdict, authorities attributed the majority of the unsolved child cases to Williams without filing additional charges. Williams has maintained his innocence while serving two life sentences.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Wayne Williams was born, raised, and operated his enterprises in Atlanta, where his arrest and 1982 conviction brought a dramatic end to the Atlanta Child Murders crisis that traumatized the metropolitan area. Williams is currently incarcerated in the Georgia state prison system and is not buried at South-View Cemetery ([FBI Serial Killers Part 5](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders)). His connection to South-View is historical, as multiple young victims of the crisis are interred on the cemetery grounds.

Name: Will Marion
Body:
Overview:
Will Marion was an African American laborer from Atlanta who was murdered by white mobs during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal beating and shooting reflect the catastrophic brutality inflicted on Black working-class residents during four days of mob terror, an atrocity that left dozens dead and damaged Atlanta's national reputation.

Life and Contributions:
Will Marion lived and worked in Atlanta during the early twentieth century. Like thousands of African American laborers during this era, Marion was part of the city's industrious Black workforce, contributing his labor to Atlanta's commercial and industrial enterprises while seeking to maintain an independent living under the oppressive restrictions of Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, inflammatory political speeches by candidates for Georgia governor, coupled with reckless, fabricated newspaper headlines alleging attacks by Black men on white women, ignited severe racial tensions. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, attacking Black laborers, streetcar passengers, and pedestrians along Peachtree, Pryor, and Decatur streets. Over the subsequent three days, roving armed mobs attacked Black homes and business districts.

Marion was caught in the path of the mob violence on September 22 and was violently assaulted, sustaining fatal injuries from gunshots and blunt force trauma. Municipal records and subsequent research confirmed that Marion died as a direct victim of the massacre. For over a century, Marion’s death was omitted from mainstream city histories until rigorous archival research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project restored his memory, identifying him as an innocent casualty of racial violence.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Will Marion lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the tragedy, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions neglected deceased African American casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds to provide solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre victims brought to its care (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Will Moreland
Body:
Overview:
Will Moreland was an African American resident of Atlanta who was ambushed and murdered by armed white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His violent death reflects the widespread terror inflicted on Black citizens during the riot, an event that reshaped Georgia politics and race relations for decades.

Life and Contributions:
Will Moreland lived and worked in Atlanta at the turn of the twentieth century, participating in the city's expanding urban economy. Like thousands of Black citizens during this period, Moreland sought to build an independent life and support his household despite the severe social, economic, and political restrictions imposed by Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, political demagoguery and sensationalized, false news reports in local white newspapers ignited severe racial hostilities across Atlanta. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, a violent mob of thousands of white men and boys swarmed downtown streets, attacking Black laborers, passengers, and passersby. Over the subsequent seventy-two hours, the mob expanded outward into residential neighborhoods, breaking into homes and firing weapons into Black households.

Moreland was ambushed and killed by mob members during the height of the violent outbreak between September 22 and September 24. His death certificate and contemporary reports documented that he succumbed to severe traumatic injuries. For over a century, Moreland’s death remained largely unacknowledged in official city histories until rigorous archival research by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project restored his memory, identifying him as an innocent victim of racial violence.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Will Moreland lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the violence, when city facilities and municipal cemeteries neglected Black casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds as a sacred haven, providing solemn Christian burials for the massacre victims (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Will Richardson
Body:
Overview:
Will Richardson was an African American grocery store owner in southwest Atlanta's Pittsburgh neighborhood whose armed defense of his business against a violent police and civilian siege in May 1902 culminated in the deadly Pittsburgh Riot. His tragic death highlighted deep racial tensions and municipal police hostility in turn-of-the-century Atlanta.

Life and Contributions:
Will Richardson was an enterprising African American merchant who operated a grocery store and residence at the corner of McDaniel and Amy streets in southwest Atlanta's working-class Pittsburgh neighborhood. In the late 1890s, Richardson had been arrested by Samuel A. Kerlin, a white Atlanta police officer, and was sentenced to months on a chain gang after Kerlin testified against him.

In the early morning hours of May 17, 1902, Richardson encountered Kerlin—then a former officer—walking along McDaniel Street. An argument erupted, Richardson threatened Kerlin, and shotgun fire was exchanged. Kerlin escaped and returned around 1:30 a.m. with police officers and armed white civilians to arrest Richardson. Richardson and several companions barricaded themselves inside the grocery store, armed with rifles and ammunition. When the posse approached, Richardson’s group opened fire, killing an officer and sparking an all-night siege.

Over several hours, hundreds of police and thousands of armed white civilians surrounded the store, trading an estimated 3,000 rounds. When gunfire failed to dislodge the barricaded men, the mob ignited the building. Richardson perished inside the inferno as the structure collapsed, and his body was almost completely cremated in the fire. Following the destruction, white mobs attempted to parade his charred remains downtown before police cordons intercepted the crowd at the city limits. Richardson died defending his life and property against armed aggression.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Will Richardson lived and operated his grocery business in Atlanta's Pittsburgh neighborhood until the violent armed siege of May 17, 1902. Following the siege, municipal police cordons intercepted a white mob attempting to parade Richardson's remains downtown, transferring his charred body by wagon to South-View Cemetery for burial (Henderson 116–17; Hartzog). His resting place at South-View connects the cemetery to the historic record of Black armed self-defense and community resistance against racial aggression during the 1902 Pittsburgh Riot.

Name: Willard L. Strickland
Body:
Overview:
Willard L. Strickland was a decorated World War II Army veteran, postal supervisor, and historic civil rights pioneer who made history in 1948 as one of the first eight African American police officers hired by the Atlanta Police Department. Strickland broke the municipal color barrier, later integrating the Decatur Police Department.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1922 in Atlanta, Georgia, Willard L. Strickland attended local public schools and completed his education at Morehouse College. During World War II, Strickland served his country with distinction in the United States Army, developing discipline, leadership skills, and an enduring commitment to public service.

In April 1948, following years of relentless civic advocacy led by Rev. William Holmes Borders and the Atlanta Negro Voters League, Mayor William B. Hartsfield and the city council agreed to hire Atlanta’s first Black police officers. Strickland was selected as one of the historic "Original Eight" Black officers. Facing severe racial restrictions, the Black officers were barred from wearing uniforms to and from work, denied the authority to arrest white citizens, and forced to work out of the basement of the Butler Street YMCA rather than the central police headquarters.

Despite these demeaning indignities, Officer Strickland served with exceptional professionalism and courage, patrolling the Sweet Auburn and Butler Street corridors and winning the deep respect of the community. In 1964, Strickland broke another racial barrier when he was hired as one of the first Black officers to integrate the Decatur Police Department. Strickland subsequently enjoyed a successful twenty-two-year career with the U.S. Postal Service as a supervisor, receiving the NAACP Honor Award for lifetime civic service before his passing in 1989.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Willard L. Strickland spent his entire life in Atlanta, courageously breaking the color barrier in municipal law enforcement in 1948 and patrolling Sweet Auburn from the Butler Street YMCA. When Strickland passed away in Atlanta in 1989 at age sixty-seven, civic and police officials honored his trailblazing career. He was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where his grave commemorates a pioneer who dismantled segregation in Atlanta law enforcement (Henderson 242–43; [AARL Strickland Papers](https://aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/25)). His resting place at South-View celebrates historic civic courage.

Name: William Barrett
Body:
Overview:
William Barrett was a seventeen-year-old African American youth from Atlanta who was abducted and murdered in May 1981, becoming one of the final victims of the harrowing Atlanta Child Murders crisis. His tragic loss occurred just as massive municipal and federal task force investigations were closing in on solving the serial disappearances.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1964 in Atlanta, Georgia, William Barrett was raised in a close-knit family and attended local public high schools. Known to his friends, teachers, and neighbors as an industrious and friendly teenager, seventeen-year-old William was preparing to enter adulthood and complete his high school education. By the spring of 1981, the city of Atlanta had been gripped for nearly two years by unprecedented fear, with dozens of Black boys and young men murdered or missing.

On May 11, 1981, William disappeared after leaving his home in Atlanta. His sudden absence prompted immediate alarms from his family and neighbors, who alerted the joint Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force. Massive search efforts were mobilized across the metropolitan area, as the entire city was on high alert with curfews and stakeouts.

Tragically, on May 12, 1981, searchers discovered William’s body on a steep wooded embankment along Winship Drive in DeKalb County. Medical examiners determined that he had suffered fatal asphyxiation. William's death was one of the very last murders linked to the crisis before law enforcement apprehended Wayne Williams on the Chattahoochee River bridge later that month. His murder was investigated by the FBI and task force detectives, leaving an indelible wound on his grieving community.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
William Barrett was an Atlanta native whose youth and tragic death occurred within the metropolitan community during the closing chapter of the 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Following the discovery of his remains, his grieving family and community held services in Atlanta. William was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where multiple youth victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were interred in sacred dignity (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His grave at South-View preserves the memory of an innocent youth taken on the eve of high school graduation.

Name: William Crogman
Body:
Overview:
William Henry Crogman was a distinguished classical scholar, educator, author, and the first African American president of Clark University in Atlanta. Serving as Clark's president from 1903 to 1910, Crogman championed liberal arts education and human dignity, providing essential civic leadership to south Atlanta following the devastating 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre.

Life and Contributions:
Born on May 5, 1841, in Philipsburg on the Caribbean island of Sint Maarten, William Henry Crogman was orphaned at age twelve. Entering maritime service, he traveled the world as a ship's cabin boy for a decade before relocating to Massachusetts to pursue education. He entered Claflin University in South Carolina, graduating with top honors in 1876.

In 1876, Crogman was appointed to the founding faculty of Clark University in Atlanta as professor of Greek and Latin literature, becoming one of the premier classical scholars in the nation. Crogman passionately argued that classical scholarship and the liberal arts affirmed the full intellectual dignity and equality of African Americans against arguments restricting Black education to manual trades. He published influential works, including *Talks for the Times* and *The Colored American*.

In 1903, Crogman made history when the Board of Trustees elected him as Clark University’s first Black president, an office he held with distinction until 1910. In late September 1906, when white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods across Atlanta and state militia raided the neighboring community of Brownsville, Crogman provided calm, steadfast leadership, working with civic leaders to protect Clark students, relieve suffering, and restore community stability. In honor of his contributions, Atlanta named Crogman Elementary School in his honor. He passed away in Kansas City in 1931.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
William Henry Crogman lived and taught in south Atlanta for more than forty-five years, shaping Clark University as professor and president and protecting the Brownsville community following the 1906 massacre. When Crogman died on April 6, 1931, at age eighty-nine, his body was returned to Atlanta for funeral services at Clark University. He was interred at South-View Cemetery, where he rests alongside fellow Atlanta University Center scholars and Brownsville leaders (Henderson 191; Bauerlein 212). His grave at South-View honors a giant of classical education and civic courage.

Name: William Holmes Borders
Body:
Overview:
Rev. Dr. William Holmes Borders was an influential Baptist minister, orator, civil rights leader, and pastor of Atlanta's historic Wheat Street Baptist Church for fifty-one years. Borders led the successful 1957 "Triple L" bus desegregation movement, integrated the Atlanta Police Department, and developed Wheat Street Gardens and Towers affordable housing.

Life and Contributions:
Born on February 24, 1905, in Macon, Georgia, William Holmes Borders was a third-generation minister. He graduated from Morehouse College in 1929 and earned a Bachelor of Divinity and Master of Arts from Garrett Theological Seminary and Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois. In 1937, Borders was called to the pastorate of Wheat Street Baptist Church on Auburn Avenue, leading the congregation until 1988.

Under Borders’s visionary direction, Wheat Street grew into a powerhouse congregation of over 5,000 members. In the 1940s, Borders led the civic campaign that compelled the city of Atlanta to hire its first eight Black police officers in 1948. On January 9, 1957, Borders launched the Love, Law, and Liberation (Triple L) campaign, leading fellow Black ministers to board segregated Atlanta city buses and take front seats. Their planned arrests sparked a federal civil rights lawsuit that permanently desegregated Atlanta transit in 1959.

Borders was also an institutional pioneer in community economic development. In the 1960s, Wheat Street constructed Wheat Street Gardens and the fourteen-story Wheat Street Towers, creating hundreds of affordable housing units, a federal credit union, and retirement facilities for low-income Black families. Borders mentored student sit-in leaders in the 1960s and served as a moral compass for Atlanta until his passing on May 11, 1993.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Rev. William Holmes Borders anchored Sweet Auburn for more than fifty years as pastor of Wheat Street Baptist Church, leading the Triple L movement and building affordable housing across the Old Fourth Ward. When Borders died on May 11, 1993, at age eighty-eight, Congressman John Lewis delivered a eulogy celebrating his prophetic leadership. A graveside service followed at South-View Cemetery, where Borders was laid to rest (Henderson 177–78). His resting place at South-View honors a legendary pioneer of Atlanta civil rights and Christian social ministry.

Name: William Welch
Body:
Overview:
William Welch was an African American laborer from Atlanta who was murdered by white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal assault reflects the catastrophic violence inflicted on Black residents during four days of mob terror, an atrocity that left dozens dead and traumatized Black communities across the South.

Life and Contributions:
William Welch lived and worked in Atlanta during the turn of the twentieth century. Like thousands of African American laborers during this era, Welch participated in the city's expanding industrial and transportation economy, seeking to earn an honest living and provide for his family despite the strictures of legal Jim Crow segregation.

In late September 1906, inflammatory political speeches by candidates for Georgia governor, coupled with reckless, fabricated newspaper headlines in local daily papers alleging assaults on white women, inflamed white racial animosity. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, an armed mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, attacking Black laborers, streetcar passengers, and pedestrians along Peachtree and Decatur streets. The mob violence quickly escalated from downtown thoroughfares into residential neighborhoods, continuing across multiple days.

Welch was caught in the path of the mob violence during the height of the outbreak on September 22. Armed rioters attacked him with blunt weapons and firearms, inflicting fatal injuries from which he died. For decades, Welch’s death was omitted from mainstream civic history until archival investigations by organizations like the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition documented his fate, ensuring that his life and tragic death were recovered for historical memory.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
William Welch lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the violence, when municipal cemeteries and public institutions neglected deceased African American casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds to provide solemn, dignified Christian burials for the massacre victims brought to its care (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.

Name: Yusef Bell
Body:
Overview:
Yusef Bell was a nine-year-old African American schoolboy from Atlanta whose abduction and murder in October 1979 became a pivotal catalyst in the Atlanta Child Murders crisis. His heartbreaking death spurred grieving mothers, led by his mother Camille Bell, to organize the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP) and demand national intervention.

Life and Contributions:
Born in 1970 in Atlanta, Georgia, Yusef Bell was the beloved nine-year-old son of Camille Bell. Known to family and neighbors in southwest Atlanta as a bright, curious, and helpful child, Yusef attended local elementary school and was well-liked throughout his community. In the autumn of 1979, subtle undercurrents of fear were beginning to grip Black neighborhoods in Atlanta following the unexplained disappearances of several youths.

On October 21, 1979, Yusef left his home to walk to a neighborhood confectionery store on McDaniel Street to purchase Bruton Snuff for an elderly neighbor. He never returned. His sudden disappearance ignited frantic searches by his mother, relatives, and neighbors across southwest Atlanta. Grieving and frustrated by the initial lack of urgent municipal response, Camille Bell began reaching out to other mothers whose sons had vanished.

On November 8, 1979, Yusef’s body was discovered abandoned in the crawlspace of the vacant E. P. Johnson Elementary School in south Atlanta. Medical examiners determined that he had died from manual strangulation. Yusef's tragic murder galvanized Atlanta's Black community. His mother founded the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP), organizing protest marches, community patrols, and national media campaigns that forced city, state, and federal officials to establish the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Yusef Bell was an Atlanta native whose childhood and tragic murder occurred in southwest Atlanta during the opening months of the 1979–1981 missing and murdered crisis. Following the discovery of his remains, funeral services were held in Atlanta. Yusef was laid to rest at South-View Cemetery, where multiple youth victims of the Atlanta Child Murders were interred in sacred peace (Henderson 6; [Atlanta Child Murders Part 18](https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018)). His resting place at South-View connects the cemetery directly to the origins of the STOP Committee and Atlanta’s collective struggle for justice.

Name: Zeb Long
Body:
Overview:
Zeb Long was an African American citizen of Atlanta who was murdered by armed white vigilantes during the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. His fatal shooting reflects the catastrophic human toll of four days of unchecked racial terror, an event that reshaped Georgia politics, voting rights, and race relations for generations.

Life and Contributions:
Zeb Long lived and worked in Atlanta during the Jim Crow era, earning an independent livelihood amidst intense municipal segregation. In early twentieth-century Atlanta, African Americans established vibrant residential neighborhoods, businesses, and fraternal orders, building community strength despite political disenfranchisement.

In September 1906, sensationalized and irresponsible newspaper headlines in local white daily publications falsely accused Black men of attacking white women, stoking virulent racial animosity throughout the city. On the evening of Saturday, September 22, 1906, a mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys swarmed downtown Atlanta, attacking Black laborers, passengers, and pedestrians. The violence quickly turned into a multi-day assault across Black residential neighborhoods.

Long was fatally targeted by armed rioters during the chaos, becoming one of dozens of casualties murdered during the outbreak of mob violence. Historical documentation compiled by the Fulton County Remembrance Coalition in their "Stories from the Soil" project confirmed Long as one of the documented fatalities of the massacre, ensuring that his life and tragic murder were preserved in historical records.

Atlanta and South-View Connection:
Zeb Long lived, worked, and was killed in Atlanta during the violent mob attacks of the 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre. In the chaotic aftermath of the violence, when city facilities and municipal cemeteries neglected Black casualties, South-View Cemetery opened its grounds as a sacred haven, providing solemn Christian burials for the massacre victims (Henderson 119; [Stories from the Soil](https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil)). South-View remains a vital site of annual civic remembrance for these tragic events.
